abunai.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's enormous shrine bell has come loose from its beam and is swinging lower with every gust, grazing the heads of the cats sunning themselves on the mossy steps below. Nobody's fixed it yet. Everyone who visits just learns to duck first and pray second — the whole shrine is quietly dangerous.
abunai.reading_mnemonic: As the bell swings past, an old priest at the shrine throws an arm out to stop a visitor from walking under it, hissing “<reading>ah-boo-nigh</reading>!” under his breath — the exact warning shape of 「<reading>あぶない</reading>」, said before anything actually falls.

achira.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane never turns to point at the shrine gate. She just tips her chin toward <vocabulary>over there (polite)</vocabulary> and lets the cats show the way.

agaru.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker's runaway balloon slips its string and drifts higher than the vending machine at the summit, then higher than the whole ridge — it doesn't stop until it's the very mark of <kanji>up</kanji> itself, floating above everything below it: to go up, rise.
agaru.reading_mnemonic: On that same trail, a hiker named Agatha grabs the balloon's string by mistake and is yanked skyward, yelling 「<reading>あがる</reading>」 as she rises past the summit — the sound of her cry, <reading>ah-ga-roo</reading>, is exactly how you say to go up, rise.

ageru-raise.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a kid raises his hand so high above his desk it nearly brushes the ceiling, then keeps going — hoisting his chair, his bag, even the wastebasket until everything in the room sits <kanji>above</kanji> where it started: to raise.
ageru-raise.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway, the same kid hoists the trophy case higher, grunting 「<reading>あげる</reading>」 with each heave, the sound landing right on <reading>ah-geh-roo</reading> — pure effort to raise something up.

ageru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she fills a basket with rice cakes and works her way down the mossy steps, pressing one into the hands of every visitor she passes — the family by the bell, the tourists taking photos, even the cats sprawled on the stones. She doesn't keep a single cake back for herself. By the bottom step the basket is empty and everyone else's hands are full.
ageru.reading_mnemonic: あげる is written exactly as it sounds — read the basket-emptying rhythm as <reading>あげる</reading>, matching the bounce of a <reading>kangaroo</reading> hopping down the steps handing things out.
ageru.description: This verb covers giving outward — you or your group giving to someone else. It carries a faint sense of conferring a favor, which can sound presumptuous aimed at someone clearly above you; a more humble word is expected in that direction.

aida.meaning_mnemonic: You already know the gate with its two doors thrown open, the sun hanging low and trapped in the gap between them. Now a duck waddles up to that same gate and refuses to pass — it just paces back and forth in the strip of light, unwilling to leave the <kanji>interval / between</kanji> the two doors. That pacing, caught-in-the-middle strip of light is the word: an interval, the between.
aida.reading_mnemonic: 間 already gives you the reading directly — the same one from the kanji's own gate-and-sun story, so 「<reading>あいだ</reading>」 is simply what you say.

aka-color.meaning_mnemonic: Back on the mountain trail, the crack in the ground still glows from the fire beneath the earth. Tonight that glow claws its way up past the trail, past the vending machine, until the whole hillside catches and everything you can see burns the same fierce <kanji>red</kanji>.
aka-color.reading_mnemonic: During the school sports field bake sale, someone leaves a tray of tomatoes baking in direct sun until the skins split and bleed everywhere. A teacher grabs one, hisses <reading>ah, car</reading> as the juice scalds her fingers, and drops it — which is exactly how you say <reading>あか</reading>, the color spreading across the whole tray.

akachan.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, by the vending machine, a hiker's toddler drops her snack and wails so hard her whole face floods the same deep, angry <kanji>red</kanji> as the ground splitting open on that hillside, glowing from the fire underneath. Nothing quiets a face that red. That furious red-faced bundle is a baby.
akachan.reading_mnemonic: The reading is exactly the pieces you already know: 赤 gives you the あか, and the childish ちゃん suffix tacks straight on after it, spelling out <reading>あかちゃん</reading>.

akai.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, that same fire-lit earth keeps cracking uphill until it reaches the vending machine improbably parked at the summit. The heat gets to the cans inside, and they burst open, spilling <kanji>red</kanji> soda down the rocks like slow lava.
akai.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer dares a coworker to eat a whole tube of wasabi filling in one bite. Halfway through, the coworker's face goes rigid and they choke out <reading>ah, kai</reading>, fanning their tongue at the till — exactly the sound of <reading>あかい</reading>, the word for red.

akarui.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi flips every switch behind the register at once, and the whole konbini goes nuclear — onigiri wrappers glowing white, the beeping till suddenly readable from across the parking lot. A moth outside faints on the spot. That's the only word for it: <kanji>bright</kanji>, blindingly, hopelessly bright.
akarui.reading_mnemonic: Koichi shields his eyes and gasps <reading>"ah, car, ooh-ee!"</reading> — the nonsense his blinded brain makes of <reading>あかるい</reading> — as the fluorescents blaze so hard they're visible from the street outside.

akeru.meaning_mnemonic: The delivery man arrives before sunrise and hauls up the konbini's rusted shutter by hand because the motor's dead again. His shoulder aches by the third pull, but the gap widens, fluorescent light spilling onto the sidewalk, onigiri shelf glowing behind the glass. He just keeps pulling until there's enough gap to walk through.
akeru.reading_mnemonic: Every morning the same delivery man hauls up Koichi's shutter by hand, and every morning his shoulder <reading>aches</reading> a little more by the third pull. He mutters the same sound through gritted teeth as the gap finally widens enough to walk through — <reading>あける</reading> — the ache and the opening worn into the same groove.

aki.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a single red leaf drifts in through the automatic door and lands square on the sensor, so the door just hangs there half-open, beeping, while more leaves blow in and pile up around the onigiri shelf until the whole floor is drifted orange. That first stubborn leaf jamming the door is autumn arriving.
aki.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the automatic door won't budge until someone finds <reading>a key</reading> taped under the onigiri shelf — it turns out to be the spare for the storeroom, left there every year once the leaves start piling up. Konbini regulars now call that leaf season <reading>あき</reading>, after the key.

amai.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a delivery van dumps a whole pallet of sugar sacks onto the onigiri shelf. One bag splits open and buries the till in white dust. The cashier can't help scooping a fingerful straight off the counter — it's pure, blinding sugar, nothing else. That's what sweet tastes like.
amai.reading_mnemonic: A woman at Koichi's konbini bites into what she assumes is a plain rice cracker and gasps <reading>ah my</reading>, eyes watering — it's actually a sugar candy in disguise. Her gasp is exactly the sound of <reading>あまい</reading>, sweet.

amari.meaning_mnemonic: Every closing shift at Koichi's konbini, the new clerk restocks the onigiri shelf and counts what's left before locking the till. Delivery day or not, the shelf never fills back up — there's just never much sitting there, and she's stopped expecting otherwise.
amari.reading_mnemonic: あまり is pure kana, written and read exactly as <reading>あまり</reading> with nothing to derive.
amari.description: あまり typically appears with a negative verb or adjective to mean not much or not very; expect it paired with a negative predicate rather than standing alone as a quantity word.

ame-v.meaning_mnemonic: You're back at the window, watching the same drops slide down the glass, one after another inside their frame. Step outside now and those drops aren't caught behind glass anymore — they're landing straight on your shoulders. What's soaking you has exactly one name: <kanji>rain</kanji>.
ame-v.reading_mnemonic: This word keeps 雨's own taught reading exactly as taught, so it reads <reading>あめ</reading> — the same sound you already tied to the drops sliding down the window frame.

anata.meaning_mnemonic: Point your finger straight at one otter in a crowd and there's no doubt left: the otter you're pointing at is <vocabulary>you</vocabulary>.
anata.description: Rarely used to address someone directly; a name or title is normally used instead.

ane.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, your <kanji>older sister</kanji> has already claimed the flattest washing stone before you're even awake, scrubbing yesterday's clothes while lecturing you for not helping. She never once asks if you mind. That unasked-for seniority, exercised at six in the morning by the water, is what (my) older sister names.
ane.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a horse comes down to drink beside her washing stone and lets out a flat <reading>ah, neigh</reading> right in her ear — which is exactly how <reading>あね</reading> sounds, and exactly why she never washes clothes there again.
ane.description: A plain, informal word for your own older sister when talking about her to someone else — not used to address her directly or to speak politely about someone else's older sister.

ani.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last good onigiri is one shelf away. Your <kanji>older brother</kanji> doesn't ask — he plants a hand on your shoulder, uses you as a step stool, and takes it while you're still off balance. That casual, lifelong right to shove you aside without apologizing is what (my) older brother names.
ani.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, he shoves past you and you catch the shelf edge with your knee. <reading>Ah, knee</reading>, you groan, doubled over by the onigiri — which is exactly how <reading>あに</reading> sounds, and exactly who just walked off without noticing.
ani.description: A plain, informal word for your own older brother when talking about him to someone else — never used to address him directly, and not the word used to speak politely about someone else's older brother (that is oniisan).

anna.meaning_mnemonic: Anna and you spot a scarecrow in a top hat on the far bank of the river, and you both call it <vocabulary>that kind of (far)</vocabulary> nonsense.

ano.meaning_mnemonic: You stand on the mountain trail and ignore everything close by. Your arm swings straight past every near rock and points at <vocabulary>that vending machine over there</vocabulary>.

ao-color.meaning_mnemonic: The sprout is still glowing over the moon, caught in that in-between shade of <kanji>blue and green</kanji>. Tonight the moonlight pulls harder than the leaves do, draining the warmth out of it until only the cool half survives — a flat, quiet, midnight blue.
ao-color.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the drinks fridge malfunctions overnight and frosts over every bottle in the back row until the glass turns an icy, unnatural shade. Koichi opens the door at dawn, sees it, and just says <reading>ow</reading> as the cold hits his hand — the sound behind <reading>あお</reading>, the word for that frozen blue.

aoi.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, that sprout's glow from over the moon drifts downstream every evening, staining the whole current the same impossible shade until the water looks like liquid moonlight. Fishermen call it the <kanji>blue</kanji> hour, and standing knee-deep in it, they're right — it's blue.
aoi.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker's boot punches straight through a rotten plank bridge over the stream. Icy water floods clear to the knee, and the shock rips out a strangled <reading>ow, eee</reading> that echoes off the rocks — exactly the sound of <reading>あおい</reading>, the word for blue.

arau.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a raccoon drags in a bicycle caked in mud, dunks it under the current, and scrubs the frame with a fistful of gravel until every speck lifts off and the metal shines wet in the sun. Rinse, scrub, repeat — that's <kanji>washing</kanji>.
arau.reading_mnemonic: The raccoon holds the dripping bike over its head and announces <reading>a raw</reading> deal, since scrubbing stripped the paint clean off. Down at the riverbank they just call the whole scene <reading>あらう</reading> now.

are.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the very top of the mountain trail is still just a dot on the ridge, too distant to name — you can only point and call it <vocabulary>that over there</vocabulary>.
are.description: Marks something distant from both you and the listener, not just from you — or a shared thing you both already know about, even out of sight.

arigatou.meaning_mnemonic: A stray cat drags a whole rice ball off Koichi's shelf and bolts up the mountain trail, and Koichi just laughs and lets it go. At the top, by the lone vending machine, the cat drops half the rice ball at the feet of a hiker who'd fed it yesterday — the closest a cat gets to saying thank you.
arigatou.reading_mnemonic: Hear <reading>ありがとう</reading> as the hiker muttering "<reading>ah-ri-gah-toh</reading>" under his breath at the cat's odd little gift, half touched, half confused.
arigatou.description: This is the plain, casual form — fine with friends, family, or a cat, but too casual for a shopkeeper, a boss, or anyone you'd address politely; those situations call for a longer, more formal version of the same word.

aru.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini has one onigiri that has sat on the same shelf for three years. It hasn't rolled off, spoiled, or been restocked — it is simply, stubbornly present, the way a rock or a receipt or a vending machine is present. Nothing with legs, nothing that breathes, just an object taking up space. That plain, unmoving presence is to exist.
aru.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, containing 「<reading>ある</reading>」.

aruku.meaning_mnemonic: Every dawn, an old monk climbs Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps at the exact same unhurried pace, one bell-toll per step, never rushing even when the temple cats race past him. Visitors say they could set their watches by him. That plodding, deliberate, one-foot-after-the-other pace up the steps is exactly what this word means: to <kanji>walk</kanji>.
aruku.reading_mnemonic: The tourists nickname the shrine monk 'the <reading>rook</reading>,' since like a chess rook he only ever creeps one square forward. Every morning the cats chant his rhythm up the mossy stairs: <reading>あるく</reading>, あるく, あるく, one slow step at a time.

asa.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>morning</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>morning</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
asa.reading_mnemonic: Koichi throws open the konbini shutters at first light and grumbles <reading>「あさ」, which sounds like 'ah, sir'</reading>, and that daily grumble is how <vocabulary>morning</vocabulary> greets him.

asagohan.meaning_mnemonic: A rooster oversleeps at Grandma Kane's shrine and wakes to the sun already glaring off the enormous bell. He bolts down the mossy steps two at a time, scattering cats, because the priest sets out the <kanji>meal</kanji> — rice, grilled fish, and miso — the instant <kanji>morning</kanji> arrives. Whoever reaches that tray first gets breakfast.
asagohan.reading_mnemonic: Every dawn a groggy monk stumbles toward the shrine gate mumbling <reading>ah, sir, go, Han</reading> at the boy stacking bowls, before Han even asks what he wants: <reading>あさごはん</reading>, already getting cold on the step.

asatte.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>day</kanji> that falls <kanji>behind</kanji> the very next one is <vocabulary>the day after tomorrow</vocabulary>.
asatte.reading_mnemonic: Koichi <reading>sautés</reading> the last onigiri filling, but the next batch won't land until <reading>あさって</reading>, when <vocabulary>the day after tomorrow</vocabulary> restocks the shelf.

ashi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, that mouth-topped pair of stopped legs is moving again, planted step after step all the way to the vending machine at the top, still barking orders down at itself with every stride. Whatever plants itself like that and carries you onward — that's your <kanji>foot</kanji>, your leg.
ashi-v.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman wades in and yelps <reading>ahh, sheesh</reading> as the icy water bites at his shins, hopping rock to rock on legs that won't go numb. By the fifth hop the whole riverbank knows the word for legs is <reading>あし</reading>.

ashita.meaning_mnemonic: The next <kanji>day</kanji> that hasn't arrived yet is always the one everyone calls <vocabulary>tomorrow</vocabulary>.
ashita.reading_mnemonic: Koichi drapes <reading>a sheet</reading> over the pastry case and promises the shelves refill only <reading>あした</reading>, when <vocabulary>tomorrow</vocabulary> finally comes.

asobu.meaning_mnemonic: At school, the recess bell rings and the whole sports field erupts — kids chasing a rolling ball, someone doing cartwheels into the sandpit, a stray dog that snuck through the gate joining every game at once. Nobody keeps score. Nobody stops. That's playing.
asobu.reading_mnemonic: A kid trips mid-cartwheel, lands face-first in the sandpit, and lets out <reading>a sob</reading> — then laughs and does it again on purpose. The whole field starts calling that stunt <reading>あそぶ</reading> for the rest of recess.

asoko.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, your guide points past every switchback you can see to a speck lost in the mist — too far from either of you to be anything but <vocabulary>over there</vocabulary>.

atama.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway of Sei's school, gym class lets out and everyone crowds through one narrow doorway at once - shoulders, bags, elbows, all jammed together. Except one part always squeezes through first, out ahead of everything else, cutting a path for the rest of the body to follow: the head.
atama.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine keeps one badly behaved llama tied up by the great bell, and it despises every visitor who gets too close, so it swings and clonks them square in the skull. The caretaker just sighs and warns newcomers the same way each time: mind <reading>a llama</reading>, or it'll crack your <reading>あたま</reading>.

atarashii-adj.meaning_mnemonic: That same person is still planted in the showroom, grinning beside their finished build, when a friend walks in and the surface throws back a mirror-perfect double of them both — two identical grinners, side by side. Nothing scuffs a mirror that clean; the whole showroom still smells of <kanji>new</kanji>.
atarashii-adj.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a delivery van drops off one unmarked box at dawn. The clerk tears it open and yelps <reading>a tortoise, eh</reading>, startled to find a factory-fresh tortoise still shrink-wrapped inside — and that startled yelp is exactly <reading>あたらしい</reading>, the word for new.

atatakai.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine the cats abandon the mossy steps every afternoon and pile onto the sun-warmed stone beside the bell instead, purring in a heap until the stone itself seems to purr back. That gentle, all-over warmth, never scalding, just comfortable, is the meaning.
atatakai.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane waves the cats off the sun-warmed stone with a cheerful farewell before heading off to buy incense, and the whole phrase comes out as one running line. Hear it as <reading>あたたかい</reading>: <reading>ah, ta-ta, kai</reading>, warm as the stone she leaves behind her.

atsui-hot.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the lone vending machine has been baking in direct sun since morning. You press a palm flat against its metal side and yank it back instantly, fingers stinging. The whole trail feels like an oven today, and that vending machine is the hottest spot on it.
atsui-hot.reading_mnemonic: You grab the vending machine's coin slot too fast and yelp <reading>“Ah, too!”</reading>, shaking out your scorched fingers. That yelp is basically <reading>あつい</reading> — the sound your mouth makes right before you remember mountain metal in the sun burns exactly like this.

atsui-obj.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer grabs a can of oden broth straight off the warmer without checking first, yelps, and juggles it hand to hand like it's on fire, blowing on her fingers. That single reflex, grab-and-drop, is the whole word: hot, the kind you find out about by touching it.
atsui-obj.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's counter, a woman named Sue reaches for the can straight off the warmer and yelps, shaking her stinging hand and hissing the same sound twice. Hear that yelp as <reading>あつい</reading>: <reading>at Sue, ee</reading>, the exact noise she makes every single time she forgets to check first.

au.meaning_mnemonic: Two people come around the same bend of the riverbank from opposite directions, both staring at the water instead of the path, and walk straight into each other. They stumble apart, startled, and there's nothing left to do but say hello. That collision, two people suddenly face to face, is what it means to <kanji>meet</kanji>.
au.reading_mnemonic: They collide so hard both yelp <reading>ow</reading> at once, then just stand there rubbing their foreheads and laughing. That startled little run-in by the river is <reading>あう</reading> — to meet.

ban-order.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, runners line up wearing paper bibs pinned on backwards, and the coach marches the row jabbing each one straight — first, second, third — until the whole line stands in strict <kanji>number</kanji> / order. Nobody has run a single step yet; the entire scene is just about getting that order right.
ban-order.reading_mnemonic: 番 takes the reading you already learned for the kanji and uses it unchanged as the word: <reading>ばん</reading>.

ban.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane rings the shrine's one enormous bell only once, right as <vocabulary>evening</vocabulary> settles over the mossy steps.

bangohan.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank at <kanji>nightfall</kanji>, a tanuki has learned exactly when the cooking fire gets left untended, and it drags the whole simmering pot toward the water to wash its paws in what's left. The family gives up chasing it along the bank and just starts cooking a second <kanji>meal</kanji>, because dinner has to happen eventually, tanuki or not.
bangohan.reading_mnemonic: The father slams the door at dusk shouting <reading>bang, go, Han</reading> at the dog racing the tanuki to the pot, and by the time the door stops rattling everyone's already sitting down to <reading>ばんごはん</reading>, tanuki-free at last.

bangou.meaning_mnemonic: At the summit of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine refuses every coin unless you first announce which slot you want, so hikers gasping from the climb start shouting out a <kanji>number</kanji> before they can get their can of coffee — the machine only understands you by your <kanji>number</kanji>.
bangou.reading_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, hikers bang on the summit vending machine's glass, yelling <reading>bang, GO!</reading> at the slot they want, and the machine finally clatters out a can once it hears 「<reading>ばんごう</reading>」 shouted correctly.

basho.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane pins a paper map to the shrine gate and stabs one finger at a single dot, refusing to move it no matter how the wind flaps the paper. Everyone who asks directions gets sent to that exact dot — the <kanji>place</kanji>, and only that <kanji>place</kanji>.
basho.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 場 read ば, plus 所 read しょ, gives <reading>ばしょ</reading>.

basu.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, something huge screeches to a stop right outside the sliding doors, tires shrieking against the curb loud enough to rattle the onigiri shelf. The doors hiss open, exhaust rolls in over the till, and a wall of tired passengers shuffles out into the fluorescent light — this rattling monster is the bus, and it stops here every hour on the hour.
basu.reading_mnemonic: バス is written exactly as it sounds, so just read it as <reading>バス</reading> — the same sound as the English word <reading>bus</reading>.

beddo.meaning_mnemonic: A monk lugs a stack of futons up the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, planning to store them by the enormous bell overnight. Before he finishes stacking, half the resident cats have already curled into the pile and refuse to move. He gives up, tucks a blanket round the edges, and leaves them the shrine's new bed.
beddo.reading_mnemonic: This word is a straight loanword from the English word for bed, written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>ベッド</reading>.

benkyou-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Sei stays in the echoing hallway of her school long after the sports field empties, hunched under a flickering light, filling page after page of a workbook with stubborn <kanji>exertion</kanji> while the caretaker locks each classroom around her. She isn't waiting for a practice or a friend to finish up — she's just studying, alone, the <kanji>strong</kanji> grip on her pencil unmoving until every problem on the page is solved.
benkyou-suru.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 勉 as べん plus 強 as きょう plus す plus る gives you <reading>べんきょうする</reading>.

benkyou.meaning_mnemonic: A boy chains his own ankle to his desk every night in the school hallway, papers piling knee-deep, refusing through sheer <kanji>exertion</kanji> to unlock the cuff until dawn. A pigeon roosts on his head, its <kanji>strong</kanji> claws locked in his hair, and won't leave either, staring at the pages until they stop turning. Neither of them moves until every problem is solved — that grinding, chained-in effort is study.
benkyou.reading_mnemonic: Every night before he chains himself down, the boy mutters the same quiet oath: '<reading>Ben, cue, oh</reading>, no distractions.' Said fast, it slides into <reading>べんきょう</reading> — the sound of him swearing himself back to the desk.

benri.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi hires a new clerk named Ben who reorganizes the whole konbini overnight. Every shelf now holds exactly what the last customer needed — umbrellas by the door on rainy days, batteries by the toy aisle, a charger built into the counter itself. Nobody has ever had to ask Ben for anything twice. That's pure <kanji>convenience</kanji> — that's what convenient means.
benri.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 便 as べん plus 利 as り gives you 「<reading>べんり</reading>」.

bentou.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the improbable summit vending machine, a hiker unzips her pack instead of buying anything. Inside sits a perfectly packed rectangular box — rice, a pickled plum, a segment of grilled fish, each one <kanji>hit</kanji>ting its slot dead center like a thrown dart — eaten cold on a rock at the top. That neat travel box is a boxed lunch.
bentou.reading_mnemonic: 弁（べん）＋当（とう）combine directly into <reading>べんとう</reading>.

betsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, two cats that look identical fight nonstop, so she builds a low wall down the middle of the mossy steps just to keep them apart — one bowl on each side, one nap spot on each side, one bell on each side. Everything about their lives gets divided into its own separate portion, one and then another entirely. That's the word.
betsu.reading_mnemonic: 別 keeps the reading you already learned for the kanji itself, carried straight through: <reading>べつ</reading>.

biiru.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail's summit reward is one vending machine, impossibly humming after two hours of switchbacks. You feed it coins with shaking hands, and instead of water it drops a cold gold can that hisses and foams straight over your boots: beer, at the top of the mountain, before you've even sat down.
biiru.reading_mnemonic: ビール is written just as it's read, kana straight through — <reading>ビール</reading> — nothing to sound out beyond what's already on the can.

bijutsu.meaning_mnemonic: A bee lands on Grandma Kane's mossy shrine wall, dips its stinger in a bowl of spilled ink, and starts slashing perfect brushstrokes across the stone — one clean stroke, then another, then a whole mountain scene. The priest stops sweeping mid-swing and just stares at the bee's art.
bijutsu.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, that same bee dips its stinger in the mud and drags it across a flat rock, calling its stripes <reading>bee-jutsu</reading> — say it fast and you've got <reading>びじゅつ</reading>, the reading for art.

bikkuri-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You're washing dishes at the riverbank when a heron that's been standing motionless for an hour suddenly explodes upward in a panic of wings and shrieks, sending dishes clattering into the water. That full-body jolt — the one where your whole body reacts before your brain has caught up — is being surprised.
bikkuri-suru.reading_mnemonic: びっくりする is written exactly as it sounds — <reading>びっくりする</reading> — no kanji to decode, just the kana as your eyes see them.

boku.meaning_mnemonic: In the thicket, the one figure still visible always answers as <kanji>me</kanji>, and when a man says it, that answer is exactly <vocabulary>I (male)</vocabulary>.
boku.description: Used mainly by men and boys speaking casually or semi-formally; women rarely use it for themselves.

booru-pen.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini till, a customer clicks a slim plastic stick against the counter, and a tiny steel ball rolls out of the tip, dragging a thin trail of blue ink across the receipt paper. Koichi doesn't blink — that rolling ball is just how a ballpoint pen writes.
booru-pen.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ボールペン</reading> is pure loanword kana, written exactly as it's read, straight from the English "ball pen," so there's nothing to decode.

boushi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that same swaddled <kanji>child</kanji> from before, arms flung out, except Grandma Kane keeps wrapping cloth around its head for warmth, spiral after spiral, until the arms vanish under the layers and only a round knit dome pokes out the top — a hat, sitting where a baby used to be.
boushi.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 帽 as ぼう plus 子 as し gives you <reading>ぼうし</reading>.

bungaku.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, someone has stacked mildewed paperbacks under the <kanji>study</kanji> canopy where the swaddled child usually sits, and the shrine cats have nested in cracked spines instead of scribbled diagrams. The child ignores the diagrams entirely, transfixed by a water-stained page of verse he can't stop rereading. When study bends toward stories instead of formulas, you get literature.
bungaku.reading_mnemonic: You already know both halves from those kanji: 文 is ぶん and 学 is がく, so they simply join as <reading>ぶんがく</reading>.

byou.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini till beeps once for every item scanned, and that single beep marks exactly one <vocabulary>second</vocabulary>.

byouin.meaning_mnemonic: A rowboat flips at the riverbank, and instead of a rescue crew, a whole hospital floats out to meet it — a full-blown <kanji>institution</kanji> for anyone <kanji>ill</kanji> enough to need it, beds lashed to buoys, an IV drip swinging from a fishing rod, a nurse checking pulses waist-deep in the current. The patient is hauled onto the nearest buoy, wrapped in a blanket, declared stable before the clipboard stops dripping.
byouin.reading_mnemonic: 病（びょう）＋院（いん）combine directly into <reading>びょういん</reading>.

byouki.meaning_mnemonic: Someone <kanji>ill</kanji> collapses on the school sports field, forehead burning, and the same swirling wisp you've seen rise off a hot bowl of rice now curls up off their skin instead — their <kanji>spirit</kanji> visibly leaking out into the air with every ragged breath. The nurse takes one look at that steam and doesn't even need to ask what's wrong: illness.
byouki.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 病 read びょう, plus 気 read き, gives <reading>びょうき</reading>.

chairo.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the <kanji>tea</kanji> urn boils over during the morning rush, sheeting hot tea across the floor, up the onigiri shelf, and onto the ceiling tiles. By closing time everything in the shop — walls, floor, Koichi's socks — has dried into the exact same <kanji>color</kanji>: brown.
chairo.reading_mnemonic: Its kanji give it away directly: 茶（ちゃ）＋色（いろ）makes 「<reading>ちゃいろ</reading>」.

chawan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats never come for the incense — they come for what's set beside it: steam curling up from a cup of <kanji>tea</kanji> next to a chipped ceramic bowl brimming with warm rice, left out every evening as an offering. By the time the bell stops ringing, every cat in the yard is circling that single rice bowl.
chawan.reading_mnemonic: The head priest only allows one bowl of rice per cat, so he stands by the bell shouting <reading>ちゃわん</reading> — which lands in your ear as <reading>Cha, one!</reading> — one cry per cat, one bowl each, no seconds no matter how loudly they beg.

chichi.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini you're bragging to the clerk about how your <kanji>father</kanji> rewired the flickering sign himself. But every time the word for father leaves your mouth it comes out clipped and small, a fast double note like a chick cheeping under the counter, because that's the plain, low-key way you refer to your own <kanji>father</kanji>, never anyone else's.
chichi.reading_mnemonic: A chick has gotten loose behind Koichi's register and won't stop cheeping two identical notes at the customers. The sound lands exactly like <reading>ちち</reading>, the same clipped double <reading>chee-chee</reading> twice in a row, and it's the one word stuck to that particular chirp from now on.
chichi.description: 父 (chichi) is the plain, humble word for your own father, used only when talking about him to people outside the family — never for someone else's father, and not usually what you'd call him to his face. お父さん (otousan) is the polite counterpart: what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father.

chiisai.meaning_mnemonic: That same delicate hook with its two flanking dots keeps shrinking with every review, the dots drawing in closer until the whole shape looks like it might blow away in a light breeze. Nothing about it ever grows back — it stays exactly <kanji>small</kanji>.
chiisai.reading_mnemonic: 小 already sounds ちい in words like this one, and さ＋い are just the ordinary adjective ending, so 小さい reads straight through as <reading>ちいさい</reading>.

chika.meaning_mnemonic: That dangling tail on the shelf mark doesn't stop at the floor — it keeps boring straight <kanji>down, below</kanji> the konbini's tile until it opens into a second, windowless shop stocked entirely in the dark. Everything down there, beneath ordinary <kanji>ground</kanji>, is underground — the basement level Koichi never mentions to customers.
chika.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 地 read ち, plus 下 read か, gives <reading>ちか</reading>.

chikai.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the bleachers were built so close to the hallway wall that runners can high-five the kids at their lockers without leaving the track. No gap, no jog required — just reach across mid-stride. That's how it feels when something sits within arm's reach, <kanji>near</kanji> enough that you never have to move your feet.
chikai.reading_mnemonic: A student presses her cheek to the hallway window, eye to eye with the bleachers just beyond the glass — <reading>cheek, eye</reading> close, nothing between them but the pane. That's the sound of <reading>ちかい</reading>, near enough to fog the glass.

chikaku.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker climbs the mountain trail for hours, certain the summit is impossibly far, only to trip over the vending machine at the top and realize it's the same one he passed at the trailhead. He'd walked in a circle the whole time. Whatever he'd been trudging toward was <kanji>nearby</kanji> the entire climb — he just never looked over his shoulder.
chikaku.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a <reading>cheeky cook</reading> has set up a stall serving free noodles to anyone who insists the summit is <reading>ちかく</reading> — nearby — even though they've clearly been climbing for hours. He never corrects them; free noodles for the delusional.

chikara-v.meaning_mnemonic: That flexed-arm stroke you already know as <kanji>power</kanji> doesn't stay still — picture it arm-wrestling every kid at Sei's school, elbow slammed onto the sports field bench, muscle bulging. It flattens every challenger the same way every time: raw <kanji>strength</kanji>, just proving itself in a bigger arena.
chikara-v.reading_mnemonic: 力 keeps the exact reading you already learned for it, so the word for power and strength is simply <reading>ちから</reading> — no new sound to memorize.

chikatetsu.meaning_mnemonic: Follow that dangling tail staked into the <kanji>ground</kanji> that always points <kanji>below</kanji> the shelf, down past the floor, down past the foundations, until you're standing on a platform lit by flickering tubes with a train roaring in out of the dark — the subway is just where below finally bottoms out.
chikatetsu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 地 read ち, plus 下 read か, plus 鉄 read てつ, gives <reading>ちかてつ</reading>.

chiri.meaning_mnemonic: An old man stands at the very top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, turning slowly to point out every river, city, and coastline visible from up there. He isn't just admiring the view — he's naming what each valley is called and, with cold <kanji>reason</kanji>, why it sits on that stretch of <kanji>ground</kanji>. That's geography.
chiri.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 地 read ち, plus 理 read り, gives <reading>ちり</reading>.

chizu.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker stalls at an unmarked fork, drops to one knee on the bare <kanji>earth</kanji>, digs a single folded sheet out of her pack, and traces the dotted line with her finger all the way to the vending machine waiting improbably at the summit. That creased sheet in her hands is the <kanji>map</kanji> that gets her there.
chizu.reading_mnemonic: At the fork she unfolds it and mutters '<reading>cheese zoo</reading>' under her breath — her own private trick for the sound — tracing the line with one finger: '<reading>ちず</reading>, cheese zoo, don't you dare blow away now.'

chizuchou.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat drags a folded sheet bigger than the mossy steps and spreads it flat across the <kanji>ground</kanji> in front of the bell. Every country, every coastline is drawn on it in ink, an enormous <kanji>diagram</kanji> of the whole world, and the cat just sits in the middle purring at it all laid out under one bell — an atlas.
chizuchou.reading_mnemonic: A tourist at the riverbank unfolds the huge sheet and squints, muttering "cheese... chew..." as she tries to fold it back along the crease. Passersby hear only <reading>ちずちょう</reading>, the <reading>cheese-chew</reading> woman fighting her map by the water.

chooku.meaning_mnemonic: A plump white hen waddles onto the classroom windowsill and lays one perfectly cylindrical, rock-hard white egg on the chalk tray. The teacher shrugs, picks it up, and starts writing the day's kanji with it — the henhouse egg works exactly like chalk once it dries stiff and white.
chooku.reading_mnemonic: チョーク is written just the way it sounds, plain katakana carrying the borrowed word straight across: <reading>チョーク</reading>.

chotto.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer asks to sample every rice ball on the shelf before buying one, but takes only the tiniest sliver off the corner of each — never a real bite, just a taste. The clerk restocks behind him without noticing anything's missing. That's the whole trick of asking for just a little: barely there, gone before you'd call it a bite.
chotto.reading_mnemonic: This word is spelled in kana exactly as it's read, with no kanji to decode: <reading>ちょっと</reading>.

dai-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby crawls into the school's echoing gym and finds it full of vending machines, washing machines, and one ancient arcade cabinet lined up like toys, each sitting on a squat stone <kanji>pedestal</kanji>. He shoves each one an inch across the floor with one finger, giggling, and by the time he's bored he's pushed every single machine in the building at least once.
dai-counter.reading_mnemonic: 台 passes through the reading you already learned for this kanji, with nothing added or swapped: <reading>だい</reading>.

daidokoro.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini has one door marked staff-only, and behind it he's wedged a stove and a cutting board on two beer crates like a makeshift <kanji>pedestal</kanji>. He fries eggs there at three in the morning, in the one <kanji>place</kanji> in the store everyone knows to find him — his whole kitchen, hidden in plain sight.
daidokoro.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from its kanji: 台 read だい plus 所 read どころ give <reading>だいどころ</reading>.

daigaku.meaning_mnemonic: The same wide-armed stretcher who's always bragging how <kanji>big</kanji> his catch was plants himself over the swaddled <kanji>study</kanji> child's roof of lesson notes and stretches even wider, insisting the canopy is huge too. He keeps stretching until the notes swell into a whole campus of towering lecture halls — the biggest school there is: a university.
daigaku.reading_mnemonic: You already know 大 as だい and 学 as がく — put them back to back, no softening needed, and you get exactly <reading>だいがく</reading>.

daijoubu.meaning_mnemonic: A delivery moped skids on the mountain trail and crashes into the vending machine at the top. Before you can flinch, the <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>husband</kanji> from next door steps out, fisherman-armed, catches both moped and driver in one arm like nothing happened, and sets them upright without spilling a single dented can. Nothing here needed fixing. That's all right.
daijoubu.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 大 as だい plus 丈 as じょう plus 夫 as ぶ gives you 「<reading>だいじょうぶ</reading>」.

dakara.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the register has a broken speaker. Instead of a plain beep, it stutters out a garbled little excuse every time someone tries to leave without paying, as if explaining itself before anyone even asks. Koichi says it always gives the reason first, then the result. That's exactly this word's job: therefore, so, here's why.
dakara.reading_mnemonic: だから is written exactly the way it sounds, so once you can read だ and から on their own, reading <reading>だから</reading> together is nothing new.
dakara.description: だから often opens a sentence on its own, almost like a blunt so? in English — fine between friends explaining themselves, but it can land as curt or impatient in a formal reply, where から attached to a full clause is the safer choice.

dandan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat climbs onto the mossy steps. Then another. Then another, each pause exactly the length of a slow drumbeat: dan... dan... dan... By the time the enormous bell finally rings, forty cats blanket the steps, and it happened so gradually that nobody ever saw the moment it became too many.
dandan.reading_mnemonic: 「<reading>だんだん</reading>」 is pure kana with no kanji hiding underneath, so you read it exactly as it's spelled, every single time.

dare.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>who</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>who</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
dare.reading_mnemonic: The old bird tilts its head at the stranger and croaks <reading>だれ</reading>, all but <reading>daring</reading> you to say <vocabulary>who</vocabulary> just walked in.

dasu.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the teacher stacks a mountain of ungraded homework by the door until the pile itself looks ready to <kanji>exit / leave</kanji> on its own. Rather than wait for that, she shoves the whole stack out into the hallway and drops a permission slip in the mailbox besides — anything that needs to go, she takes out and sends. That's the meaning: to take out, to send.
dasu.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the fastest kid at school, <reading>dashes</reading> for the door the instant the bell rings, worksheets flying out of his open bag behind him. Teachers have started calling it his name for the move: <reading>だす</reading> — always mid-dash, always flinging something out as he goes.

deguchi.meaning_mnemonic: Two mountains stacked one on top of the other are already more <kanji>exit</kanji> than anyone wants to climb, so the exhausted hiker at Koichi's konbini rest stop bolts for the nearest gaping <kanji>mouth</kanji> of a doorway instead of scaling a third summit. Two mountains too many plus a wide-open mouth: that's the exit.
deguchi.reading_mnemonic: 出 read で and 口 read ぐち combine exactly as taught, giving <reading>でぐち</reading> straight from the parts you already know.

dekiru.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a kid who's wiped out on the skateboard deck all week finally lands the trick clean in front of the whole class. The board goes still under their feet — quiet, no more falling, no more trying. It's not luck; they can do it now, and the trick itself is finished.
dekiru.reading_mnemonic: できる is pure kana — sound it out as <reading>できる</reading>, the crowd's murmur when the trick lands clean: <reading>deck-hero</reading>.
dekiru.description: This word also functions as the potential form of the verb 'to do,' so it can mean either 'able to do something specific' or simply 'possible' depending on context. The thing that's possible is marked differently than a normal direct object, which trips learners used to English's straightforward 'can.'

demo.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school there's one rule painted on the gym wall: everyone runs the lap. But the gym teacher stands at the start line every single morning with a raised hand and a face that says otherwise — some days he waves the slowest kid through, no lap required, no explanation given. The rule always holds, but there's always one however waiting at the start line.
demo.reading_mnemonic: でも is pure kana, so it's read exactly as spelled: <reading>でも</reading>, no hidden readings to work out, just say what you see.
demo.description: でも usually opens a sentence to mean but or however, but attached straight after a noun it switches jobs entirely and means even — even a cat, even me — with no contrast implied at all.

denki.meaning_mnemonic: That storm-bred bolt punches through the rain and drives into a lightbulb on the ceiling, filament screaming white. Beside it, the curl of <kanji>spirit</kanji> that always rises off a hot bowl of rice streams upward too, feeding the glow. <kanji>Electricity</kanji> plus that rising energy floods the room: electricity, light.
denki.reading_mnemonic: 気 already lends you Kiki's giggly き, and 電 gives you でん — line them up and you get <reading>でんき</reading>, electricity.

densha.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the overhead cart — that boxy frame with its axle drawn straight through, the <kanji>vehicle</kanji> shape you already know — gets struck by the same jagged bolt that cracks out of the rain-soaked sky, feeding it pure <kanji>electricity</kanji>. Sparks race down the axle and the whole cart screams off along the tracks, electrified into a train.
densha.reading_mnemonic: <reading>でんしゃ</reading> is just 電's でん plus 車's しゃ said back to back — the readings you already know, joined.

denwa-suru.meaning_mnemonic: The storm outside Koichi's konbini keeps cutting the lights, and every time the <kanji>electricity</kanji> flickers back on, the till phone is already ringing with some caller mid-sentence, still going, spinning story after story down the wire as if the connection had never dropped at all. Electricity carrying someone's endless <kanji>talk</kanji> straight into your ear — that's what it means to phone.
denwa-suru.reading_mnemonic: でんわする is just the readings you already know, stacked in order: 電 as でん, 話 as わ, plus する tacked on the end — read them straight through and you get <reading>でんわする</reading>.

denwa.meaning_mnemonic: The lightning that split the sky over your rain-streaked window doesn't fade at the glass — it dives down a wire and into a box on the desk. Out of the earpiece pours that same restless <kanji>talk</kanji>, tongue wagging nonstop, riding pure <kanji>electricity</kanji> into your ear. That's a telephone: talk carried on a bolt of electricity.
denwa.reading_mnemonic: 電 already gives you でん and 話 already gives you わ — stitch them together and you get <reading>でんわ</reading>, telephone.

denwabangou.meaning_mnemonic: The storm's <kanji>electricity</kanji> knocks the lights out at Koichi's konbini, and in the sudden dark the till clerk won't stop the <kanji>talk</kanji>, tongue wagging as he shouts whose <kanji>turn</kanji> it is and which <kanji>nickname</kanji> to dial into the dead payphone. Nobody asked, but now you have his phone number.
denwabangou.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 電 read でん, plus 話 read わ, plus 番 read ばん, plus 号 read ごう, gives <reading>でんわばんごう</reading>.

depaato.meaning_mnemonic: A tower shop devours entire departments whole — one floor is nothing but shoes, the next is only teapots, and a man in a necktie gets trapped between six escalators that all disagree about which way is up. Every level swallows a different specialty until the whole building is just department after department stacked to the ceiling: a department store.
depaato.reading_mnemonic: デパート is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>department</reading> and you've already said <reading>デパート</reading>, no decoding needed.

deru-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the bell rings and the hallway fills instantly, everyone funneling toward the same doorway like those two stacked mountains finally toppling outward under their own height. There's no lingering once the peaks give way — the whole crowd is already <kanji>exit / leave</kanji>, headed out.
deru-v.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stray kangaroo nicknamed <reading>Day Roo</reading> has wedged itself under the enormous bell, cats piled on its back. Grandma Kane rings the bell once. The kangaroo startles, hops clear of the mossy steps, and that's how you <reading>でる</reading> when you're stuck.

do-degree.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the microwave beeps and someone keeps sliding in the same lump of dough, cranking the dial past a new temperature mark and checking it once, twice, three times before it's ready. Each check is one pass at a certain heat, and stacking up those passes is exactly what times / degrees means.
do-degree.reading_mnemonic: 度 keeps the reading you already learned for the kanji itself, carried straight through: <reading>ど</reading>.

doa.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini only has one way in: an automatic slab that slides aside the instant someone steps close, breathing out a soft whoosh right where the shop meets the street. New hires hear that whoosh and just call it what it sounds like, unchanged from English — a door.
doa.reading_mnemonic: This word is a loanword straight from English, written in kana exactly the way it sounds — read <reading>ドア</reading> just like the English word door that it borrows.

dochira.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail forks below the summit, one path to the vending machine, the other into a ravine. The peeling sign nailed there only ever asks <vocabulary>which way</vocabulary>.

doko.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi circles his own konbini three times, demanding an answer from every empty shelf to the one question he keeps repeating: <vocabulary>where</vocabulary> is the till key.

donata.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the priest bows to each donor and asks, with great formality, <vocabulary>who (polite)</vocabulary> has left an offering today.
donata.description: The polite way to ask someone's identity — reserved for strangers, customers, or phone calls, not for close friends.

donna.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine only stocks unlabeled cans, so you have no idea <vocabulary>what kind of</vocabulary> drink you are about to buy.

dono.meaning_mnemonic: You freeze at the onigiri shelf in Koichi's konbini. Your finger hovers rack to rack, and you can't land on <vocabulary>which onigiri</vocabulary> you actually want.

dore.meaning_mnemonic: Every onigiri on Koichi's konbini shelf looks identical, so pointing at the whole row is the only way to ask <vocabulary>which one</vocabulary> you actually want.
dore.description: Assumes three or more options; English "which one" doesn't carry that count.

dou.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine on the mountain trail sells nothing but raw dough, and every hiker who buys one just stands there wondering <vocabulary>how</vocabulary> that is supposed to be lunch.

doubutsu.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school announces a surprise visit from the local shelter, and by lunchtime every hallway smells like fur and nervous energy. Rabbits loose in the gym, a goat near the vending machines, a parakeet shrieking over the PA — every one a <kanji>thing</kanji> that won't hold still, some fresh <kanji>move</kanji> setting off the next alarm. Whatever has fur, feathers, or four legs and doesn't belong indoors — that's animal today.
doubutsu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 動 read どう, plus 物 read ぶつ, gives 「<reading>どうぶつ</reading>」.

doumo.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till won't stop beeping — somehow he's rung up the same rice ball five separate times. Rather than work out how it happened, he just presses his hands together toward the register and mutters a loose, all-purpose noise of gratitude at the mess he's made, one sound doing double duty for both the mystery and the thanks.
doumo.reading_mnemonic: どうも is pure kana, read just as written — sound out <reading>どうも</reading> the way Koichi mutters it, a low <reading>dohh-moh</reading> rolled out under his breath at the register.
doumo.description: This word covers two unrelated jobs: a vague intensifier meaning "somehow" or "quite," and a casual, often incomplete way of saying thanks — like saying "thanks" without finishing "thank you very much." Used alone it's breezy and informal, not something you'd offer a boss or a stranger you owe a real apology to.

doushite.meaning_mnemonic: A restless ghost haunts Grandma Kane's shrine, moaning though, stay at every visitor without ever explaining itself, until the cats spend the whole night yowling <vocabulary>why / how come</vocabulary>.

doyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: The startled <kanji>weekday</kanji> pheasant finally settles down to dig in the <kanji>earth</kanji>. That digging <kanji>day</kanji> is <vocabulary>Saturday</vocabulary>.

e-picture.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing school hallway, someone taped up a drawing so bad the paper itself seems embarrassed to hold it. Every student who passes stops, tilts their head, and produces the exact same reaction — because what's supposed to be a horse has four legs, three ears, and no clear idea which end is which.
e-picture.reading_mnemonic: 絵 keeps the reading you already learned for the kanji itself, carried straight through: <reading>え</reading>.

ee.meaning_mnemonic: Near the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, one hiker collapses onto a rock and asks if the other wants to stop too. The other doesn't even break stride, just tosses back a lazy eh — yeah, obviously, why else would there be a vending machine all the way up here.
ee.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly as it sounds — the hiker's lazy <reading>eh</reading> stretched out on the trail gives you the reading <reading>ええ</reading>.
ee.description: This is a softer, more casual yeah than the standard yes — natural between friends or equals in relaxed conversation, but it can sound too casual toward a stranger, a boss, or a teacher, where the more formal option is safer.

eiga.meaning_mnemonic: You're stuck at a bus stop in the rain, and the drugstore across the street has a demo screen in its window that never turns off — passersby keep pausing mid-stride, faces lit blue, unable to look away from the flickering rectangle. The wet glass <kanji>reflects</kanji> each passerby as a moving <kanji>brush-stroke</kanji>. That instinctive freeze, everyone briefly captured by a moving picture, is a movie.
eiga.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 映 read えい, plus 画 read が, gives <reading>えいが</reading>.

eigakan.meaning_mnemonic: Every night, folding chairs fill Koichi's konbini parking lot — instant ramen cups, someone's dog draped over a cooler. A bedsheet clipped to the delivery truck catches the shutter light's <kanji>reflection</kanji>, resolving into a <kanji>picture</kanji> as Koichi's annexed lot becomes one sprawling <kanji>building</kanji> — a cinema built from nothing but a parking lot and a bedsheet.
eigakan.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from its kanji: 映 read えい, 画 read が, and 館 read かん combine to give <reading>えいがかん</reading>.

eigo.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a transfer student's mouth won't stop — one open mouth stacking speech on speech, then another mouth joining in, piling word after word into a whole <kanji>language</kanji>. But every syllable that tumbles out is rolled and foreign, all flat vowels and hard Rs the local kids can't place. That foreign stack of speech is English.
eigo.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 英 as えい plus 語 as ご gives you <reading>えいご</reading>.

eki.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning another <kanji>station</kanji> platform fills with hoofprints instead of footprints — the local horses treat the place like open pasture. Today one gallops so hard it clears the ticket gates and skids onto a departing train, mane flying. Staff gave up chasing them years ago.
eki.reading_mnemonic: 駅's own taught reading carries straight over unchanged, so <reading>えき</reading> is exactly what you already know it to be.

ekiin.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning the galloping <kanji>station</kanji> horse thunders onto the platform, and it isn't the conductor who deals with it — it's the whistle-blowing <kanji>employee</kanji> in uniform whose laminated badge swings on a lanyard as they chase it back off the tracks before the first train arrives. Radio crackling, cap crooked, unbothered by any of this: that worn-out but unshaken figure is your station staff.
ekiin.reading_mnemonic: Over the radio the worker's reply crackles back garbled, just an <reading>echo in</reading> the tunnel — but that crackly <reading>えきいん</reading> is on every platform of this line, herding lost passengers back before the doors slide shut.

en-money.meaning_mnemonic: You already know this shape: a single shiny coin flattened into a square frame, round enough to pass for a <kanji>circle</kanji>. That coin never needs to be anything grander — one coin sitting in one frame is worth exactly one <kanji>yen</kanji>, and it always has been.
en-money.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the kanji's own taught sound: 円 is read <reading>えん</reading>, exactly as you already learned it for the coin in its square frame.

enpitsu.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway of Sei's school, a boy chews the eraser end of a thin gray stick down to nothing, tapping the point against his desk until it snaps clean in half during the exam — the exact anxious shape and worry of a pencil.
enpitsu.reading_mnemonic: 鉛 (えん) plus 筆 (ぴつ) combine directly to give <reading>えんぴつ</reading>.

erabu.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the onigiri shelf holds forty identical triangles, and the till keeps beeping impatiently. A tired shopper stands frozen, picking one up, putting it back, picking up another, until she finally commits — she has to choose, and the beeping won't stop until she does.
erabu.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, <reading>a rabbit</reading> hops up the mossy steps, surrounded by cats, and must pick just one to sit with. It circles them twice, muttering <reading>えらぶ</reading>, choosing, before flopping down beside the one-eared tabby.

erebeetaa.meaning_mnemonic: A vending machine sits at the very top of the mountain trail, impossible to reach on foot. Some hiker gave up climbing years ago and bolted a box to the cliff face that just goes straight up, dinging at each impossible landing until the doors slide open right onto the summit. That box is the elevator.
erebeetaa.reading_mnemonic: エレベーター is a katakana loanword straight from English, so saying <reading>elevator</reading> is saying <reading>エレベーター</reading> — the sound is the whole word, no decoding needed.

esukareetaa.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps got tired of climbers stopping to catch their breath, so one day the whole staircase started crawling upward on its own, each step sliding onto the next in an endless diagonal parade. The shrine cats ride it like a conveyor belt straight past the enormous bell. That self-walking staircase is the escalator.
esukareetaa.reading_mnemonic: エスカレーター is a katakana loanword straight from English, so saying <reading>escalator</reading> is saying <reading>エスカレーター</reading> — the sound is the whole word.

fooku.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till clerk jabs a four-pronged skewer into the rotating hot dog case just to see what happens, and the sausage spins loose, flies across the aisle, and lands spiked upright on the onigiri shelf like a tiny flag. Four sharp points, one impaled sausage: that whole ridiculous skewer is a fork.
fooku.reading_mnemonic: <reading>フォーク</reading> is written exactly as it sounds - a borrowed word, so it is simply the English fork clipped down into kana, nothing to decode.

fuben.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine atop the mountain trail is supposed to be pure <kanji>convenience</kanji>, but it has one working button, and it dispenses only cold soup on the hottest day of the year. Hikers queue anyway since it's the only machine for two hours either way, and every one of them mutters the same thing on the way down. Nothing up there works the way it should. That's inconvenient.
fuben.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 不 as ふ plus 便 as べん gives you 「<reading>ふべん</reading>」.

fuku.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine cats go bare all year, until the coldest morning, when she drapes a tiny knitted sweater over every single one. They strut past the enormous bell stiff-legged, dressed head to tail, mossy steps turned runway. None of them asked for clothes, but none of them takes them off either.
fuku.reading_mnemonic: 服 keeps the reading you already learned for the kanji itself, carried straight through: <reading>ふく</reading>.

fun-counter.meaning_mnemonic: The woodcutter owns no clock. One clean swing through a log takes him exactly one <kanji>minute</kanji>, so when the villagers ask how long the noodles need, he answers in logs and starts chopping. Twelve leaning <kanji>parts</kanji> later the noodles are done: count the halves, halve the count, and you have counted minutes.
fun-counter.reading_mnemonic: This is just 分 wearing its taught reading, so a number plus <reading>ふん</reading> counts your minutes.
fun-counter.description: Attaches to a number to count minutes and to give clock times. The sound shifts after several numbers — one, three, four, six, eight and ten — so those number-plus-minutes combinations are worth learning as fixed forms rather than assembling them.

fun.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>minute</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>minute</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.

fune.meaning_mnemonic: An otter drags every barrel and plank he can find onto the riverbank, lashing them together into a lopsided raft before the current rises further. He shoves off with a broom for a paddle — proof that any floating hunk of junk counts as a ship the moment it carries someone somewhere.
fune.reading_mnemonic: The ferryman blows through a battered <reading>funnel</reading> to signal departure, and the honk that comes out lands squarely as <reading>ふね</reading> — the noise every boat on this river makes before it pushes off from the dock.

furu-rain.meaning_mnemonic: Inside Koichi's konbini, the ceiling mascot's stuffing has sprung a slow leak, and tufts drift down over the onigiri shelf like a private snowfall that never reaches the door. The till keeps beeping through it as customers brush fluff off their shoulders. Whatever comes down from above, steadily and without asking, is what <kanji>falls</kanji>.
furu-rain.reading_mnemonic: Customers call that drifting stuff the mascot's <reading>fur</reading>, and the clerk mutters the word every time it happens — <reading>ふる</reading> — since in this konbini it never rains, it just falls.
furu-rain.description: This verb is reserved for rain and snow falling from the sky — it doesn't extend to objects falling in general, so don't reach for it when something merely drops or tips over.

furui-adj.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine borrows that same mouth held up by ancient crossbeams — its bell hangs from timber so weathered the wood has gone the color of ash. Cats doze in the beam's shadow, moss creeps up every post, and the mouth beneath keeps repeating the same worn story to anyone who'll listen: this whole place is <kanji>old</kanji>.
furui-adj.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats gather around a chest nobody has opened in decades. The oldest tom, a scraggly cat named <reading>Fur Louie</reading>, wedges the lid open with one paw, and the hinge lets out a groan that sounds exactly like <reading>ふるい</reading>, the word for old.

futatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>two</kanji> kanji doesn't change to make <vocabulary>two things</vocabulary> — it already means exactly that on its own.
futatsu.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, an owl in the rafters gives two flat <reading>hoots</reading> every night. The cats insist it's actually saying <reading>ふたつ</reading> — announcing <vocabulary>two things</vocabulary> to no one in particular.
futatsu.description: This belongs to the native Japanese counting series for objects, used as a general default counter when no specific counter word applies.

futsuka.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>two</kanji> flat lines slide under the <kanji>day</kanji> mark without changing shape. That doubled mark means <vocabulary>two days</vocabulary> have passed.
futsuka.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a hiker known as <reading>Foot Sucker</reading> steps in mud on <reading>ふつか</reading>, and the mud won't let go for the full <vocabulary>two days</vocabulary>.

fuyu.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the sports field freezes so hard overnight that someone's abandoned soccer ball is stuck fast to the ice, and the whole team spends morning practice tiptoeing across the frozen grass in their socks because their shoes keep sliding out from under them. That bone-deep, everything-locked-solid freeze is winter.
fuyu.reading_mnemonic: On the frozen sports field, Sei skids into a snowbank and pops up gasping <reading>phew, you</reading> nearly took me out — his teammate had shoved him from behind. The whole team started yelling <reading>ふゆ</reading> at each other for every shove after that, all winter long.

gaikoku.meaning_mnemonic: The person from the slanted gate keeps walking, past their own fence, until the open air runs out at someone else's <kanji>country</kanji> — walls so tall they wrap an entire nation. They step through the gap still headed <kanji>outside</kanji>, and now they're standing in a foreign country.
gaikoku.reading_mnemonic: This one's regular: 外 already reads がい and 国 already reads こく, so stacked together they simply give you <reading>がいこく</reading>.

gaikokujin.meaning_mnemonic: Follow the <kanji>person</kanji> already mid-stride past the slanted gate, headed <kanji>outside</kanji> — but this time they don't stop at the fence. They keep walking until the walls that wrap an entire <kanji>country</kanji> shrink into a smudge on the mountain trail behind them. Striding clean outside your own country's walls is what makes you a foreigner.
gaikokujin.reading_mnemonic: Each kanji keeps its taught reading in a row — 外（がい）＋国（こく）＋人（じん） — giving you <reading>がいこくじん</reading> straight down the line.

gakkou-v.meaning_mnemonic: The swaddled <kanji>study</kanji> child, still parked under its canopy of scribbled lesson notes, gets carried to the courtyard and set at the foot of the one great <kanji>school</kanji> tree. Roots tangle around the roof of notes, a bell rings somewhere in the branches, and the courtyard fills with kids at recess — canopy and tree have grown into one building: a school.
gakkou-v.reading_mnemonic: You already know 学 as がく and 校 as こう — chain them together (がく softens to がっ before こう) and you get exactly <reading>がっこう</reading>.

gakusei.meaning_mnemonic: The child camped beneath that roof of scribbled notes refuses to go home, and overnight the desk starts to feel like part of them — that's daily <kanji>study</kanji>. But they're not finished growing: the same soil that turns a seed into <kanji>life</kanji> is still working underneath them, a person still half-sprouted, still becoming. That's a student.
gakusei.reading_mnemonic: 学 gives がく and 生 supplies the same せい you already know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student, combining exactly into 「<reading>がくせい</reading>」.

gatsu-month.meaning_mnemonic: That same crescent moon now hangs painted above the calendar taped beside Koichi's till, one wedge inked in for every lap it makes across the sky. Shoppers glance up between onigiri runs to see which wedge is lit, using the moon exactly as before — just to name the <kanji>month</kanji> instead of the night.
gatsu-month.reading_mnemonic: Koichi refuses to update that calendar one day at a time — he's too <reading>gutsy</reading> for that. Once every full moon he tears off an entire wedge in one motion, grunting <reading>がつ</reading> as the paper rips clean away.

genki.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's rice bowl breathes out that same curling <kanji>spirit</kanji> steam every morning, but today it rises so fast and so high it nearly knocks the bell clean off its hook. She grins — a bowl steaming that lively means the person eating it is healthy and lively too.
genki.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the kanji readings you already know: 元 as げん plus 気 as き gives you 「<reading>げんき</reading>」.

genkin.meaning_mnemonic: Under Koichi's konbini till sits that same roof-covered stash of gleaming <kanji>money</kanji>, kept buried safe the way it's always been. One slow night the clerk actually digs it up, counts every bill by hand, and slaps the stack flat on the counter — no card, no swipe, just physical bills you can hold. That dug-up, countable stack is cash.
genkin.reading_mnemonic: Ken forgets his card at the konbini every single week, so the clerk just sighs, '<reading>again, Ken</reading>?' and taps the register for cash instead. That resigned sigh is exactly the sound of <reading>げんきん</reading> — same till, same excuse, every time.

getsuyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>moon</kanji> claims the earliest <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji>, ahead of the sun, and that day is <vocabulary>Monday</vocabulary>.

ginkou.meaning_mnemonic: The figure who's always mid-stride, legs split wide, leaning into the step, never leaves the building — he paces the lobby, stamping passbooks between strides because he won't stand still long enough to finish one. Customers behind him catch the same itch to <kanji>go</kanji> before their money finishes counting — a building built around cash that never sits still.
ginkou.reading_mnemonic: 銀（ぎん）＋行（こう）combine directly into <reading>ぎんこう</reading>.

go-shujin.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> who strides in the door each night doesn't get his coat off before he's handed a list — go find the shoes, go find the remote, go find out why dinner's late. Everyone in the house treats him like hired help with a wedding ring: that's the respectful title for someone's husband.
go-shujin.reading_mnemonic: ご stays ご, 主 gives しゅ, and 人 gives じん — stacked together they produce <reading>ごしゅじん</reading>.
go-shujin.description: This is the respectful term for someone else's husband, used when talking to or about the listener's family — not the word you'd use for your own husband. It leans on 主人 (master), so some speakers now avoid it for the gendered assumption baked in.

go-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>five</kanji> kanji never grew into anything else, so it and the <vocabulary>five</vocabulary> word mean exactly the same thing.

gochisousama.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a fat cat licks its bowl of dried fish clean, then rolls over on the mossy steps in a stretch that looks exactly like a deep, satisfied bow. Every cat there does the same roll once the bowl is empty, as if the shrine teaches manners. That lazy roll is the whole phrase: thanks for the meal, already finished.
gochisousama.reading_mnemonic: Written exactly as it sounds — read the kana straight through and you get 「<reading>ごちそうさま</reading>」.

gogo.meaning_mnemonic: Once the clock falls <kanji>behind</kanji> <kanji>noon</kanji>, every hour left in the day counts as <vocabulary>afternoon</vocabulary>.

gohan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps end at a single offering bowl the cats can never quite reach: a small mound of plain white rice, steaming, set out fresh every morning. It isn't a snack and it isn't a whole feast — it's simply what's due at mealtime, the actual cooked rice sitting there and the <kanji>meal</kanji> built around it, both at once.
gohan.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ごはん</reading> is just ご as written plus 飯's reading はん, chained straight together.
gohan.description: This word literally names plain cooked rice, but in everyday speech it just as often means a full meal in general, not only the rice itself — asking someone if they've had gohan yet is asking whether they've eaten at all, breakfast, lunch, or dinner alike.

gomennasai.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a delivery cart clips the onigiri shelf and forty rice balls roll toward the door. The clerk doesn't shout — he just bows lower and lower, repeating the same syllables, until the last onigiri stops at a customer's shoe. That ritual of taking full blame for something rolling away from you is: I'm sorry.
gomennasai.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it sounds, kana all the way through, so there's no puzzle to solve — just recognize <reading>ごめんなさい</reading> on sight and you already have the reading.

gozen.meaning_mnemonic: Every hour that still stands <kanji>front</kanji> of <kanji>noon</kanji> counts as <vocabulary>morning</vocabulary>, before lunch begins.

gyuunyuu.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, the morning delivery crate holds little paper cartons, so cold they sweat in the sun. A kid downs one in one gulp, gets a white mustache, and holds up the empty carton proudly to the whole team: milk.
gyuunyuu.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ぎゅうにゅう</reading> is just 牛's reading ぎゅう plus 乳's reading にゅう, chained together as written.

ha-tooth.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine dispenses exactly one item that day: a single chipped <kanji>tooth</kanji>, still faintly rattling, ejected after the last hiker crunched down on a stone hidden inside their rice ball. Everyone just runs a tongue along their own teeth, checking for the gap where a tooth used to be.
ha-tooth.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the nurse lets out one flat sound every time a kid limps in clutching their jaw — a startled <reading>ha</reading>, stretched thin like a gasp with nowhere to go. That same deadpan <reading>は</reading> is the whole word: the sound she makes over a broken tooth is the reading for tooth itself.

haburashi.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini vending machine jams and spits out nothing but bristled sticks — hundreds of them, rattling into the till tray while the beeping never stops. Koichi tries one on his molars out of curiosity and it actually works. By morning he's stacked them by the onigiri shelf with a hand-written label: <kanji>tooth</kanji>brush, one per customer.
haburashi.reading_mnemonic: The stickers on Koichi's new stock just say <reading>はブラシ</reading> — he sounded it out as 'ha' for the gap-toothed grin on the box art and 'brush' for the bristles, so regulars just call them <reading>ha-brush</reading> and never mispronounce the label again.

hachi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>eight</kanji> kanji is the <vocabulary>eight</vocabulary> word too — no separate story needed, they were always the same character.

haha.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, among the mossy steps and the cats sprawled everywhere, your <kanji>mother</kanji> doubles over laughing at some joke only she finds funny, the sound bouncing flat off the one enormous bell. That plain, unpolished laugh is exactly the humble word you use for your own <kanji>mother</kanji>, never for anyone else's.
haha.reading_mnemonic: Her laugh rings off the shrine bell as two dry, identical beats, <reading>ha-ha</reading>, the same flat sound as <reading>はは</reading>, over and over until the cats scatter. It's a plain, low sound on purpose, nothing decorative, matching the plain word it belongs to.
haha.description: 母 (haha) is the plain, humble word for your own mother, used when speaking about her to people outside the family — never for someone else's mother, and not typically what you call her to her face. It contrasts with お母さん (okaasan), the polite form used to address your own mother directly or refer to someone else's.

hai-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane lines up cups of water along the mossy shrine steps for the cats, refilling one from the well every time a cat drinks it dry, over and over until the whole row is gone again. She never counts the cats — she counts the cups she's had to refill, one cupful after another, until the well runs low.
hai-counter.reading_mnemonic: 杯 keeps the reading you already learned for the kanji itself, carried straight through: <reading>はい</reading>.

hai.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the priest swings the enormous bell and calls the roll for the cats scattered across the mossy steps. Each cat shoots a paw straight up the instant its name rings out — an immediate, unmistakable yes, no hesitation, no exceptions.
