hai.reading_mnemonic: This word is written just as it sounds — picture each cat's paw shooting <reading>high</reading> the moment its name is called, and you have the reading <reading>はい</reading>.

hairu-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a tiny torii gate stands guard in front of the lone vending machine. You duck your head low, just like the ducking figure who taught you to <kanji>enter</kanji>, and step through the narrow gate into the clearing — the machine already humming, waiting.
hairu-v.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a regular everyone greets with <reading>Hi, Rue</reading> slides open the onigiri case and folds herself in beside the salmon triangles. Koichi doesn't look up from the beeping till; he just mutters <reading>はいる</reading> as the glass slides shut on her.

hajimaru.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, out on the sports field, a hedgehog referee named Hazy Maru raises the starting horn over a line of runners. Nobody steps forward, nobody says go — the instant the horn sounds, the race just <kanji>begins</kanji> on its own, runners lurching off before they've even decided to move. That's what beginning looks like when nothing and nobody has to make it happen.
hajimaru.reading_mnemonic: Hazy Maru raises the horn and bellows <reading>Ha, Jimmy, Maru!</reading> across the field before anyone can move, and the racers bolt not because he counted down but because his shout already sounded like the race starting itself: <reading>はじまる</reading>.

hajime.meaning_mnemonic: At the foot of the mountain trail, a hiker adjusts her boots, looks up at the impossibly steep path, and takes exactly one step. That single step, before the vending machine at the top is even a speck, is the whole <kanji>beginning</kanji>.
hajime.reading_mnemonic: At the starting line on Sei's sports field, the coach cups his hands and shouts <reading>ha, Jimmy!</reading> to the runner who hasn't noticed the race started. Jimmy bolts — that shout is 「<reading>はじめ</reading>」, the beginning.

hajimemashite.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's first day at the new school, the hallway echoes so much his greeting bounces back before he finishes it. He bows to the wrong homeroom twice, and each time the whole class stands and returns the same ritual line anyway — the one you say only once, to someone you're meeting for the very first time: nice to meet you.
hajimemashite.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it sounds, kana all the way through, so there's no puzzle to solve — just recognize <reading>はじめまして</reading> on sight and you already have the reading.

hajimeru.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the register at Koichi's konbini, a raccoon clerk named Meru Jimson grips the ancient till with both paws and physically shoves its lever forward, forcing the beeping to life stroke by stroke. Nothing in this shop starts on its own — she has to <kanji>begin</kanji> it herself every morning, hauling the whole shift into motion by hand before a single customer walks in.
hajimeru.reading_mnemonic: The clerk grunts <reading>Ha, Jimmy, Meru!</reading> every single morning as she wrenches the till's lever down, and regulars have started timing their onigiri run to that grunt — the sound that means she's deciding, on purpose, that the day is now <reading>はじめる</reading>.

hako.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, you press the button for water. It grinds, hesitates, then drops a plain taped-shut carton instead, tumbling down the last few steps ahead of you. Nobody asked for this. The machine just started calling every carton a box, and now so does everyone who climbs the trail.
hako.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Koichi wades in to cool a crate of drinks and comes out numb to the elbow. He yelps <reading>"Ha, cold!"</reading> so sharply that the fishermen nearby start calling the crate itself by that yelp, and the name sticks as <reading>はこ</reading>.

hakobu.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a turtle has apparently opened a ferry service: every evening it surfaces with someone's forgotten sandal balanced flat on its shell, swims it dead straight across the current, and leaves it on the far rock before turning back for the next one. Nobody asked it to. It just carries things from one bank to the other, and that's the whole job.
hakobu.reading_mnemonic: Fishermen at the riverbank cheer <reading>Ha, Cobo!</reading> every time the turtle noses a lost sandal off the rocks and paddles it across dead level, and once it lands safely on the far side, they call the whole ferry-run <reading>はこぶ</reading>.

han-time.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>half</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>half (past)</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
han-time.description: This word means "half past" an hour, not half of a general quantity — it always attaches to a time, never a whole object.

hana-nose.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron plants itself ankle-deep and points its long beak straight up, sniffing the air to check whether the water's too cold to cross before wading in. That beak does the one job it's built for — smelling out trouble first — which is exactly what a nose is for.
hana-nose.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a new transfer student named Hannah presses her face to the cafeteria window, sniffing out the menu before anyone announces it. The other kids nickname her <reading>はな</reading> on the spot — that <reading>Hannah</reading>-nose never misses a smell, even through glass.

hana-v.meaning_mnemonic: Under the fluorescent glare of Koichi's konbini, someone has wedged a single potted plant by the onigiri shelf: one stem leaning hard to the side, its bloom spilling clean over the pot's rim. Customers keep stopping mid-reach for rice balls just to stare at it. Stem below, blossom bursting above — a <kanji>flower</kanji> where nobody expected one.
hana-v.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane finds a single bloom growing out of a crack in the shrine's mossy steps and gasps '<reading>hah-nah</reading>,' the breath she makes whenever a cat brushes her ankles. That gasp becomes <reading>はな</reading>, the shrine's word for the flower nobody planted.

hanashi.meaning_mnemonic: That same mouth still hasn't stopped, and now its stories have an audience: the cats at Grandma Kane's shrine gather on the mossy steps every evening because one of them just won't quit <kanji>talking</kanji>, spinning fresh stories about a fish the size of the bell. Nobody's ever proven a word of it, but nobody leaves either.
hanashi.reading_mnemonic: Every time the storytelling cat starts up again, Grandma Kane calls out from the steps, <reading>Hannah, she</reading> really said that? — and the phrase blurs into <reading>はなし</reading>, the very story the whole shrine has gathered on the mossy steps to hear.

hanasu-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a mouth keeps releasing stacked lines of speech across the water, one slab after another, while right beside it a tongue wags nonstop, egging it on for more. Between the two of them the water is drowned out entirely — this is what it sounds like when someone won't stop <kanji>talking</kanji>. That endless back-and-forth is what it means to speak.
hanasu-v.reading_mnemonic: Hana, a heron who wades the riverbank, opens her long beak and lets out a honk that sounds exactly like <reading>はな</reading>, then finishes it off with a brisk <reading>す</reading> snap of her bill — together that's <reading>はなす</reading>.

hanbun.meaning_mnemonic: Han the half-and-half chef cleaves the crossed matchsticks down the middle, one perfect <kanji>half</kanji> either side of the beeping till. The woodcutter, unimpressed, sets a log by the onigiri shelf and drops it into two leaning <kanji>parts</kanji>. Two men, two clean cuts, and the konbini floor is nothing but half.
hanbun.reading_mnemonic: 半 gives its はん and 分 its ぶん with no surprises, so the word is simply <reading>はんぶん</reading>.

hantai.meaning_mnemonic: Two teams line up on opposite banks of the river, rope pulled taut between them, boots dug into the mud, each side straining directly against the other's pull. Neither team gives an inch — that dead-even standoff, everyone pulling the opposite way from everyone else, is exactly the picture for opposite, against.
hantai.reading_mnemonic: The referee, nicknamed <reading>hun-tie</reading> because his necktie unravels every time he blows the whistle, screams <reading>はんたい</reading> whenever one team yanks in the exact opposite direction from the other.

harau.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till beeps and beeps at a customer already halfway out the door, arms full of onigiri he never scanned. The clerk has to haul him back by the collar before he'll dig out his wallet. Nobody leaves that counter until the beeping stops — you always have to pay.
harau.reading_mnemonic: The clerk hauls him back by the collar, shouting that he'll <reading>haul</reading> him to the register himself if he has to. Coins finally hit the counter. The whole scrambling scene is <reading>はらう</reading> — to pay.

haru-attach.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi finds the drink-cooler's price sticker curling up at the corner, licks the back of a fresh one from the roll, and presses it down flat against the glass with his whole palm until every corner is glued flat. That's sticking something into place for good — to stick, to paste.
haru-attach.reading_mnemonic: Koichi keeps a toy <reading>harpoon</reading> by the register and spears each curling flyer clean onto the corkboard so it stays flat, muttering <reading>はる</reading> under his breath with every satisfying thunk.

haru.meaning_mnemonic: Every year on the mountain trail, the vending machine at the top freezes solid through winter — until one morning the ice around its buttons melts, a marmot pokes its head out of a burrow beside it, and the whole slope turns to mud and green shoots overnight. That sudden thaw, when everything wakes up at once, is spring.
haru.reading_mnemonic: A groundhog named Haru climbs out of her burrow on the mountain trail every thaw and bellows a cheerful <reading>halloo</reading> across the valley to announce she's awake. Everyone down at the shrine started calling that first warm shout <reading>はる</reading>, and the name stuck.

hashi-bridge.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a delivery cart stalls at the water's edge, wheels churning mud. Someone drags two empty vending-machine crates out, sets them end to end across the current, and rolls the cart straight over the water without a splash. The crate-line stays there after — a bridge, built out of pure stubbornness.
hashi-bridge.reading_mnemonic: A cook at the riverbank burns a batch of <reading>hash</reading> browns and, furious, flings them one by one across the current. They land in a perfect line, crisp edge to crisp edge, and someone simply walks across on the hash line — which is exactly how you say <reading>はし</reading>.

hashi-chopsticks.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the only vending machine sits with two thin metal prongs sticking out where the coin slot should be — the last hiker jammed his chopsticks in there trying to pry loose a stuck can. Nobody's fixed it since; they just call it the chopsticks machine.
hashi-chopsticks.reading_mnemonic: By the time a hiker drags themselves up to that machine, all they can manage is a rasping <reading>はし</reading> — it comes out as <reading>ha-shh</reading>, half word, half exhale — right as they spot the two chopsticks still propping the jammed coin door open.

hashiru.meaning_mnemonic: Sei is already late for practice when the coach spots him at the classroom door. There's no time to warm up, so he just bolts, straight down the echoing hallway and out onto the sports field, arms pumping, shoes slapping tile and then grass. The coach doesn't even blink. That flat-out, no-warning sprint across the field is to run.
hashiru.reading_mnemonic: As Sei rockets across the field, the announcer's shout comes out garbled through the loudspeaker — all anyone hears is <reading>ha-shee-roo</reading>, over and over, close enough to <reading>はしる</reading> that the whole team starts using it as their word for tearing across the grass.

hataraku.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi unlocks the konbini at six to find last night's clerk still behind the till, sleeves rolled, restocking the onigiri shelf for the fourth time since closing. He offers to send her home; she just points at the line forming outside and grabs another crate. Some people rest between shifts. She has never once learned how — she just works.
hataraku.reading_mnemonic: The new clerk at Koichi's konbini won't leave the <reading>hot rack</reading> of oden warming by the till, muttering <reading>はたらく</reading> under her breath as she flips skewers past midnight, refusing every break Koichi offers.

hatsuka.meaning_mnemonic: The two raccoons are still hunched over their cold noodle broth, each guarding its snapped chopstick — the same two you met before. Every <kanji>day</kanji> new sun through the window finds them arranging the four chopstick halves into one perfect cross, the shape of <kanji>ten</kanji>, then doubling that cross because there are <kanji>two</kanji> raccoons at the table. After twenty of these sunrises nobody has eaten a single noodle: the twentieth day.
hatsuka.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer grabs coffee straight off the warmer and spills it across the hood of his parked <reading>hot car</reading> right by the beeping till. Twenty days running he does this at checkout, and the staff now just call it <reading>はつか</reading> — the 20th, twenty days of the same scalded hood.

hayai-early.meaning_mnemonic: Same sun-over-the-stick you already know: it's cresting the horizon so <kanji>early</kanji> that your alarm hasn't even gone off. You're blinking awake in a grey pre-dawn kitchen, coffee not ready, socks mismatched — the sun got here first, and now everything today has to start this <kanji>early</kanji> just to keep up with it.
hayai-early.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the sports field sits empty except for one runner already warming up before the gates even open. The groundskeeper spots the shape moving in the dark and shouts <reading>hi, yay</reading> in surprise, which is exactly <reading>はやい</reading>, the word for early.

hayai-fast.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a leaf drops onto the current and is gone before it finishes falling — past the washing stones, under the bridge, out of sight in one blink. Nothing on that water ever holds still long enough for a second look.
hayai-fast.reading_mnemonic: A boy leaps off the riverbank shouting <reading>hi-yah!</reading> and is already underwater before the shout finishes echoing off the far bank — that's the speed of <reading>はやい</reading>, gone before the sound catches up to him.

heta.meaning_mnemonic: That same <kanji>hand</kanji> that should hold steady instead droops <kanji>down</kanji> below the table, fingers trembling as it fumbles the teacup and sends it crashing to the floor. Everyone at the table agrees: this hand is unskillful, hopelessly bad at absolutely everything it touches.
heta.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow tries to toast a marshmallow and instead sets the whole power line ablaze, dropping the charred stick into the river below. The other birds start calling him a total <reading>hater</reading> of marshmallows, squawking 「<reading>へた</reading>」 every time he lights another one on fire.

heya-bangou.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the gym gets carved overnight into a maze of tiny <kanji>section</kanji>s, each one boxed under its own little <kanji>roof</kanji>, none of them labeled, so students keep wandering into supply closets looking for homeroom. The janitor storms through stapling a <kanji>number</kanji> to every single door until each one wears its room <kanji>number</kanji> like a name tag.
heya-bangou.reading_mnemonic: A hall monitor at Sei's school bellows through a megaphone, <reading>hey, uh — bang, GO!</reading>, banging a gong before sprinting off, and the scrambling classroom just catches her cry fading down the corridor: 「<reading>へやばんごう</reading>」.

heya.meaning_mnemonic: Past the mountain trail's improbable vending machine, someone has wedged a plain door straight into the rock face, walling off a <kanji>section</kanji> of cliff under a stone <kanji>roof</kanji>. Push it open and there's nothing dramatic inside — just four walls, one chair, and quiet, built for the sole purpose of finally sitting down after the climb: a room, carved out of nowhere in particular.
heya.reading_mnemonic: The hiker collapses through that door, drops her pack, and sighs <reading>hay, yeah</reading> — worn out enough that even four bare walls feel like paradise. That sigh is exactly how you say <reading>へや</reading>, room, once you're finally inside one.

hi-sun-v.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the same window with a bar across it that you already know: the <kanji>sun</kanji> is climbing into the frame right now, filling the room with morning light. That one image was always doing double duty — window, bar, climbing sun — and standing alone it's already the whole word for sun and <kanji>day</kanji>, no second kanji needed to lean on.
hi-sun-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is written with the very kanji you already read as <reading>ひ</reading>, so the sound carries straight over — no new reading to learn.

hidari-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, in the middle of shop class, someone braces a carpenter's square hard against a plank so it won't slip while a friend saws — the same tensed grip as before, the arm that isn't doing the cutting. That steadying arm is always the one on the <kanji>left</kanji>, holding everything still so the other hand can work.
hidari-v.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a mender called <reading>He-Dolly</reading> sits on the mossy steps stitching a rag doll the cats keep stealing. One cat yanks the thread until the enormous bell rope snags the doll and hoists it. He lunges, misses, and from the dirt he groans <reading>ひだり</reading>.

higashi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning that same tree at the horizon snags the sun in its branches again, right on schedule. You watch it happen daily: the sun claws its way through the tangle, breaks free, and you know exactly which direction you're facing when it does — <kanji>east</kanji>.
higashi-v.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a regular leans on the onigiri shelf by the door until the till beeps in protest. He lets out a burp that fogs the glass, and the clerk mutters <reading>he-gassy</reading>. That mutter is <reading>ひがし</reading>.

hikaru.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the steep mountain trail, the one lonely vending machine keeps its light on all night, a single bright square glowing over the dark ridge. Hikers exhausted from the climb spot it from three switchbacks away before anything else on the mountain — the machine's whole purpose, up here, is simply to shine.
hikaru.reading_mnemonic: The hiker who restocks that machine is named <reading>Hikaru</reading>, and climbers joke that both he and the machine do the same job on that ridge: <reading>ひかる</reading>, shining so you don't miss the top.

hiki.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, Sei is trying to wash one stray cat, but it wriggles free and suddenly there are three more identical stray cats streaking off between the rocks, all soaked and furious. She gives up chasing them individually and starts tallying the whole dripping mob as small animals (counter).
hiki.reading_mnemonic: Every time a cat darts past her soaked sleeves, Sei yelps "<reading>hick</reading>!" in surprise, and by the third one darting past the rocks she's just counting the startled yelps out loud: <reading>ひき</reading>.

hikidashi.meaning_mnemonic: Your dresser has a wooden box wedged into it like a second peak stacked on the mountain of drawers above it. Tug the handle and the box finally does what its shape always threatened: it does its best <kanji>exit / leave</kanji> impression, sliding all the way out and dumping your socks on the floor. That sliding box is the drawer.
hikidashi.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just those pieces stacked together: 引 read ひ, plus き, plus 出 read だ, plus し, which gives <reading>ひきだし</reading>.

hikouki.meaning_mnemonic: The restless figure who can't stand still — always mid-stride, always about to <kanji>go</kanji> somewhere — sprints down a runway and just keeps going, faster and faster, until the ground drops away entirely and he's roaring into the sky strapped inside an airplane.
hikouki.reading_mnemonic: Line up the readings you already know — 飛 as ひ, 行 as こう, 機 as き — and they simply become <reading>ひこうき</reading>.

hikui.meaning_mnemonic: A heron at the riverbank refuses to use the tall bridge and instead wades under a footbridge built barely above the water. Every step forces its neck down further, until it's hunched practically flat against the current, its whole body folded so low its beak skims the surface.
hikui.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit vending machine, delivery boy Ren has to duck so far under its low overhang that he grunts <reading>“he, coo, we”</reading> each time — the exact sound of <reading>ひくい</reading>, because everything up here, the ceiling included, is built low.

hima.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school lets out early with no explanation, and the hallway that's usually echoing with footsteps goes completely silent. Sei sits alone on the steps with an entire afternoon and nothing scheduled in it, swinging a bag back and forth just to have something to do. An empty stretch with nowhere to be — that's free time.
hima.reading_mnemonic: Sei texts a friend just one word: <reading>he, ma</reading> — short for hey, ma, guess what, she's about to waste the whole afternoon. Drag those two sounds together and it's <reading>ひま</reading>, said by someone who has absolutely nothing to do and all day to do it in.

hiragana.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field the coach gives up on straight chalk lines and starts dragging the chalk into loose, looping curves instead — no sharp corners anywhere, just soft rounded strokes bending back on themselves. That rounded, curling script the coach just invented by accident is exactly what this word names: hiragana.
hiragana.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it's read, all in kana: <reading>ひらがな</reading>.

hiroi.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane climbs the mossy steps expecting another cramped little shrine room, but the doors swing open onto a courtyard so wide the enormous bell looks like a pebble sitting in the middle of it. The cats scatter in every direction because there's finally room to run. She just stands there with her arms out, turning in a slow circle: wide, spacious, wide, spacious.
hiroi.reading_mnemonic: A tiny hero marches up Grandma Kane's steps expecting a cramped little shrine and instead finds a whole valley behind the gate, room enough to get lost in. He plants his flag and shouts so the cats can hear it too: <reading>hero</reading>, <reading>ひろい</reading>, this place just keeps going.

hiru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>daytime</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>noon</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
hiru.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's vending machine, a <reading>hero</reading> refuses to climb until 「<reading>ひる</reading>」 strikes, since he only fights at <vocabulary>noon</vocabulary>.

hirugohan.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the <kanji>daytime</kanji> sun sits flat overhead as the sports field empties for the lunch bell, and a stray dog times its raid perfectly, snatching a tray straight off the picnic table mid-sprint. Kids chase it in a lap around the track, but the dog is faster than any of them expect, gone with the whole <kanji>meal</kanji> before anyone's fork is even out.
hirugohan.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ひるごはん</reading> chains 昼's reading ひる, plus ご, plus 飯's reading はん, exactly as written.

hito.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, someone rounds the corner: just two legs mid-stride, a body carried along above them, heading forward without dragging anything else behind. Strip away every job title, every role, every name — what's left striding down that hallway is simply a <kanji>person</kanji>.
hito.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a lone figure climbs the mossy steps at dusk, no name tag, just a shape moving past the cats. One cat swats at a bare foot and the figure yelps <reading>he-toe</reading>, which is exactly the sound of <reading>ひと</reading>, the word for person.

hitori-de.meaning_mnemonic: The goat abandons her one-contestant stage and packs it in, but the only <kanji>person</kanji> who ever bought a ticket — a lone figure with two legs striding forward — has already left too, walking the <kanji>one</kanji> straight line of dirt without another soul in sight. That's alone: one person, nobody else.
hitori-de.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 一 read ひと, plus 人 read り, plus で, gives <reading>ひとりで</reading>.

hitotsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>one</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>one thing</vocabulary> word share the very same stroke: nothing was added, nothing was changed.
hitotsu.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the tired cashier rings up a single item by barking <reading>ひとつ</reading>, which comes out sounding like <reading>hit two</reading>, and hands over exactly <vocabulary>one thing</vocabulary>.
hitotsu.description: One of the native Japanese counting words for generic objects, used instead of the ordinary number words when there is no specialized counter for whatever is being counted.

hoka.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, one umbrella turns up in the lost and found every rainy week, and every student swears, straight-faced, that it belongs to someone else — never mine, always another person's. By the end of term nobody remembers whose it actually was, just an endless chain of pointing at whoever's standing nearby. That endless deflection is the word: other.
hoka.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a peddler named Hoka the hawker never sells you anything from his own cart — he waves you further up the path, insisting you buy from the other hawker instead. Every climber ends up chasing an <reading>hoka</reading> who doesn't exist. His name says it plain: <reading>ほか</reading>.

hon-counter.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till has jammed with a single receipt spooling endlessly onto the floor — a long white ribbon of paper, thin as the line marking a tree's roots. The clerk keeps stacking these long unrolled strips like planks, and pretty soon he's counting them the same way he'd count <kanji>books</kanji>: as long objects (counter).
hon-counter.reading_mnemonic: 本 already reads ほん from book / origin, so the counter for long objects keeps that same reading: <reading>ほん</reading>.

hon.meaning_mnemonic: At the school, Sei kneels by the tree with that single flat line marking its <kanji>origin</kanji> and presses a stack of blank paper flat against the mark. When she peels the pages away, the origin's whole shape has bled through onto every sheet, and she staples the stack edge to edge — a bound stack of someone's origin, pressed flat and readable, is exactly what a book is.
hon.reading_mnemonic: 本 keeps the reading you already learned for it — read it as <reading>ほん</reading>.

hontou-ni.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi finds a battered <kanji>book</kanji> behind the konbini till and swears its water-stained page is the exact <kanji>origin</kanji> of the beeping glitch everyone blames on ghosts. He traces the story back to that origin page, hands it to the manager, and his guess <kanji>hits</kanji> the mark exactly — he's telling the truth, really and truly.
hontou-ni.reading_mnemonic: Koichi drops to one knee at the shrine, hand flat on his own kneecap, swearing <reading>honest to knee</reading> — <reading>ほんとうに</reading> — that the till really did start beeping on its own, while Grandma Kane just stares at the kneeling man.

hoshi.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi strings cheap fairy lights along the konbini ceiling, but half of them burn out by midnight, leaving a scatter of tiny bright points against black tile. Late customers buying onigiri look up and see a private sky punched with pinholes of light, one fixed point at a time. That single point of light, sitting alone in the dark, is exactly the word: star.
hoshi.reading_mnemonic: Two hikers reach the mountain trail's summit vending machine at last light. One collapses against it, and her friend blurts <reading>Whoa, she's</reading> done — then both look up to find a single point of light waiting over the ridge: the <reading>ほし</reading> that guided the whole climb.

hoshii.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a kid presses against the sports-field fence eyeing another team's shiny new ball, arms not quite reaching through the wire, face doing all the talking. Nobody has to ask what that expression means — wanting something you can't yet have looks the same on everyone.
hoshii.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Grandma Kane eyes the far bank where the mushrooms grow thick and sighs 「<reading>ほしい</reading>」 to no one in particular — '<reading>oh, she</reading>' really does want to cross, and the current is just fast enough that wanting has to be enough for today.

hoteru.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini run for onigiri turns into an all-nighter when the shelves multiply into fluorescent corridors, till after till after till, until he realizes he's wandered into a lobby lined with beds instead of shelves — he's checked into a hotel without meaning to.
hoteru.reading_mnemonic: ホテル is a loanword written exactly as it sounds, straight from the English <reading>hotel</reading> — just recognize 「<reading>ホテル</reading>」 as the borrowed sound and move on.

hou.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman raises his hoe like a compass whenever someone asks which way to wade across. He never points with his hand — only the hoe, tilted toward whichever <kanji>direction</kanji> the current looks calmest that day — and that single tilt is the only answer anyone gets.
hou.reading_mnemonic: He grunts one flat <reading>ほう</reading> as the hoe swings — the same clipped sound as saying <reading>hoe</reading> with your mouth barely open — and that grunt-and-tilt is the whole direction anyone needs at the crossing.

hyaku-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hundred</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>hundred</vocabulary> word are the very same thing, nothing added and nothing changed.

ichi-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>one</kanji> kanji is just that single flat line. Read on its own, it is simply the word <vocabulary>one</vocabulary>, so the kanji and the word are exactly the same.

ichiban.meaning_mnemonic: The goat's one-contestant talent show finally gets real judges. They tally the votes, find there is only <kanji>one</kanji> name on the ballot, and rank her <kanji>number one</kanji> without protest. She was always going to be the most decorated goat on the plain, and now it's simply official.
ichiban.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old angler weighs every catch twice, then declares his own the <reading>いちばん</reading> — the <reading>itchy bun</reading> of fish, unbeatable — before anyone else can even measure theirs.

ie.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a hermit crab stops dragging its blistered shell. It wedges into a hollow rock at the trail's edge, lines up four pinecones in the doorway like doormats, and won't budge again. That hollow rock, doormats and all, is officially somebody's <kanji>house</kanji> — the crab has made itself a home.
ie.reading_mnemonic: A builder named Ei nails one crooked wall onto that same hollow rock and steps back beaming, waiting for someone to ask about the roof. Instead he throws both arms up and shouts <reading>いえ</reading>, which lands on the ear exactly like an English <reading>yay</reading>, and declares the one wall a finished house.

ii.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat sniffs the offering bowl and gives two sharp nods — one for the taste, one for the temperature — before curling up satisfied on the mossy steps. Two nods, two syllables: いい, いい. Whatever survives a cat's judgment twice over earns the simplest verdict there is — good.
ii.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds, said twice over: <reading>いい</reading>.
ii.description: いい is the casual, everyday word for good, but it conjugates oddly: the negative, the past, and the te-form all switch to a different stem instead of building directly off いい itself — one of the few adjectives in Japanese that bends this way.

iie.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the summit vending machine jams on the same drink three times running. You don't bother explaining — you just fold your arms, stretch your mouth into a long groan, and shake your head slowly. That stretched, reluctant groan is the whole word: no.
iie.reading_mnemonic: いいえ is spelled exactly as it sounds, no hidden readings to untangle — read the kana <reading>いいえ</reading> straight through, drawn out like the groan <reading>ee-yeah</reading> you just gave that stubborn machine.
iie.description: This is the standard textbook "no," but it leans formal and can sound blunt if used bare — Japanese speakers often soften a refusal or deny a compliment with it rather than flatly reject something, so it does more polite work than the English word suggests.

iin.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school converts the equipment closet into a one-desk clinic every flu season — a cot and a nurse standing in for the absent <kanji>doctor</kanji>, treating every complaint with the same orange lozenge. Sei fakes a stomachache to skip laps, then turns pale for real when the lozenge turns out to be mislabeled wasabi candy. Word spreads until the closet is treated like its own <kanji>institution</kanji>, hand-lettered sign and all: clinic, enter at your own risk.
iin.reading_mnemonic: The nurse only ever answers <reading>いいん</reading> — 'yes, fine' — no matter the symptom, patting the cot and repeating <reading>'ee-een, ee-een'</reading> like a metronome until whoever's sick just gives up arguing and lies down.

ikaga.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi is so eager to please every customer that he never just asks outright; he bows first, and only then wonders aloud <vocabulary>how (polite)</vocabulary> he can help you today.
ikaga.description: This is the polite version of the plain how, used when making an offer or asking someone's preference, such as with a guest or customer. The plain form is what you would use with close friends instead.

iku-v.meaning_mnemonic: That stick figure who's always mid-stride, the one who can never <kanji>go</kanji> two seconds without moving to the next place, finally shoulders a bag and walks straight out the door one morning. You watch the doorway swing shut behind them. That's the whole word: to go.
iku-v.reading_mnemonic: It's simply the taught <reading>い</reading> reading of 行 that Koichi already uses, plus く, spelling out <reading>いく</reading> exactly as the kanji already taught you.

ikura.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tub of salmon roe sits with no price tag, so you hold it up to the cashier and ask <vocabulary>how much</vocabulary>.
ikura.description: いくら for how much is an exact homophone of いくら, the everyday word for salmon roe — a genuine coincidence in real Japanese, not just this story's invention.

ikutsu.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank you keep saying eek at every coot that paddles past, until you've lost all track of <vocabulary>how many / how old</vocabulary> the chicks trailing behind them are.
ikutsu.description: This one question word covers two different English words: asking how many of something there is, and asking someone's age. Context tells you which sense is meant, since there is no separate word for each.

ima.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>now</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so whenever you say it, that is the only moment it ever points to.
ima.reading_mnemonic: A hiker at the mountain trail's vending machine slams the button and shouts <reading>いま</reading>, sounding just like shouting <reading>I'm-a</reading> grab this drink, because <vocabulary>now</vocabulary> is the only moment worth waiting for.

imi.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one particular cat never blinks — it just stares at whatever offering was left on the mossy steps, as if grading its <kanji>taste</kanji>. Visitors have taken to leaving notes asking the cat what it's thinking. It never answers, but everyone leaves convinced that unblinking stare carries the real point of the offering — its meaning.
imi.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from its kanji: 意 read い plus 味 read み give <reading>いみ</reading>.

imouto.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the small girl who insists on carrying her own backpack up the mountain trail, refuses help, then sits down halfway and cries until someone caves and carries both the backpack and her. That stubborn, still-needs-looking-after littlest-girl energy is exactly a younger sister.
imouto.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the small girl stubs her toe on a root and yelps three sharp sounds — <reading>ee, moh, toe</reading> — before anyone can catch her. The hiker behind logs it plainly as <reading>いもうと</reading>, the toe-stubbing little sister, and keeps climbing.

inu.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening a dog parks himself outside Koichi's konbini, nose pressed to the glass, staring at the onigiri shelf like it personally wronged him. He never begs, never barks — just stands there radiating quiet judgment until someone caves and brings one out. That silent, immovable stare is what dog means here.
inu.reading_mnemonic: A new part-timer trips over the dog camped by Koichi's door and asks if he's some kind of mascot. Koichi shakes his head: he's just <reading>いぬ</reading>, plain and simple, and the easiest way to hold onto that is to hear it as <reading>in new</reading> — like he wandered in new and never left.

ireru-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the little figure who ducks under doorways to <kanji>enter</kanji> on its own is stalling by the onigiri shelf. You plant a hand on its back and shove — bent double, it goes through anyway, disappearing into the back room. You didn't just watch it enter this time; you made it happen. You put it in.
ireru-v.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Eri catches a slippery <reading>eel</reading> that keeps trying to escape. She has one hand free and a bucket ready, so before it can wriggle off she says '<reading>いれる</reading>' and drops it straight in.

iriguchi.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini has one doorway low enough that you have to duck your head to step through — that's the ducking figure who <kanji>enters</kanji>. Beyond it the sliding doors gape like a giant <kanji>mouth</kanji>, wide open all night, swallowing customers whole. Duck, then get swallowed by the mouth: that gaping doorway is the entrance.
iriguchi.reading_mnemonic: Koichi hangs a mock sign over the gaping doorway reading <reading>いりぐち</reading>, joking it looks like the entrance to an <reading>eerie Gucci</reading> boutique — pure velvet-rope energy for a konbini. Duck under, get swallowed by the mouth, and you've found the entrance.

iro.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the onigiri shelf overnight, and by morning every wrapper is a wildly different hue — lime green, shocking pink, traffic-cone orange — clashing under the fluorescent lights. Customers stop dead in the doorway, dazzled by the sheer <kanji>color</kanji> of it all.
iro.reading_mnemonic: Koichi finds a gloomy donkey named <reading>Eeyore</reading> wandering the konbini aisle. Under the fluorescent lights his gray coat lights up with every hue on the shelf, and his mournful name sounds just like the word for it: <reading>いろ</reading>.

iroiro.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine improbably parked on the mountain trail, an old peddler unrolls a blanket covered in buttons, each one a different <kanji>color</kanji> — red, teal, one just paint-spattered — insisting every single one does something different. You press three at random and get juice, a whistling kettle, and a burst of confetti. Nothing on that blanket matches anything else. That is the entire idea of various.
iroiro.reading_mnemonic: A parrot at Koichi's konbini refuses to say any word once — it repeats everything twice, tilting its head each time like it's testing a new shade of the same phrase. Ask it to name anything and out comes the doubled echo, <reading>いろいろ</reading>, sounding just like calling a <reading>hero, hero</reading> across the aisle.

iru-exist.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine has a cat that has lived among the mossy steps for as long as anyone remembers. It breathes, blinks, occasionally swats the enormous bell, proof that something living is here, right now, unlike the stones around it. That ongoing presence, breath and all, is to exist.
iru-exist.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, containing 「<reading>いる</reading>」.

iru-need.meaning_mnemonic: You're packing for a weekend trip and your friend keeps grabbing things off the shelf — a hairdryer, three paperbacks, a spare umbrella. You take each one back and set it down: not necessary. Then you get to the phone charger and stop. That one you keep. That's the line between wanting something and actually needing it.
iru-need.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a lost <reading>eel</reading> flops out of a hiker's water bottle, gasping — it needs water right now or it's finished. The hiker jams coins into the improbable vending machine, and the eel wheezes out the sound of its own need: 「<reading>いる</reading>」.

isha.meaning_mnemonic: A goldfish that stopped blinking gets carried into the clinic, though goldfish famously have no eyelids. The receptionist doesn't even look up — stranger visits happen weekly. When your name is finally called, the person in the white coat with a stethoscope swinging off one ear is exactly who you came for: the <kanji>doctor</kanji>.
isha.reading_mnemonic: 医 gives い and 者 gives しゃ, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>いしゃ</reading>.

isogashii.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the final bell rings and she is somehow expected to be three places at once: the sports field, the office, and the echoing hallway, all before the gate locks. She sprints the same loop between them so many times she forgets which errand she already finished. That constant, overlapping scramble is what busy means here.
isogashii.reading_mnemonic: Sei pants <reading>ease over, gosh, she!</reading> jogging past the sports field for the third time — close enough to <reading>いそがしい</reading> that it's basically her out-of-breath way of saying busy.

isogu.meaning_mnemonic: The last train chimes its warning right outside Koichi's konbini, and you abandon your basket mid-scan, shove past the onigiri shelf, and pelt for the platform doors as they begin to slide shut. There's no time left to think — only to hurry.
isogu.reading_mnemonic: A cat bolts down the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine for no reason at all, and you chase after it shouting '<reading>easy, go, easy, go!</reading>' — <reading>いそぐ</reading> — sprinting the whole way down before the enormous bell finishes its first toll.

issho-ni.meaning_mnemonic: The goat's one-contestant show attracts a crowd of hopefuls, but she won't compete against them — she drags them all onto the <kanji>one</kanji> stage at once and calls it a single unified act. There's no more soloist, only one crowded platform, everyone lumped together under her name.
issho-ni.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the whole team squeezes onto one bench, knee to knee, yelling <reading>いっしょに</reading> — which the coach mishears as <reading>a show, knee!</reading> — but that tangled pile-up on one bench is exactly the point: everyone crammed in together.

isu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a heavy wooden seat with a tall carved back, and look closely — the carving is shaped exactly like a swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms flung wide the way it always reaches. Those flung-out arms become the armrests, the swaddling becomes the seat, and the whole piece of furniture is built around that one reaching shape: a chair.
isu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 椅 read い, plus 子 read す, gives you <reading>いす</reading>.

itadakimasu.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountaintop vending machine, a hiker finally reaches the summit and presses both palms flat together before tearing into the rice ball — a silent thanks to whoever grew the rice and carried it up that slope. Only after that press of palms does the first bite happen. Press, then bite: let's eat, thanks for the food.
itadakimasu.reading_mnemonic: Written exactly as it sounds — read the kana straight through and you get 「<reading>いただきます</reading>」.

itai.meaning_mnemonic: Somewhere on the steep mountain trail, a hiker stubs bare toes on the vending machine's metal base and folds instantly in half, hopping in a tight circle with both hands clamped around the foot, teeth gritted, unable to manage a single word except the one that means painful.
itai.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the sliding door snags his necktie just as he steps through, yanking him back against the onigiri shelf. He yelps 「<reading>いたい</reading>」, wrestling the <reading>tie</reading> free from the still-beeping door, no dignity left in the fluorescent glare.

itsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat sits under the enormous bell all day. It keeps asking いつ, itchy to know exactly <vocabulary>when</vocabulary> the bell will ring.

itsuka.meaning_mnemonic: Watch the <kanji>sun</kanji> rise <kanji>five</kanji> separate times over the konbini roof, and you have counted <vocabulary>five days</vocabulary>.

itsumo.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine has cats sprawled on every mossy step, and no matter which morning you visit, rain, festival day, ordinary Tuesday, they are always there in the exact same spots, as if none of them ever left at all.
itsumo.reading_mnemonic: いつも is plain kana, read and written exactly as <reading>いつも</reading>, with nothing to derive.

itsutsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>five</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>five things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
itsutsu.reading_mnemonic: The mascot at Sei's school is so <reading>itchy</reading> that five spots erupt down its costume. That's exactly <vocabulary>five things</vocabulary> the coach counts as <reading>いつつ</reading> in his logbook.

ittekimasu.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi bursts out of his konbini mid-shift, legs split wide in that stride you know as <kanji>go</kanji> — off to restock from the vending machine down the road. He shouts through the door that he's <kanji>going</kanji>, but the shout carries a promise to come right back. That's what you say the instant you're the one walking out.
ittekimasu.reading_mnemonic: Koichi ducks out of his konbini mid-shift, the till still beeping, and nearly eats the shop key he was locking up with. He spits it into a clump of shrine-cat moss on the mat and yells <reading>eat-teh-key-muss</reading>, which is exactly the sound of <reading>いってきます</reading>.

iu-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stone mouth carved into the old bell pushes out one neat stacked layer of speech every time a cat brushes past it, like it's reading off a single fixed line it memorized decades ago. It never adds anything, never explains, it just delivers that one word again and again. That single fixed word, pushed out and done, is what it means to <kanji>say</kanji> something.
iu-v.reading_mnemonic: Ichi the shrine cat only ever meows one clipped sound, a flat <reading>ee-oo</reading> that the cats around the bell have started imitating, and that sound is exactly <reading>いう</reading>.

ji-oclock.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till clock is nothing but that same sun-in-a-window face from the shrine, glowing under fluorescent lights instead of sky. The beeping till freezes the instant the hand lands square on a number, and Koichi calls out that exact moment — not a stretch of <kanji>time</kanji>, just the single instant the sun-face points to.
ji-oclock.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 時 was already taught as <reading>じ</reading>, and that's exactly the reading this word keeps, unchanged.

jibun-time.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>minute</kanji> sliced off of <kanji>time</kanji> tells you exactly what <vocabulary>time (of day)</vocabulary> it is.

jibun.meaning_mnemonic: The woodcutter is dividing the day's woodpile, and the sword is doing the arithmetic. Every log comes down into two leaning <kanji>parts</kanji>: one part for the village, one part he plants his boot on. The sword <kanji>understands</kanji> the rule immediately and never miscounts — the half with a boot on it is oneself.
jibun.reading_mnemonic: 自 gives じ and 分 gives ぶん, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>じぶん</reading>.
jibun.description: It points at whoever is speaking or being talked about, so it comes out as myself, yourself, or herself depending on the sentence. In casual speech it also works as a plain, slightly blunt word for I.

jikan-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, the sun crawls across the sky the way it does at the shrine, ticking off <kanji>hours</kanji> like a clock reflected in the water. Between one splash of laundry and the next, the gate-shaped gap of caught sunlight marks the <kanji>interval</kanji> you were gone, and you realize you've lost several whole hours just watching the current.
jikan-counter.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 時（じ）plus 間（かん）simply combine, giving you <reading>じかん</reading> straight from readings you already know.

jikan.meaning_mnemonic: How much <kanji>time</kanji> sits in the <kanji>between</kanji> of two moments is exactly <vocabulary>time / hours</vocabulary>.

jisho.meaning_mnemonic: Long after the <kanji>write</kanji> sun has sunk below your notebook and your hand is still moving on its own from that daily ritual, the pile of scribbled pages has grown so thick it needs its own spine. You bind the whole towering stack into one fat volume you flip through every time you're stuck on a word — a book that exists only to make writing easier: a dictionary.
jisho.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from its kanji: 辞 read じ plus 書 read しょ give <reading>じしょ</reading>.

jitensha.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the overhead cart shape — axle through the center, wheels braced on either side, the same boxy frame you already know as a <kanji>vehicle</kanji> — comes loose from its cart body and rolls itself up the mossy steps on just its two wheels, each one spinning through the same dizzy <kanji>revolve</kanji> as before, wobbling past the enormous bell while cats scatter. No engine, no rails, just those wheels pedaling themselves uphill: a bicycle.
jitensha.reading_mnemonic: A cat at Grandma Kane's shrine watches the wheels totter past the bell and yowls, 'jitters... shaa!' as they nearly tip into the moss. That startled <reading>jitters-sha</reading> cry is exactly how you say bicycle: <reading>じてんしゃ</reading>.

jouzu.meaning_mnemonic: That <kanji>hand</kanji> you'd normally hold out for a shake instead shoots straight <kanji>up</kanji>, higher than everyone else's, catching every ball a street juggler throws without even glancing at it. The crowd realizes this hand belongs to someone truly skillful — good at whatever it touches.
jouzu.reading_mnemonic: At the edge of the mountain trail, a keeper named <reading>Joe's zoo</reading> trains a monkey to pour tea without spilling a drop. Hikers stop climbing just to watch, murmuring 「<reading>じょうず</reading>」 every single time the cup fills clean to the brim.
jouzu.description: Used to praise someone else's skill — saying this about your own ability comes across as boastful, so speakers reach for a different word when the skill being described is their own.

jugyou.meaning_mnemonic: Picture Sei's school clanging its bell for third period. Every desk snaps upright at once, notebooks flip open, and forty pens move in the same held breath as the teacher starts writing on the board — that shared, synchronized scramble to take down everything before the bell rings again is exactly a class, a lesson.
jugyou.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 授 as じゅ plus 業 as ぎょう gives you <reading>じゅぎょう</reading>.

junbi-suru.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a bee named June spends the whole climb before the cold sets in — stocking the hive, patching every gap, checking the vending machine at the top for one last snack. Getting everything lined up and ready before the real thing starts is exactly what to prepare means.
junbi-suru.reading_mnemonic: Nothing irregular here: 準 is じゅん, 備 is び, plus する, and the whole word reads <reading>じゅんびする</reading>.

juu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ten</kanji> kanji is simply the <vocabulary>ten</vocabulary> word. There is one mark and one meaning, nothing extra to remember.

juusho.meaning_mnemonic: A courier at the riverbank keeps miscounting his stack of parcels, so he starts tying each one to a labeled post driven into the bank, one per house upstream where a family has settled in to <kanji>dwell</kanji>, until every home along the water has its own numbered post marking the exact <kanji>place</kanji> its mail belongs — its address.
juusho.reading_mnemonic: On the riverbank, the courier hollers a <reading>zoo show</reading> parade of names through his megaphone before untying the last parcel — the post reads 「<reading>じゅうしょ</reading>」, the address stamped in waterproof ink, and off he paddles.

kaban.meaning_mnemonic: After the last bell at Sei's school, someone crams gym shoes, dog-eared workbooks, and a crumpled umbrella into one straining canvas sack, then wrestles the zipper shut over the bulge as it clears the sports field. That overstuffed sack slung over a shoulder is just a bag doing its job.
kaban.reading_mnemonic: <reading>かばん</reading> is plain kana, written exactly as it sounds, no kanji reading to derive here.

kado.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini sits right on the corner, and a delivery van cuts the turn too sharp. It clips the onigiri shelf through the window, spins once, and wedges itself nose-first into the exact corner of the building — where it stays, blocking the corner entrance for the rest of the shift.
kado.reading_mnemonic: The van's <reading>car door</reading> pops open on impact and won't shut again — it hangs there at the corner of the konbini like a broken wing. Koichi just tapes a sign to it: this is the corner now. That crumpled car door is exactly how you remember <reading>かど</reading>.

kaeru-change.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a courier frog named Kaera swaps one basket for another on every crossing — rice one way, laundry the other, never both at once. She doesn't just move things, she <kanji>changes</kanji> what's in someone else's hands entirely. That deliberate swap is what the word teaches: something changes because someone changed it.
kaeru-change.reading_mnemonic: Kaera the frog announces each swap with a croak that sounds like <reading>かえる</reading> — the vendors nearby just call her <reading>Kaera</reading>, and the name stuck to the sound itself.
kaeru-change.description: This is the transitive verb — you change something (someone changes their mind, changes the schedule), always with an object. There's a separate intransitive partner meaning something changes on its own; that one takes a different reading, so don't reach for this word when nothing did the changing.

kaeru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The same weary traveler from 帰's story finally reaches the little house, drops the walking stick on the step, and collapses through the door without even taking off his shoes. That homeward pull was never about the walking — it's the whole shape of <kanji>return</kanji>, and once it starts pulling, stopping halfway was never on offer.
kaeru-v.reading_mnemonic: 帰 already supplies かえ here and る supplies る, so return home comes out as <reading>かえる</reading> — the same reading you learned for 帰, just running straight into the verb ending.

kaesu.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the many cats steals an offering plate from beneath the enormous bell, but the mossy steps make for a terrible getaway. Guilt, or maybe just clumsiness, wins out, and by dawn the cat has quietly carried the plate all the way back to the exact spot it took it from.
kaesu.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat flings a fish bone past the enormous bell, and every time it sails back into her paw the bell gives one clean "<reading>kay-essu</reading>" clang. That clang is <reading>かえす</reading>, the sound of something coming right back to where it started.

kagaku.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>study</kanji> canopy over the swaddled child is stacked with scribbled diagrams, but tonight he isn't reading them — he wires two batteries to a fork and dunks it in a puddle by the riverbank, just to see the duck jump. Poking the world until it reacts, then writing down what happened, is exactly what grows under that roof in the <kanji>department</kanji>: science.
kagaku.reading_mnemonic: Take the kanji in written order and the reading follows: 科 as か, then 学 as がく, giving <reading>かがく</reading>.

kagetsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the caretaker never repaints the mossy steps one moon-turn at a time. He waits, letting several full turns of the <kanji>month</kanji> stack up unnoticed among the cats, then tallies the whole stretch off in a single breath before finally ringing the bell.
kagetsu.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cats have grown <reading>cagey</reading> about the caretaker's tenure, counting his moon-turns in murmurs of <reading>かげつ</reading> each time another stretch gets added to his tally before the bell ever rings.

kagi.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail is, inexplicably, padlocked. A hiker pats down every pocket of their khaki trousers, harder and harder, until deep in the last one something small and metal turns up — the only thing standing between them and a can of tea: the key that finally opens the lock.
kagi.reading_mnemonic: The hiker digs through <reading>khaki</reading> pocket after khaki pocket, patting each one flat, until the last gives up a small metal shape with a jingle. That frantic pocket search is <reading>かぎ</reading> — the key that finally unlocks the padlock chaining the vending machine shut.
kagi.description: In Japanese, 鍵 covers both the physical key and the lock it opens — context decides which one is meant, where English normally reaches for two separate words.

kai-floor.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a vending machine bolted to the mountain trail, one machine bolted onto every single <kanji>storey</kanji> as hikers climb. They count out loud passing each one: first machine, second, third, all the way to the summit. By the top nobody's counting mountains anymore — they're counting floors (counter), one per machine.
kai-floor.reading_mnemonic: 階 is a single-kanji word, so the reading you already learned for that kanji is the whole word: <reading>かい</reading>.

kai-times.meaning_mnemonic: A hamster spins its wheel in tight, dizzying circles while its keeper stands by with a clicker, tallying each lap out loud. Nobody cares how far the hamster actually traveled — only how many circuits it completed, because that count is the only thing anyone bothered measuring: times, plain and simple.
kai-times.reading_mnemonic: 回 keeps the reading you already learned for the kanji itself, carried straight through: <reading>かい</reading>.

kaidan.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail swaps its steep dirt slope for a perfectly cut staircase overnight, one vending machine still stranded at the very top like nothing changed. Climbers now count each step aloud by <kanji>storey</kanji>, waiting for a <kanji>grade</kanji>, relieved someone finally built proper stairs instead of a slope.
kaidan.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 階 read かい, plus 段 read だん, which gives <reading>かいだん</reading>.

kaigi.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the teachers get summoned into the echoing hallway every Friday, and nobody wants to go. The moment the doors seal shut, someone always groans one flat, defeated "geez." That groan is the whole room's opinion of the <kanji>meet</kanji>ing they're now stuck in.
kaigi.reading_mnemonic: You already know both halves: 会 is かい and 議 is ぎ, so they snap together as <reading>かいぎ</reading>.

kaimono-suru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>buy</kanji> reach — cowrie shell out, slid across the counter — doesn't stop at one purchase. Basket after basket, shell after shell, the hand keeps reaching, sliding, reaching again, aisle after aisle, until the counter is buried under shells and every lumpy unlabeled <kanji>thing</kanji> from the lost-and-found bin. That endless string of buying, one purchase chasing the next with no end in sight, is what it means to shop.
kaimono-suru.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 買 read か, plus い, plus 物 read もの, plus す, plus る, gives <reading>かいものする</reading>.

kaimono.meaning_mnemonic: You walk into Koichi's konbini planning to grab one thing, but the cowrie shell in your hand won't stop moving — you <kanji>buy</kanji> the onigiri, then the drink, then the umbrella by the door, sliding shell after shell across the till until your arms are full of bags. That endless chain of buying, one <kanji>thing</kanji> after another, is shopping.
kaimono.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches above Koichi's konbini, bags overflowing, screeching <reading>かいもの</reading> — it lands on your ear like <reading>kie, moan, oh</reading>, her call every time she swoops down to buy one more thing.

kaisha.meaning_mnemonic: The landlord insists the view improves productivity, so the office gets hauled up the steep mountain trail — desks wedged between boulders, the printer jamming two switchbacks from the top. The boss holds the <kanji>meet</kanji>ing by the vending machine, tapping his coffee like a whiteboard. A hiker asks if this is really a company. It is.
kaisha.reading_mnemonic: 会（かい）＋社（しゃ）combine directly into <reading>かいしゃ</reading>.

kaishain.meaning_mnemonic: Every floor the elevator stops at, the same tired figure in a grey suit steps on to <kanji>meet</kanji> whoever is waiting, straightens a laminated badge on a lanyard, staples one form, and steps off two floors later to do it all again. Nobody remembers his name, only his badge and his sigh. That endless loop of suit, badge, and paperwork is exactly what the word means: company <kanji>employee</kanji>.
kaishain.reading_mnemonic: His badge, half-covered by his tie, reads <reading>Kai Shain</reading> in blocky letters — no one at the company can pronounce it right, but everyone recognizes that a <reading>かいしゃいん</reading> like him has been riding this elevator since it was installed.

kakeru-call.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the ancient payphone by the door refuses to connect unless you shout the right word into the receiver before dialing. Everyone in line has learned the trick by now: say it loud, then the call goes through. Mumble it, and the line just stays dead — you have to properly make the call.
kakeru-call.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so there is nothing to decode — just read <reading>かける</reading> straight through and that is the whole reading.

kaku.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at your desk the sun sinks below your notebook exactly like it always does, and the instant its last light fades your hand starts moving on its own, filling line after line in the dark with no lamp to help. That daily blackout scribbling, repeated night after night, is the whole ritual of learning to <kanji>write</kanji>.
kaku.reading_mnemonic: Perched on the power line above Koichi's konbini, Kaa the crow burns through a stack of receipt paper with tiny flame-puffs, scorching every sheet into a <reading>khaki</reading> brown before it hits the ground. She calls the color <reading>かく</reading>, insists it counts as her handwriting, and refuses to use ink like everyone else.

kamera.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist raises a boxy black gadget with a glass eye at the enormous bell and shouts the thing's own name at it. The flash pops, every cat on the mossy steps freezes mid-leap, and the little screen lights up with the shot: a camera, catching cats that never agreed to sit still.
kamera.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, no kanji to decode — just say what you see: <reading>カメラ</reading>.

kami-hair.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the resident cats leaps onto a visitor's shoulders and burrows straight into the long dark strands hanging past her collar, kneading and refusing to leave. Grandma Kane just laughs, ringing the mossy steps clean, and says the cat has finally found the hair it always wanted to nest in.
kami-hair.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane calls that shrine cat <reading>Cami</reading>, and Cami spends every visit nesting in the same visitor's <reading>かみ</reading>, purring against her scalp. Grandma Kane rings the enormous bell to shoo her off, but Cami just digs deeper into the かみ and refuses to move.

kami-paper.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats leap along the mossy steps and swat every fortune slip off the branches, until by dusk the ground is drifted white with thin square sheets — not snow, just fallen <kanji>paper</kanji>, blanketing the whole shrine before Grandma Kane can ring the bell.
kami-paper.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches a cat pawing through the drifted fortune slips and snaps, come, me! — meaning drop it and follow her to the shrine office. <reading>かみ</reading> is that snap: <reading>come-me</reading>, aimed at a cat sitting on a pile of shrine paper.

kanashii.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the cats knocks the rope loose from the enormous bell, and it stops ringing altogether. The cats line up on the mossy steps and stare at the dead bell like mourners at a funeral, not one of them moving. That flat, drawn-out stillness is what sad means here.
kanashii.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sighs over the silenced bell, <reading>kahh, nuh, sheesh</reading> — nearly the sound of <reading>かなしい</reading> itself, as if the whole shrine were groaning out the word for sad.

kanban.meaning_mnemonic: A washed-up <kanji>plank</kanji> keeps drifting back to the same spot on the riverbank no matter how far downstream the current drags it, until someone finally hauls it out, props it upright in the mud, and nails a warning to it. Within a week every angler on the bank reads it before casting a line — the plank has become the riverbank's one official signboard.
kanban.reading_mnemonic: Anglers just call the plank <reading>かんばん</reading>, shorthand born from an old fisherman grumbling <reading>'can ban'</reading> fishing here since the current keeps wrecking his line, and the name outlasted his complaint by years.

kangaeru.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports field, the visiting kangaroo mascot stops mid-hop and just stands there, chin dipped, replaying the coach's instructions before committing to a single bounce. It refuses to move again until it has turned the play over enough times to be sure. Working something out fully before acting on it is what it means to think something through.
kangaeru.reading_mnemonic: The mascot pauses so long that the crowd starts chanting <reading>かんがえる</reading>, kan-ga-eh-ru, which to the visiting parents sounds exactly like <reading>kangaroo</reading> — and it really is one, still working through the play call before it dares to jump.
kangaeru.description: 考える describes working through a problem step by step — reasoning, weighing, deciding — rather than a passing feeling or fleeting thought. Reach for this one when actual mental effort is involved.

kanji-word.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's lone vending machine, every button is carved with dense, stroke-packed marks instead of pictures — no plain lines anywhere, just rows of intricate symbols crammed into a space built for a simple picture. Whatever you call that whole crowded family of written characters, this word is it: kanji.
kanji-word.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 漢 read かん, plus 字 read じ, gives <reading>かんじ</reading>.

kanojo.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi points across the konbini at the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> restocking the onigiri shelf, arm sweeping the row into place. <kanji>He</kanji> doesn't explain, just tilts his head and grins: that's the one he's been talking about all week. You don't need more than that look to know she's his girlfriend, and now you know who she is too.
kanojo.reading_mnemonic: 彼 gives かの and 女 gives じょ, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>かのじょ</reading>.

kao.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat named Botan leaps onto the offering bowl and stares down at the water pooled inside it, hunting the strange animal staring back. It takes three tail-lashes before Botan realizes the intruder blinks whenever she blinks — it is her own face, staring up out of the water.
kao.reading_mnemonic: A cow wanders into Grandma Kane's shrine and butts the shrine bell aside just to see what's cooking. The monk grabs the <reading>cow</reading> by the horns and yells right into its <reading>かお</reading> — but its blank face never changes.

karada.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, the gym teacher lines everyone up and makes them stretch every part at once — arms, legs, back, neck — until the whole trembling row moves as a single shuddering unit. She points down the line and names it plainly: the <kanji>body</kanji>, all of it, working together.
karada.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher barks that this drill works the whole <reading>car, duh</reading> — she means the whole <reading>からだ</reading>, obviously, and nobody laughs because she's still holding the whistle. からだ, she repeats, jabbing a finger at each kid's ribs to prove her point.

karai.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker reaches the vending machine improbably parked at the top of the mountain trail and buys the only can left. The first sip is a wall of salt, like drinking the ocean. Two steps later the chili catches up and torches the back of her throat. She sits down hard on a rock, fanning her mouth. That drink was spicy, and it was salty.
karai.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a jeep pulls alongside the hiker, and the driver leans out and offers her a ride: <reading>car ride</reading>, he calls, grinning around a mouthful of chili peppers. That's the sound of <reading>からい</reading>, spicy, salty.
karai.description: This word covers two distinct sensations English keeps separate — spicy-hot (a chili pepper) and salty (over-salted soup). Which one a speaker means comes entirely from context, not from the word itself.

kare.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>he</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>he / boyfriend</vocabulary> are exactly the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
kare.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker points at a shape trudging up and asks <reading>かれ</reading>. It sounds just like <reading>car, eh</reading>, and she means only the <vocabulary>he / boyfriend</vocabulary> who promised to meet her there.

kariru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, you forgot your umbrella and it's pouring. The priest keeps a bin of spares by the mossy steps and lets you take one, no questions, as long as you understand it's not a gift — you're borrowing it, and it goes back tomorrow.
kariru.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the temple cats treats a fallen toy <reading>car</reading> like the greatest find ever, dragging it around all day — but by evening it always drops it back on the steps, because even a cat instinctively knows how to <reading>かりる</reading>.

karui.meaning_mnemonic: Sei sprints across the sports field hauling what should be a heavy gym bag, except someone swapped the weights inside for empty juice cartons overnight. He practically floats down the track, arms pumping, feet barely tapping the ground between strides: light, light, light, he could carry ten of these.
karui.reading_mnemonic: Cara chases Sei down the echoing school hallway with the swapped-out gym bag and can't believe how little it weighs on her shoulder. <reading>Cara</reading>, we're winning this race, she yells back at him, we're so <reading>かるい</reading> today, かるい as air.

kasa.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the sky cracks open and dumps a whole second river down onto the first one. A fisherman yanks a bent bamboo frame out of his tackle box, stretches waxed paper across the ribs, and pops it open over his head just before he's soaked through — that bent, stretched frame is an umbrella.
kasa.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the rain arrives as one long <reading>cascade</reading> — clip off just the front half, said fast, and you get <reading>かさ</reading>, the umbrella the fisherman snaps open to survive it.

kasu.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, everyone forgets a pencil at some point, and there's always one kid by the window who has extras. She holds one out without a word, already expecting it back before the bell rings — that's exactly what it feels like to lend something.
kasu.reading_mnemonic: At school, Sei <reading>casts</reading> a glance at her spare pencil, then slides it across the desk to a friend who forgot theirs, saying '<reading>かす</reading>' — a quick loan she fully expects back by the end of class.

kata-person.meaning_mnemonic: A customs officer refuses to ever say the word "<kanji>person</kanji>" — it's beneath the dignity of his line. Instead he stamps each passport with a flourish and announces "next, esteemed guest," bowing a fraction lower for the elderly and exactly the same for everyone else. That stiff, formal way of naming someone is the word itself.
kata-person.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tailor sets up shop by the onigiri shelf, snipping fabric with a huge <reading>cutter</reading>. Every customer who walks in gets bowed to and called "esteemed <reading>かた</reading>" before he measures their shoulders for a suit nobody asked for.
kata-person.description: As "person," 方 is a polite, formal register word — used to respectfully describe someone else (a customer, a stranger, an elder), not to refer to yourself or to talk casually about friends.

katakana.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the exhausted night clerk restocks imported snacks and refuses to write in curves. Every foreign product label gets stamped out in blocky, straight-edged letters, like they were sliced with a paper cutter instead of drawn by hand. That sharp, angular script reserved just for foreign words is katakana.
katakana.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds, 「<reading>カタカナ</reading>」.

kau-v.meaning_mnemonic: You spot something you want and reach for the cowrie shell that's stood in for money since forever, laying it flat on the counter and sliding it across before you can lose your nerve. Shell handed over, prize now in your other hand — that whole exchange, shell for object, is exactly what it means to <kanji>buy</kanji>.
kau-v.reading_mnemonic: Outside Koichi's konbini, Kaa the fire-breathing crow hops from the power line to the beeping till and pecks a cowrie shell into the slot. A puff of flame singes the onigiri shelf. She lets out a long <reading>caw</reading>, which is exactly the sound of <reading>かう</reading>.

kawa-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, you crouch to rinse your hands and watch three currents braid together exactly the way you learned to see them: three flowing lines side by side. Cup your palms and the water doesn't care about the drawing — it just runs, cold and fast, over your fingers. That current has a name: <kanji>river</kanji>.
kawa-v.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Koichi wades in to save a floating onigiri wrapper and the current yanks his sandal off. He hops on one foot yelling '<reading>kah-wah</reading>!' at the water, and that yelp is <reading>かわ</reading>, the word for the current that just robbed him.

kawaii.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stray kitten totters down the mossy steps, misjudges the very last one, and rolls the rest of the way, ending up flat on its back among the resident cats with all four paws in the air. Nobody laughs. Nobody could. It is somehow the single cutest thing that has ever happened on those steps.
kawaii.reading_mnemonic: かわいい is already exactly what it sounds like — kana straight through, with no kanji hiding a different pronunciation underneath, so the word you say and the word you read are simply 「<reading>かわいい</reading>」.

kawaru.meaning_mnemonic: You watch an intersection from the corner for a full minute: the light is red, then amber, then green, then back to red, cars stopping and starting each time. Nothing about the pole itself moves, yet everything it signals is different every time you look. That shifting-in-place is the meaning: to <kanji>change</kanji>.
kawaru.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports field, someone drives a tiny toy car through a puddle shaped exactly like a <reading>car wash</reading>, and it rolls out a completely different color than it went in. Sei blinks at the repainted car and mutters that everything on this field has just <reading>かわる</reading>, changed.

kayoubi.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Fire</kanji> catches on the next <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> it can reach and burns straight through it, leaving <vocabulary>Tuesday</vocabulary> scorched.

kaze-cold.meaning_mnemonic: Sei collapses face-down on the school field after the last sprint of practice, soaked in sweat. A cold wind knifes across the grass the instant she stops moving, and by evening she's shivering under three blankets with a raw throat and a fever — a cold caught in one gust of <kanji>wind</kanji>.
kaze-cold.reading_mnemonic: Sei's coach wraps her scraped knee in gauze at the edge of the field, and the wind — <reading>かぜ</reading> — snatches the loose end and flaps it like a flag. She hisses '<reading>gauze</reading>' through her teeth, kaze, the same wind that left her sick the next morning.
kaze-cold.description: 風邪 is written with the same character as 風, 'wind' — colds were traditionally believed to be carried in on a bad wind, which is also why the everyday expression for catching a cold literally means 'to be hit by wind.'

kaze-wind.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the automatic door sticks open and a sudden gust roars in, sending the entire onigiri shelf toppling and every plastic bag in the store leaping off its hook at once. He just stands at the till, beeping through the chaos, muttering that it's too much <kanji>wind</kanji> for one small door.
