kaze-wind.reading_mnemonic: Koichi swears the same draft <reading>causes</reading> the shelf to fall every single morning, and he's taken to yelling <reading>かぜ</reading> at the door like it's a curse word, until the whole konbini staff starts shouting it whenever a gust rolls through.

kazoku.meaning_mnemonic: Zookeeper Zoe stopped filing her animals by species years ago. Now every enclosure is sorted by family: otters piled into one <kanji>house</kanji>, meerkats packed into one den, and the daily headcount sheet has only one column, because at her zoo the only unit that ever matters is the whole family showing up together.
kazoku.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 家 read か, plus 族 read ぞく, gives <reading>かぞく</reading>.

keikan.meaning_mnemonic: Someone's been dumping fish traps along the riverbank at night, and every trap turns up empty by morning except the one time a figure in a sharp uniform wades in at dawn, hauls the traps out by hand, and confiscates the lot without a word. That quiet, uniformed figure standing ankle-deep in river mud is exactly what the word means: police officer.
keikan.reading_mnemonic: 警 gives けい and 官 gives かん, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>けいかん</reading>.

keitai.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the new clerk Kei ties his phone to his belt with butcher's string before every shift, certain he won't survive the beeping till without it. By closing time the string has looped him to the register three times over, and everyone has stopped calling it a phone — it's just his mobile phone now.
keitai.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 携 as けい plus 帯 as たい gives you <reading>けいたい</reading>.

kekkon-suru.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, a hiker collapses to one knee in front of the lone vending machine, holds up a coin like a ring, and asks it to supply him forever. The machine accepts, clunking out two canned coffees like vows exchanged. That absurd, binding transaction at the top of the mountain is what it means to marry.
kekkon-suru.reading_mnemonic: 結 read けっ plus 婚 read こん plus す plus る is simply <reading>けっこんする</reading>.

kesu.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the summit vending machine's fluorescent panel flickers and dies in a gust of wind at the exact moment a hiker rubs yesterday's chalk arrow off the rock beside it with his thumb. Bulb dark, chalk gone, both within the same breath of wind — that's the meaning: to turn off, to erase.
kesu.reading_mnemonic: The ranger who patrols the mountain trail is named Kesu, and hikers joke that wherever he walks, lights die and marks vanish behind him. Whisper <reading>けす</reading> and picture him snapping his equipment <reading>case</reading> shut — every switch he touches goes dark, every chalk line under his boot disappears.

ki-tree-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one trunk splits the mossy steps clean in half, roots shoving down into the stone and branches spreading wide over the enormous bell. Cats scatter into its shade every afternoon. There's no need to explain what's growing there — trunk, roots, branches, unmistakably a <kanji>tree</kanji>.
ki-tree-v.reading_mnemonic: 木 keeps the same reading you already learned for the character itself — <reading>き</reading>, the same <reading>key</reading> sound, home to Kiki the tree spirit.

kibun.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail the woodcutter's sword drops a log into two leaning <kanji>parts</kanji>, and a curl of warm steam lifts out of the fresh cut. He leans in and sniffs it. Sulky pine today. That rising <kanji>spirit</kanji> off the split wood is the log's mood, and it sets his feeling for the whole afternoon.
kibun.reading_mnemonic: 気 hands over its usual き and 分 its ぶん, so nothing bends here: the word is read <reading>きぶん</reading>.
kibun.description: 気分 covers your general mood or how you feel physically — good, bad, off — rather than an emotion aimed at a particular person or thing. Saying your 気分 is bad most often means you feel unwell.

kiiro.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till jams and won't stop printing. Receipt after receipt spools out under the fluorescent lights, each one dyed a violent, glowing <kanji>color</kanji>, until the whole counter disappears under a drift taller than the onigiri shelf — every scrap of it the exact same yellow.
kiiro.reading_mnemonic: A canary lands on Koichi's till and pecks at the same <reading>key</reading> over and over, then hops along the counter in a tidy <reading>row</reading> of yellow feathers — key, row, <reading>きいろ</reading> — and won't budge until someone finally calls it by that color.

kikoeru.meaning_mnemonic: Your ear is still pressed against that cold gate from before, straining for whispers — except this time you don't have to strain. The sound comes straight through the wood on its own: footsteps, a slammed door, someone calling your name, all loud enough to reach you without you having to <kanji>hear</kanji> for it. When sound arrives like that, unbidden, it's simply audible.
kikoeru.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, Kiki the tree spirit lives in the old cedar beside the vending machine. A hiker stops to buy a drink. The wind hits the branches and she giggles <reading>Key, Koeru</reading>, and it <reading>きこえる</reading> even over the machine's hum; he nearly drops his canned coffee.

kiku-v.meaning_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit presses her ear against the gate of the shrine one more night, straining to catch the whispers behind it. But tonight she can't just stay quiet about it — she raps on the wood and demands to know what they're saying. Pressing an ear to a gate gets you two things: you listen, and eventually you have to <kanji>ask</kanji>.
kiku-v.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit giggles every time the wind <reading>kicks</reading> up, which is the only signal she needs to start <reading>きく</reading>ing at the gate again.

kimi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>mister</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>you (familiar)</vocabulary> are exactly the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
kimi.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a stranger jabs a finger at your chest and barks <reading>きみ</reading>, which lands like <reading>key, me</reading>. He means exactly the <vocabulary>you (familiar)</vocabulary> standing in front of him, nobody else in the store.

kimochi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>spirit</kanji> puffing off your rice bowl never behaves the same way twice — some mornings it billows thick and warm, curling lazily upward; other mornings it comes out thin and jagged, quick to vanish. Whatever shape that rising wisp takes right now is exactly what you <kanji>hold</kanji> inside: your feeling, your mood.
kimochi.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 気 read き, plus 持 read も, plus ち, gives <reading>きもち</reading>.

kinou.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>day</kanji> that already slipped past you, gone before you could grab it, is <vocabulary>yesterday</vocabulary>.
kinou.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank someone fishes a soggy calendar page out of the water and reads <reading>きのう</reading> off it, sounding like a rusty <reading>key</reading> to a day already washed downstream, and that lost page is <vocabulary>yesterday</vocabulary>.

kinyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> finally pays out in solid <kanji>gold</kanji>, and that payday is <vocabulary>Friday</vocabulary>.

kippu.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank crossing, the ferryman won't push off until every passenger hands him a small paper stub, <kanji>cut</kanji> cleanly in half at the perforation. No stub, no ride across — that torn scrap clutched in your hand is the ticket.
kippu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the ferryman drops each torn stub into a rusty tin he calls his '<reading>key pool</reading>,' clinking it in with a grin and calling out '<reading>きっぷ</reading>, another one for the pile' before shoving off.

kirai.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till keeps beeping over the same soggy egg sandwich nobody buys. A customer picks it up, wrinkles her nose, and shoves it back onto the shelf for the third time today. The clerk sighs and admits the whole town has quietly decided this sandwich is disliked.
kirai.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane holds up a shrine key and swears it opens the bell tower, but it's obviously the wrong one — a <reading>key lie</reading> if she's ever told one. The cats hiss at her fib. Everyone at the shrine mutters 「<reading>きらい</reading>」 about that key, because nobody trusts a liar's key twice.

kirei.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one battered vending machine stands against the mist — and someone climbs all the way up every single morning just to wipe its dusty glass front until it gleams, though nobody has ever explained why. Spotless glass, spotless coin slot, spotless everything, on a trail where nothing else is. That is pretty / clean.
kirei.reading_mnemonic: きれい is written and read exactly as it looks, straight kana with no hidden reading to derive — just remember 「<reading>きれい</reading>」 as is.

kiru-cut.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a fallen vine blocks the only path to the vending machine at the top. Someone has already sliced clean through it in one motion — the two halves swing apart like saloon doors — and past the gap, the thirsty hikers finally reach the machine. The vine had to be <kanji>cut</kanji> before anyone could pass.
kiru-cut.reading_mnemonic: Kiroo the kangaroo guards that same mountain vine. When a hiker gets close, she rears back and yells '<reading>KEY-roo</reading>!' before one clean kick slices the vine in half — it is her signature move, and hikers now mutter <reading>きる</reading> to themselves before every cut, copying the kangaroo's battle cry.

kiru-wear.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the gym locker room has one communal hoodie that never gets folded — it just gets pulled straight over whoever walks in first, backwards, arms flailing through the wrong holes. By the time the whistle blows, someone is standing there with the top half properly on, however wrong it looks underneath.
kiru-wear.reading_mnemonic: Kiroo the kangaroo also keeps a spare hoodie in Sei's locker room, and every morning she wrestles it over her head shouting '<reading>KEY-roo</reading>!' with one ear stuck in a sleeve. Students now mutter <reading>きる</reading> under their breath while dressing, copying the muffled cry from inside the hoodie.

kissaten.meaning_mnemonic: Sei ducks out of gym class through a gap in the fence and ends up in an impossibly quiet <kanji>shop</kanji> three streets over — dim lighting, one old man refolding the same newspaper over a steaming pot of <kanji>tea</kanji>, a menu of drinks nobody at school has heard of. It is a coffee shop, and gym period never felt shorter.
kissaten.reading_mnemonic: 喫（きっ）＋茶（さ）＋店（てん）combine directly into <reading>きっさてん</reading>.
kissaten.description: きっさてん usually points at an old-style Japanese coffee shop — dim, quiet, often decades-old — rather than a modern chain cafe.

kita-v.meaning_mnemonic: The two figures are still on that frozen bench, spine to spine, too stubborn to face the wind. A postman trudges by and asks which way is <kanji>north</kanji>. Neither turns around — they just jab a thumb back over the shoulder, into the gale that's been freezing them all along, and that's your answer.
kita-v.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing hallways of Sei's school, the janitor <reading>Keeter</reading> is oiling lockers when his key ring slides into a floor drain. He lies flat, arm down the grate, fishing through gum. When the keys snag, he just pants <reading>きた</reading> into the tiles.

kitanai.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone has left a bicycle half-buried in the mud, its wheels crusted brown, a plastic bag snagged on the handlebars flapping in the current. A heron lands on the seat, takes one look at the muck dripping off every spoke, and flies straight back off without touching it. Even the heron won't go near something that dirty.
kitanai.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Grandma Kane spots the mud-crusted bicycle and asks who left it there. A boy points at his friend and blurts <reading>Kit, uh, not I!</reading> — which is exactly how you say <reading>きたない</reading>, dirty.

kitte.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, beside the one improbable vending machine, a <kanji>hand</kanji> <kanji>cuts</kanji> a small sticky square from a roll and presses it flat onto the corner of an envelope before shoving the envelope into the summit mailbox — the little square that lets it travel: a postage stamp.
kitte.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker keeps licking the vending machine's sticky squares instead of buying tea, and the vendor barks <reading>quit it</reading> — she finally buys one properly, licks it once, and presses it onto her postcard: a <reading>きって</reading>.

ko-counter.meaning_mnemonic: A vending machine at the top of the mountain trail dispenses nothing but pebbles, buttons, and dice — one at a time, plink, plink, plink. A hiker feeds it coins just to watch the tiny things drop, because that machine only deals in small objects (counter), and it refuses to give you anything bigger.
ko-counter.reading_mnemonic: The hiker mutters "<reading>ko</reading>-<reading>ko</reading>-<reading>ko</reading>" every time another <reading>こ</reading> pebble clatters into the tray, counting them off one clunk at a time, her breath fogging the cold mountain air as the tray slowly fills up.

kochira.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sweeps one arm toward the shrine steps and the stranger beside her in one motion. Wherever that arm lands, path or person, is <vocabulary>this way / this person</vocabulary>.

kodomo-v.meaning_mnemonic: That swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms still flung wide from its own story, wriggles loose right in Koichi's konbini and topples half the onigiri shelf reaching for it. The till beeps in protest as a clerk calls out for whoever's kid this troublemaker belongs to — arms flailing, wrapping gone, still unmistakably a child.
kodomo-v.reading_mnemonic: This word takes 子's reading こ and adds 供's reading ども, giving 「<reading>こども</reading>」: child.

koe.meaning_mnemonic: A lone hiker stands at the edge of the mountain trail and lets out one enormous shout at the far canyon wall — not words, just raw sound thrown as hard as he can throw it. A beat later it comes back, fainter but unmistakably the same sound. That thrown, bounced-back sound, and nothing else, is what this word simply means: voice.
koe.reading_mnemonic: The hiker is named <reading>Coe, eh</reading> — that's literally how he introduces himself, flat and dragging the vowel out. So when he shouts into the canyon and the sound flies back at him a beat later, it comes back as <reading>こえ</reading>: his own voice, thrown at rock and handed right back to him unchanged.

koko.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine you stop on one mossy step and plant both feet. You thump the stone under you and mean exactly <vocabulary>here</vocabulary>, nowhere else.

kokonoka.meaning_mnemonic: Cross off <kanji>nine</kanji> boxes on the calendar, one for every <kanji>day</kanji>, and you have marked off <vocabulary>nine days</vocabulary>.

kokonotsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji still means the same nine, and adding つ turns it into <vocabulary>nine things</vocabulary>. You're counting objects now, not just naming the number.
kokonotsu.reading_mnemonic: Koichi won't ring up a sale until <reading>ここのつ</reading> <reading>coconuts</reading> are stacked beside the till. Nine dusty coconuts is his idea of a proper <vocabulary>nine things</vocabulary> display.

kokuban.meaning_mnemonic: The soot-caked village wall from the fire that turned everything <kanji>black</kanji> gets sawed down into a <kanji>plank</kanji> and hauled to school. Bolted to the front of the classroom, chalk dust just adds more soot on top of soot, so the teacher's writing surface ends up exactly the color the village already was: a blackboard.
kokuban.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 黒 read こく, plus 板 read ばん, gives <reading>こくばん</reading>.

komaru.meaning_mnemonic: You are locked out of your apartment in the rain, keys sitting in plain view on the kitchen counter through the window, phone dead, neighbor not home. You stand under the awning testing the same doorknob for the tenth time, and this exact useless loop is the meaning: to be troubled.
komaru.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a scruffy kangaroo blocks your way, its fur knotted with burrs. You crouch down and <reading>comb a roo</reading> right there on the gravel, and the line of hikers behind you groans, thoroughly <reading>こまる</reading> at the wait.

kome-v.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the mountain trail, past the last switchback, hikers find the one vending machine standing improbably at the summit. Its slots hold no soda or tea — only small bags of hard, pale grains, unwashed and uncooked. A disappointed hiker buys one anyway, shakes it like a maraca, and trudges back down still hungry: uncooked rice.
kome-v.reading_mnemonic: A hiker at the summit rattles her bag of grains and mutters '<reading>Comb</reading> through this later,' annoyed she packed the wrong snack. That mutter is exactly <reading>こめ</reading> — uncooked rice, the kind you rinse before cooking, not eat straight from the bag.

konbanwa.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi flips the konbini sign to closed at dusk, but the shrine cat slips in first, same time every night, tail curling around the onigiri shelf as the till gives its last beep. He never shoos it. He just crouches, says the one line reserved for exactly this hour, and lets it out: good evening.
konbanwa.reading_mnemonic: This one is pure kana, said exactly as it looks: <reading>こんばんは</reading> reads like "<reading>cone-bahn-wah</reading>" — sound it out and you're already saying good evening.
konbanwa.description: This greeting only works after dusk, when the sky has actually gone dark — it is not a general-purpose hello, and it is never used to say goodbye, even though it looks like it could close a conversation.

konbini.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's shop never closes, the till beeps without pause, and the onigiri shelf by the door restocks itself like clockwork at three in the morning. Someone pays a phone bill at the register while another customer photocopies a form, all before the entry chime finishes ringing. That does-everything, always-open little shop is a convenience store.
konbini.reading_mnemonic: コンビニ is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>conveni</reading>, short for convenience, and you've already said <reading>コンビニ</reading>.

kongetsu.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Now</kanji> lands on whichever lap of the <kanji>month</kanji> the moon is currently making, and that lap is <vocabulary>this month</vocabulary>.

konna.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi holds up a rice ball that got sat on and refuses to sell <vocabulary>this kind of</vocabulary> onigiri. He waves it at the shelf like evidence.

konnichiwa.meaning_mnemonic: Right at midday, Grandma Kane rings the shrine's one enormous bell and every cat on the mossy steps looks up at once. She doesn't say a word to any of them — she just nods at the sun sitting directly overhead, because this greeting only comes out when the day is that bright and that high: hello, said squarely in the afternoon.
konnichiwa.reading_mnemonic: こんにちは is plain kana, read exactly as written with no hidden readings to decode: <reading>こんにちは</reading>, pronounced like <reading>kon-nee-chee-wah</reading>.
konnichiwa.description: This greeting is tied to daylight hours — roughly late morning through early evening — and isn't the everyday word you'd say to family at home or close friends you see constantly; it's for acquaintances, strangers, and daytime encounters generally.

kono.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school you snatch up your own notebook and refuse to loosen your grip, because <vocabulary>this (+ noun)</vocabulary> only works with something actually in your hand.

konshuu.meaning_mnemonic: The moment <kanji>now</kanji> falls on is always inside one lap of the <kanji>week</kanji>, and that lap is <vocabulary>this week</vocabulary>.

koohii.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps furiously at three in the morning as a zombie-eyed customer clutches an empty paper cup, breathing out fumes so bitter the onigiri shelf seems to lean away from him. He doesn't order food. He doesn't speak. He just raises the cup, and the cashier refills it without a word: coffee.
koohii.reading_mnemonic: コーヒー is written exactly the way it sounds, straight through in kana — <reading>コーヒー</reading> — nothing here to decode, just read it aloud.

kooto.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine sells exactly one item: a stiff paper coat that unfolds like a cardboard crane. You climbed up in a t-shirt, so you feed it your last coins, unfold it, and stop shivering immediately. Up here, that stiff paper garment has one name and one job — it's your coat.
kooto.reading_mnemonic: コート is kana, so it is pronounced exactly as it looks — no kanji hiding a different sound. Read the four characters straight through and you get <reading>コート</reading>, the loanword transcription of English 'coat.'
kooto.description: コート is a loanword that also means "court," as in a tennis court — the two senses share one spelling and one sound, and only the surrounding sentence tells you whether someone is putting one on or standing on one.

koppu.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the hot-drink machine drops every order with a hollow knock — kop — straight into a plastic cup waiting below. Regulars just call the whole machine 'the koppu machine,' since that's the sound the cup makes catching the drink every single time.
koppu.reading_mnemonic: コップ is written exactly as it sounds — <reading>コップ</reading> — a katakana borrowing of the English word <reading>cup</reading>, no decoding needed.

kore.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi grabs the onigiri closest to his hand at the register and holds it straight up without even glancing at the shelf. Whatever sits right beside you is always <vocabulary>this one</vocabulary>.

kotae.meaning_mnemonic: A fisherman at the riverbank refuses to reel in anything until the river tells him something back. He shouts a question at the current, waits, and eventually a smooth stone washes up at his boots with a single word scratched into it. He pockets the stone before he even looks at the fish — to him, that scratched stone is the answer.
kotae.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman is named Kota, and every time a stone washes up he reads the word aloud, then tacks on his own tic: '<reading>Kota, eh?</reading>' Said quickly on the riverbank, that slurs into <reading>こたえ</reading> — his own name fused with the answer he just fished out.

kotaeru.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's teacher lobs a question across the sports field like a ball, slow and looping, and it takes forever to come back. But when it does, it isn't a mumble — it's one clean shout that cracks down the echoing hallway and lands exactly where it's supposed to. That single confident shout, sent back only once someone is sure of it, is what it means to answer.
kotaeru.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the kid everyone calls Kota is a hero for one reason: he's always first to shout back when the teacher lobs a question across the field. Say it fast — Kota, hero — and it flattens into <reading>こたえる</reading>, the <reading>Kota, hero</reading> whose reputation depends on never letting a question sit unanswered.

koto.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the gossip cat drags in a folded cot every evening and refuses to say a word until you're sitting on it. Only then does she report the day's <kanji>matters</kanji> — who fought, who left an offering, what toppled off the shelf — never a solid object you could hold, only something that happened.
koto.reading_mnemonic: Every night the cat pats the cot twice before she'll talk, announcing the news with a soft double knock: "<reading>こと</reading>, <reading>こと</reading>" — the same sound as tapping a <reading>cot</reading>, her signal that a matter is about to be reported.

kotoba.meaning_mnemonic: The mouth is still stacking layers of speech, but this time it doesn't stop where a single sentence would end — it keeps piling layer on layer, far past what one thought needs. That endless stack of <kanji>say</kanji> becomes an entire language, and every layer in it, taken alone, is a word.
kotoba.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's cat drags a tiny stolen <reading>coat</reading> across the shrine steps, and the temple goat trailing behind lets out one flat <reading>baa</reading> like a complaint. Coat, baa — say it fast and you get <reading>ことば</reading>, the word for word itself.

kotoshi.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever year is <kanji>now</kanji> is simply this <kanji>year</kanji> — nothing else counts as <vocabulary>this year</vocabulary>.
kotoshi.reading_mnemonic: A tailor named <reading>Coat, She</reading> sews exactly one <vocabulary>this year</vocabulary> label, stitching 「<reading>ことし</reading>」 into the collar and burning every other date.

kouban.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a lost tourist rings the enormous bell for directions, and others queue behind her, each waiting their <kanji>turn</kanji> like numbered slips from a dispenser. A patient officer steps from his booth, cats streaming past, and points down the street to the actual police box — the booth that rescues people from ringing the wrong bell.
kouban.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from its kanji: 交 read こう plus 番 read ばん give <reading>こうばん</reading>.
kouban.description: A 交番 is a small neighborhood police post, usually staffed by one or two officers, common on street corners and near stations — not the blue British police telephone box the English name might bring to mind. Locals stop by for directions about as often as for anything police-related.

kouen.meaning_mnemonic: A city block gets squeezed between an office tower and a train station, so someone covers it in grass, wedges in three benches and a rusty swing set, and leaves the gate open for pigeons and toddlers to fight over the last patch of shade. That leftover square of green boxed in by concrete is a park.
kouen.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from its kanji: 公 read こう plus 園 read えん give <reading>こうえん</reading>.

koutei.meaning_mnemonic: The same lone tree from the <kanji>school</kanji> <kanji>courtyard</kanji> is still there, except now the walls are gone — just open dirt stretching out around the trunk, kids sprinting circles around it during recess, using the roots as home base for tag. Bare ground ringing that one tree is the schoolyard.
koutei.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, restless behind the konbini register, wheels a folding <reading>table</reading> out to that dirt yard to sell onigiri at recess — the kids call it Koichi's <reading>table</reading> so often it's worn down to <reading>こうてい</reading>, the reading for schoolyard.

ku-num.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>nine (alt)</vocabulary> word point at the same idea, character for character.

kubi.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker finally reaches the summit vending machine and cranes forward so far to read the buttons that his head tips back on a long thin stalk, wobbling like it might snap clean off. Everyone behind him on the trail stares at that one stretched, straining neck.
kubi.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the trail, the hiker wedges his head into a stone <reading>cubby</reading> beside the vending machine to get a closer look, and now his <reading>くび</reading> is stuck fast in the gap. He twists his くび side to side, but the cubby holds on tight.

kuchi-v.meaning_mnemonic: That open square is still hanging there mid-yawn, exactly as you left it — nothing has been drawn inside it, because nothing needs to be. A hole with nothing inside was already the whole idea: it's just a <kanji>mouth</kanji>, caught wide open and refusing to close until you've said the word for it.
kuchi-v.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer's mouth hangs open under the buzzing lights, coughing, insisting he caught the <reading>cooties</reading> from someone's open <reading>くち</reading>. Koichi shoos him out before the till starts beeping and restocks the onigiri.

kudamono.meaning_mnemonic: After the last steep switchback of the mountain trail, a hiker collapses in front of the one vending machine improbably waiting at the top, expecting a cold drink — and finds every slot loaded with the same unlabeled <kanji>thing</kanji>: apples and oranges. Too worn out to complain, he buys one standing there. What that machine stocks at the summit is fruit.
kudamono.reading_mnemonic: Staring at the slots, the hiker <reading>could-a moaned</reading> about the missing drinks, but he's too exhausted to do more than mutter it under his breath, and that tired, flattened mutter comes out sounding just like <reading>くだもの</reading> — the fruit waiting at the top of the trail.

kumo.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine bell rings on its own one grey morning, and by the time she reaches the mossy steps, a thick grey mass has rolled in low overhead, swallowing the roofline whole and turning every cat on the steps into a silhouette. She squints up and just calls it the cloud sitting on her shrine.
kumo.reading_mnemonic: One of Grandma Kane's shrine cats, a fat grey tom the neighborhood calls Moe, sits on the mossy steps and coos up at the grey mass rolling over the bell. Regulars say he's only saying <reading>coo, Moe</reading>, but it comes out sounding exactly like <reading>くも</reading>, so that's what everyone calls the cloud too.

kurai.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's enormous bell goes silent at dusk, and the mossy shrine steps dissolve into shadow so complete you hear the cats climbing before you ever see them. You feel your way up by touch alone, one hand on stone you can't find with your eyes. That's the word for pitch-black: dark.
kurai.reading_mnemonic: A cat yowls <reading>"coo, why…"</reading> somewhere on the shrine steps — the sound that scratches itself into your head as the reading <reading>くらい</reading> — right before it vanishes completely into shadow, leaving only its voice behind.

kureru.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the curry machine glitches. Instead of dropping the packet into the bin like it does for everyone else in line, it swivels, hums, and fires a steaming pouch of curry straight into your hands — skipping every other customer, no request made, no line waited in. Nobody arranged it. Something simply gave itself to you.
kureru.reading_mnemonic: くれる is pure kana — no kanji to decode — so just sound out <reading>くれる</reading> as the curry machine's hiss: say <reading>curry-roo</reading> fast and you have it exactly right.
kureru.description: This verb only works when the giving benefits you or your in-group — someone does something for your side. A different verb covers everyone else giving to a third party, so it's easy to reach for this one in the wrong direction as a beginner.

kuro-color.meaning_mnemonic: The soot from that fire settles over the village for good, and when someone finally tries to repaint the signpost, every color left in the tin has merged into a single sludge — dip the brush anywhere and it comes out the same <kanji>black</kanji>.
kuro-color.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, someone's boot skids off a loose rock and comes back caked in tar-dark mud from ankle to knee. Scraping at it against the vending machine does nothing but smear it further, and they growl <reading>coo row</reading> under their breath — exactly the sound of <reading>くろ</reading>, the word for that filthy, unmistakable black.

kuroi.meaning_mnemonic: The village elder tosses one more log onto that sooty communal fire, and a startled cat bolts straight through the ash pile chasing a moth. It streaks across every wall and rooftop on its way out, smearing soot over the parts the smoke hadn't reached yet, until the whole huddled village is stained one uniform <kanji>black</kanji>.
kuroi.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, someone tips over a jar of ink kept for painting new charms, and it floods across the mossy steps toward a dozing cat. The cat bolts upright trailing inky pawprints and yowls a ragged <reading>coo, roi</reading> as it flees — exactly the sound of <reading>くろい</reading>, the word for black.

kuru-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the crossroads, the tree spots someone trudging up the mountain trail, footsore and ready to quit, and doesn't wait politely — it stretches a branch out like a beckoning arm and hauls them under its shade before they can even ask. That's the tree's whole personality: it never chases anyone anywhere, it only ever makes people <kanji>come</kanji>.
kuru-v.reading_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads spots a straggler still dragging up the trail and calls out <reading>coo, roo</reading> until they finally give in and come sit in its shade — that giving-in is exactly <reading>くる</reading>.

kuruma.meaning_mnemonic: Outside Koichi's konbini, under the buzzing fluorescent sign, that same overhead cart shape — axle through the middle, wheels flanking each side, the boxy frame all around — rolls up to the beeping till lane itself, engine running. Nobody laid a track out here, just four wheels parked on the apron: a <kanji>car</kanji>, plain and simple.
kuruma.reading_mnemonic: This is the same 車 you already read as くるま, so the word for car is simply <reading>くるま</reading> — the reading you learned with the kanji itself.

kusuri.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the medicine shelf sits past the onigiri, a lonely row of blister packs nobody touches — until 2 a.m., when someone stumbles in hacking and coughing, sweeps the whole row into a basket, and pays without a word. That row of boxes is the <kanji>medicine</kanji>.
kusuri.reading_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the shelf with only a <reading>cursory</reading> glance, tossing boxes on by feel. A customer mumbles '<reading>くすり</reading>, please' without looking up either — both of them running on autopilot at 2 a.m., neither one fully awake.

kutsu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the mountain trail, steep and endless, with that one vending machine impossibly balanced at the summit. A hiker collapses beside it, kicks off two mud-caked boots, and buys a can of tea instead of anything to eat. He drinks, sighs, and never puts the boots back on — leaves them right there under the machine as shoes for whoever runs out of nerve next.
kutsu.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail vending machine, a scruffy crow named Kutsu lands on the boots someone abandoned there and calls out sharply, <reading>coo-tsu, coo-tsu</reading> — the exact sound of <reading>くつ</reading>, over and over, guarding them like his own shoes now.

kuukou.meaning_mnemonic: A city block gets flattened overnight — grass paved over, buildings hauled off — replaced by flat runway under an <kanji>empty</kanji> stretch of sky. Nowhere to sit, nowhere to shop, just tarmac waiting for the next jet to lift into all that emptiness. That whole open, sky-swallowed lot is what people mean by airport.
kuukou.reading_mnemonic: 空（くう）＋港（こう）combine directly into <reading>くうこう</reading>.

kyonen.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>year</kanji> already scratched onto the shield-board and left behind you is <vocabulary>last year</vocabulary>.

kyou.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> you are standing in belongs to whichever <kanji>day</kanji> the sun happens to be up, and that day is <vocabulary>today</vocabulary>.
kyou.reading_mnemonic: Sei's teacher circles the date on the board and calls out <reading>きょう</reading>, which sounds exactly like calling <reading>cue</reading> for the pop quiz, because <vocabulary>today</vocabulary> is officially starting.

kyoudai.meaning_mnemonic: Picture two toddlers wedged together at Koichi's konbini, gripping the same onigiri, each wailing that the other one started it. One throws back a gaping yawn like the <kanji>older brother</kanji> who owns the place, while the other trails a loop of cord like the <kanji>younger brother</kanji> showing off a stolen bow. Neither releases, and the clerk just watches the same tantrum play out twice — that tangled squabble is what siblings means.
kyoudai.reading_mnemonic: 兄 gives its reading きょう and 弟 gives だい, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>きょうだい</reading>.

kyoukasho.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>teach</kanji>er drops a heavy book from the <kanji>department</kanji> on your desk before the sun even starts sinking outside the window. Every page is already crammed with lessons, leaving blank space below each one just so you can <kanji>write</kanji> your answers there — and that crammed, half-finished book is exactly what a textbook is for.
kyoukasho.reading_mnemonic: This word is three known readings in a row: 教 as きょう, 科 as か, and 書 as しょ, making <reading>きょうかしょ</reading>.

kyoushitsu.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane has turned the mossy steps behind her shrine's enormous bell into rows of little desks, and every cat in the neighborhood sits at one, tails curled, waiting for her to tap the bell between lessons the same way she's always used that crack to <kanji>teach</kanji>. Rows of desks boxed into that temple <kanji>room</kanji>, cats included, is what a classroom looks like here.
kyoushitsu.reading_mnemonic: Before each drill she holds up a <reading>cue sheet</reading> so the cats know which trick comes next — read her handwriting on it fast and it comes out <reading>きょうしつ</reading>, the reading for classroom.

kyuu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>nine</vocabulary> word are the exact same character, doing the exact same job.

machi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Hover over that same grid again — fields squared off on the left, the straight road cutting through on the right. Now watch it fill in: roofs go up along the road, a bakery claims the corner, kids race bikes past the fields. Roads plus fields plus everyone building a life between them — that's a <kanji>town</kanji>.
machi-v.reading_mnemonic: A courier named <reading>Machi</reading> pedals through the grid every morning, roofs and bakery and kids on bikes rushing past. She shouts the name of the sprawl the moment she crosses the gate — <reading>まち</reading> — and drops her bike to finish the delivery on time.

mada.meaning_mnemonic: The clock over Sei's sports field already says race time, but Sei is still on the bench, still knotting one shoelace, still not standing up. Everyone else is lined up at the start line waiting on her. The whistle hasn't blown, because for her it's still, stubbornly, not yet time.
mada.reading_mnemonic: 「<reading>まだ</reading>」is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so you just read it as it appears — no kanji to decode.

mado.meaning_mnemonic: Picture someone at Grandma Kane's shrine so furious that a cat knocked over the offering bowl that they wrench open the wooden frame set into the wall and shout their outrage straight at the sky — mad, then oh, right as the frame swings wide. That opening they're yelling through, moss creeping up its sill, is a <kanji>window</kanji>.
mado.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches the cat sprawled across her offerings again and goes properly <reading>mad, oh!</reading> — the shout tears out of her as she yanks the wooden frame in the shrine wall wide open to chase it out. That startled yell is <reading>まど</reading>: the window she just threw open.

madoguchi.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi cuts one narrow slot into his konbini's front glass so customers never have to walk inside - just an open <kanji>mouth</kanji> in the pane, nothing else. You slide your money through it, a voice on the other side takes your order, and that slot is the service <kanji>window</kanji>.
madoguchi.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 窓 read まど, plus 口 read ぐち, which gives <reading>まどぐち</reading>.

mae.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that storefront awning again, jutting out over the sidewalk with its two-legged display stand planted beneath it. It's built to be the very first thing anyone sees, standing out in <kanji>front</kanji> of the shop, met <kanji>before</kanji> a single customer crosses the threshold. Whatever greets you first, whatever juts out ahead of everything else, is the front — the before.
mae.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a regular named Ma lunges past the onigiri shelf by the door, racing the beeping till. The automatic door catches her coat, yanks her off her feet, and she snaps <reading>mah-eh</reading> — which is exactly <reading>まえ</reading>, the word for the front.

magaru.meaning_mnemonic: Inside Koichi's konbini, a shopping cart with one stuck wheel refuses to go straight, swerving hard into the onigiri shelf every time it nears the corner. The clerk gives up steering it normally and yanks it sideways right at the corner, spilling rice balls everywhere as it finally turns.
magaru.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the clerk yells <reading>mug a roo</reading> every time the cart nearly rams a customer, and the wheel screeches <reading>まがる</reading> as it swerves around the corner just in time, rice balls flying off the shelf behind it.

mai-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane is fanning herself at the shrine with what she insists is one paper fan, except the wind keeps peeling it apart into more and more identical flat sheets, scattering across the mossy steps. The cats bat each sheet flat against the stone, and she ends up having to tally the whole scattered stack as flat objects (counter).
mai-counter.reading_mnemonic: One cat pins a sheet down and lets out a flat, dragged-out "<reading>maaai</reading>" every time another one lands, so Grandma starts counting them by that cry: <reading>まい</reading>, <reading>まい</reading>, <reading>まい</reading>.

maiasa.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini shutter grinds open at <kanji>every</kanji> <kanji>morning</kanji>'s first light, and that daily grind is <vocabulary>every morning</vocabulary> itself.

maiban.meaning_mnemonic: The shrine bell at Grandma Kane's rings out <kanji>every</kanji> single time the sun goes down, and that relentless repeat is <vocabulary>every night</vocabulary>.

mainen.meaning_mnemonic: Notch <kanji>every</kanji> ban onto the <kanji>year</kanji> board and the tally becomes <vocabulary>every year</vocabulary>.

mainichi.meaning_mnemonic: Slap <kanji>every</kanji> ban onto the calendar and it covers <kanji>day</kanji> after day, which is just <vocabulary>every day</vocabulary>.

maishuu.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Every</kanji> <kanji>week</kanji> loops back to Monday like a stubborn circle, and that loop is <vocabulary>every week</vocabulary>.

maitsuki.meaning_mnemonic: Cover <kanji>every</kanji> lap the <kanji>month</kanji> moon makes and you get <vocabulary>every month</vocabulary>.

man-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>ten thousand</vocabulary> word never needed to separate, so they never did.

mannaka.meaning_mnemonic: That same spear, driven clean through the mouth-shaped opening, doesn't stop at one skewer — it pins three coins to the shrine step in a perfect row, and no matter how Grandma Kane's cats bat at the ends, the spear always balances dead level at its <kanji>middle, inside</kanji> point. Whatever sits there, exactly equidistant from both edges, is the center — the <kanji>true</kanji> middle.
mannaka.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 真 read ま, plus ん, plus 中 read なか, gives <reading>まんなか</reading>.

marui.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the enormous bell has been struck by centuries of visitors until every corner has worn away entirely — no edges, no angles, just one smooth curve running all the way around it. The monks pat it fondly and call it perfectly round.
marui.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a fat cat refuses to leave the bell stand, curling tighter every time a visitor claps. The old monk sighs, 'you get <reading>more roly</reading> every day' — and that mumbled phrase is how you remember <reading>まるい</reading>, round.

mata.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer buys the exact same onigiri, eats it on the curb, forgets he ever ate it, and shuffles straight back inside to buy the exact same onigiri. The till beeps the identical price for the fourth time that hour. He always does it again.
mata.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, <reading>また</reading>, so there's nothing to decode — just read it as it looks.

matsu.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sits on the mossy shrine steps with her hands folded, cats draped over her feet like she isn't going anywhere. Whatever she's expecting hasn't come yet, so she just sits, still as the bell beside her. That stillness, held on and on without complaint, is what it means to wait.
matsu.reading_mnemonic: A cat wanders up and tries to strike a <reading>match</reading> against the shrine bell, hoping to hurry things along, but Grandma Kane doesn't even blink. She's content to <reading>まつ</reading> as long as it takes.

mazu.meaning_mnemonic: Before ringing the enormous bell at Grandma Kane's shrine, every visitor pauses to clap twice and bow — first of all, that; only then the pull on the rope. One tourist skips straight to the bell and yanks it, and the cats scatter hissing, because he never did it first of all.
mazu.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, <reading>まず</reading>, plain and phonetic all the way through.

mazui.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine improbably parked at the top of the mountain trail, you buy the last can — mystery flavor, no label — and immediately regret existing. Your face does something involuntary. That single working button might be a war crime. That's bad-tasting.
mazui.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it sounds — just say <reading>まずい</reading>, nothing to derive, nothing hiding underneath.
mazui.description: Beyond food, まずい is also the everyday word for a situation gone wrong or awkward — closer to "uh-oh, bad" than to bad cooking. Someone muttering it while staring at a spilled drink or a missed deadline is using this same word, not talking about taste at all.

me-v.meaning_mnemonic: Above the register at Koichi's konbini hangs a security frame with two little dots for pupils, tilted so it looks like it's staring you down while you pick between the onigiri and the beeping till. That frame with pupils staring back is exactly the <kanji>eye</kanji> watching every customer who lingers too long.
me-v.reading_mnemonic: 目 already gives you this reading on its own — め is exactly how 目 reads by itself, so the <reading>め</reading> here is that very same reading, unchanged.

megane.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the librarian's eyesight gives out mid-shelving, so she bends two empty onigiri wrappers from Koichi's konbini into perfect circles, wires them together with a stray chopstick, and hooks the whole rig over her ears. The blur snaps into focus at once — she has just invented glasses.
megane.reading_mnemonic: A new student at Sei's school keeps insisting she isn't wearing glasses, but every teacher squints at her face and asks, <reading>Meg, uh, nay?</reading> — which is exactly how you say <reading>めがね</reading>, the glasses she is obviously wearing.

michi-v.meaning_mnemonic: You keep following that winding <kanji>road</kanji> up the mountain trail, switchback after switchback, until it stops being a hiking route — a delivery scooter buzzes past, a mailbox appears at the bend, gravel turns to pavement. It isn't a trail anymore; it's somebody's street. That's the word: <kanji>road</kanji>, the ordinary road or street right outside a door.
michi-v.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a guide named <reading>Michi</reading> waits at the one bend with a signpost, shouting directions before hikers wander off. Everyone who reaches her calls it by her name — the winding <reading>みち</reading> that got them there safely.

midori.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman's tackle box tips into the shallows. When he fishes it back out, every hook, weight, and bobber inside has come up coated in the same slick pond algae, dripping one uniform green, until the whole box is just a soggy green mess sitting in the reeds.
midori.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a woman knocks three times on her boathouse door — <reading>me, dough, ree</reading> — and waits so long for an answer that pond algae creeps up the door itself, turning it the same green as the water: <reading>みどり</reading>.

mieru.meaning_mnemonic: That <kanji>see</kanji>-eye on its pair of little legs wanders off one day and climbs to the very top of a hill, right out in the open. Now it doesn't matter who looks up — from the village, from the school field, from the riverbank — that eye is standing right there in plain sight. It's stopped just doing the looking and started being the thing everyone can look at: visible.
mieru.reading_mnemonic: 見（み）＋える gives you 「<reading>みえる</reading>」 regularly — the same み you already know from 見, plus the える ending this whole verb family wears.

migi-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer jams an arm into the vending slot up to the elbow, fishing after a stuck onigiri — the same fingers-into-open-mouth shape as before, working itself free all over again. It's always the dominant one doing this kind of stunt, which is why that grabbing hand is the <kanji>right</kanji> one.
migi-v.reading_mnemonic: On the steep mountain trail, a hiker named <reading>Miggy</reading> stops to retie a shoe and sits squarely on a thistle. She rockets upright with the lace still looped around her ankle, dragging the shoe, and hisses <reading>みぎ</reading> all the way to the top.

mijikai.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps and spits out a receipt that stops after two centimeters, cut off mid-word before the total even prints. The clerk tugs at the paper, but that's all there is — the roll's been swapped by mistake, and every single receipt today comes out stubby, clipped, cut short.
mijikai.reading_mnemonic: Jika, the new clerk, tries to introduce herself, but the till keeps beeping over her: '<reading>Mi, Jika</reading>—' is all that gets out before she's cut off. Her own clipped name is the whole lesson — that stubby, chopped-off sound is <reading>みじかい</reading>.

mikka.meaning_mnemonic: That stubby ladder of rungs you know as <kanji>three</kanji> lines up beside the <kanji>day</kanji> mark. Three rungs stacked on one day column add up to <vocabulary>three days</vocabulary>.

mimi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the mountain trail, that dangling flap of skin catches the sudden beep of the vending machine echoing off the rock face before your eyes even register the machine is there. The flap swivels toward the sound like it has a mind of its own — proof that the whole point of an <kanji>ear</kanji> is hearing first, seeing second.
mimi-v.reading_mnemonic: 耳 already reads みみ on its own, so the <reading>みみ</reading> in this word is that same reading, said once for the character and now doubled for the word.

minami-v.meaning_mnemonic: That tent is still pitched with its wind chime jingling under the roof, planted on the sunniest patch of ground you could find. You keep dragging the stakes further and further along, chasing the warmth, until the chime is going nonstop in the soft breeze — and dragging a tent that far only points one way: <kanji>south</kanji>.
minami-v.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, Nami keeps kicking the lone vending machine until cans rain down the slope. A hiker ducks and yells <reading>me-nami</reading> as a can clips his ear, which is exactly the sound of <reading>みなみ</reading>.

minna.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the tinny loudspeaker crackles once and a single voice booms through every aisle at the same instant, announcing a surprise scavenger hunt: onigiri, umbrellas, batteries, go. Every last customer looks up from what they're doing in the same second - not some of them, not most of them. Everyone.
minna.reading_mnemonic: みんな is written exactly the way it sounds, plain kana with nothing hiding underneath, so the word simply is its own reading: <reading>みんな</reading>.

miru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that stood up on legs is exhausted from all its walking, so it stops in the middle of the road and just stands there. It doesn't blink, doesn't turn away, doesn't do anything else at all — it just plants its legs and looks. That is all this word ever asks of you: to <kanji>see</kanji>.
miru-v.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the guide Mia unpacks a cracked hand mirror instead of a map and holds it up to the sun, tilting it at hikers below. She calls down that all she needs is a <reading>mirror</reading>, the sound of <reading>みる</reading>, and spends the whole afternoon flashing light across the valley instead of guiding anyone up.

mise.meaning_mnemonic: A hand-painted sign hangs above one sliding door: vegetable bins spill onto the pavement, a bell over the frame jingles nonstop, and the till keeps popping open from coins going in and out all day. Nothing about the place is fancy — just one small room built around handing things to people for money. That room is a <kanji>shop</kanji>.
mise.reading_mnemonic: A tiny shopkeeper mouse rings up every sale by squeaking the price twice, so customers just call the cramped counter <reading>mice, eh</reading> — say it fast enough and you get <reading>みせ</reading>, the shop everyone in town swears is run entirely by rodents.

miseru.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that grew legs doesn't just wander off to <kanji>see</kanji> things for itself — sometimes it marches straight up to you, plants itself in front of your face, and refuses to leave until you've looked too. Dragging what it saw over so someone else can see it as well is exactly what it means to show something.
miseru.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 見 as <reading>み</reading> plus the ending せる tacked on, giving you <reading>みせる</reading> straight from the reading you already know for “see”.

mitsukeru.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that stood up on legs to <kanji>see</kanji> everywhere finally spots what it's after. It stops walking, plants its legs flat on the ground, and refuses to budge until you notice what it's staring at. That sudden dead stop, legs locked, eye fixed — that's the exact feeling of finding something you'd been hunting for.
mitsukeru.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting dog, patrols his wall of antique swords at dusk and sniffs a scabbard stuffed with leftover sausages. He barks <reading>meats-care</reading> at any hand that comes near, which is exactly the sound of <reading>みつける</reading>.

mittsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>three</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>three things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
mittsu.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a forgotten baseball <reading>mitt</reading> holds <vocabulary>three things</vocabulary> the same customer left behind. The till clerk marks it <reading>みっつ</reading> without looking up.

mizu.meaning_mnemonic: You're back at the riverbank where the streams splash outward in every direction, cold spray hitting your face. Cup your hands in that spray, and the streaks resolve into something you can actually drink: <kanji>water</kanji>.
mizu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a keeper named <reading>Miss Zoo</reading> dives in after an escaped otter. She surfaces coughing, gasping that she swallowed a mouthful of <reading>みず</reading>, spits it out, and trudges home soaked to teach the otter a lesson.

mizuumi.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the top of the mountain trail expecting the usual lone vending machine, but instead the whole crater ahead is filled with still, glassy water stretching out to the far ridge — too big for a pond, too walled-in for the sea. You have found a lake.
mizuumi.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, a hiker introduces herself between gasps as <reading>Missy Umi</reading>, then points down at the water filling the crater below. Out of breath, her name and the word for what she's pointing at blur into one: <reading>みずうみ</reading>.

mochiron.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer asks the clerk if the mochi by the register is actually fresh. The clerk, a rice-cake vendor everyone calls Ron, doesn't even glance up — restocking that shelf every single hour is his whole job. Obviously it's fresh. Of course it is.
mochiron.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>もちろん</reading> sounds just like the confident vendor's name, <reading>Mochi-Ron</reading>, shrugging off the question.
mochiron.description: This is a confident, assertive of course — fine with friends or in casual replies, but answering a boss or teacher with it can come across as presumptuous, so softening the tone or adding a more formal ending is often safer.

mokuyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>tree</kanji> finally grows tall enough to shade a whole <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji>, turning it into <vocabulary>Thursday</vocabulary>.

mondai.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine doesn't dispense drinks anymore. Every button jams, spits out a folded riddle instead — each one stamped with a single <kanji>topic</kanji>, and nothing else — and demands you solve it before it will even consider a refund. Hikers arrive thirsty and leave with an armful of only more of these — unanswered <kanji>questions</kanji> and problems, stacked one on top of the last.
mondai.reading_mnemonic: A sticker on the machine reads, in block letters: '<reading>MONDAY</reading> deliveries only — no drinks.' Grumbled enough times on the hike back down, that word wears smooth into <reading>もんだい</reading>, the exact sound of every problem the machine caused.

mono.meaning_mnemonic: Momo, the konbini clerk, hates chaos. Every dropped umbrella, chipped mug, and lost sock that wanders onto her counter gets a paper tag and a spot on the shelf, no matter what it is. She never asks what it means or why it's there — a thing is a thing, and every <kanji>thing</kanji> gets labeled and shelved.
mono.reading_mnemonic: Momo stamps each tag with a flat moan: "moooono." Customers assume she's exhausted, but it's just her filing chant — one long <reading>moan</reading> for every <reading>もの</reading> she catalogs, thing after thing after thing.

morau.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a heron stands perfectly still while the current drifts small fish toward its beak. It never wades in, never chases, never hunts — it just waits at the same spot every morning, and the river keeps delivering. Everything the heron eats today, something else caught for it first.
morau.reading_mnemonic: もらう is pure kana, read straight through: sound out <reading>もらう</reading> as the heron's stomach grumbling <reading>more, ow</reading> each time a fish arrives late.
morau.description: This verb marks receiving, and it stretches beyond objects — you can 'receive' a favor or an action someone did for you, not just a physical thing. The person you received it from is the one who benefited you, which trips learners moving directly from English 'get.'

motsu.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine finally appears, and the hiker who has been dreaming about it for two hours locks both arms around it like it might disappear. She doesn't buy anything from it, she just holds it, arms full of cold metal and victory, refusing to let go. That grip is to <kanji>hold</kanji>, to have.
motsu.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the hiker's boot skids on a patch of moss. She grabs another clump of <reading>moss, too</reading>, both fists closing around it so she doesn't tumble down the slope. Holding two fistfuls of moss, too, that grip is <reading>もつ</reading>, the sound of hands that refuse to let go.

motto.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail dispenses one can, then rattles and drops a second on top of it, then a third, refusing to stop even after the hiker steps back and holds up both hands. It just keeps deciding that whatever amount already exists, there needs to be more.
motto.reading_mnemonic: もっと is pure kana, so <reading>もっと</reading> is read exactly as it's spelled — no hidden reading to work out here.

mou.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini gets exactly one onigiri delivery a day. You wander in at noon expecting a full shelf, but it's already bare — the whole batch sold out before the till even finished beeping. Koichi just shrugs: the next batch arrives soon, but for now, you're already too late.
mou.reading_mnemonic: 「<reading>もう</reading>」is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so you just read it as it appears — no kanji to decode.

muika.meaning_mnemonic: The lid that turns eight into <kanji>six</kanji> clamps shut on one more <kanji>day</kanji>, and that trapped day makes <vocabulary>six days</vocabulary> in all.

musuko.meaning_mnemonic: That same swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms flung wide, has somehow hauled itself up the whole mountain trail and is now feeding coins into the vending machine at the summit like it owns the place. A hiker asks the panting father trailing behind whose kid that is. He beams, chest out — that's his son.
musuko.reading_mnemonic: At the summit, the father spots a moose eyeing his boy's snack and bellows <reading>Moose, Coe!</reading> — the name of the trail's resident moose, shouted fast and clipped. That exact bark, <reading>むすこ</reading>, is what every hiker on this mountain learns to recognize as a warning about his son.

musume.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a girl in oversized cleats trips over the finish-line ribbon and drags the whole banner down with her. A woman in the stands leaps up, mortified and delighted at once, shouting across the entire field for her — this ribbon-tangled little disaster is her daughter.
musume.reading_mnemonic: Still tangled in ribbon, she turns to the snack table and asks sweetly, <reading>Mousse, may?</reading> — polite as anything in the middle of a disaster. That well-mannered request, <reading>むすめ</reading>, is the reading you're listening for.

muttsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>six</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>six things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
muttsu.reading_mnemonic: A stray <reading>mutt</reading> wanders into Grandma Kane's shrine and steals <vocabulary>six things</vocabulary> off the offering step. The cats hiss, but she only sighs <reading>むっつ</reading> as it bolts.

muzukashii.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a cow wearing a muzzle plants its hooves at the steepest switchback and refuses to go one step further, not even toward the vending machine improbably waiting at the top. Coaxing it up that last stretch turns out to be nearly impossible, which is what difficult means here.
muzukashii.reading_mnemonic: The hiker groans <reading>muzzle-cow-she!</reading> at the stubborn animal — near enough to <reading>むずかしい</reading> that it becomes her word for anything this hard, from then on.

nagai-adj.meaning_mnemonic: That same bearded elder from before is leaning on his stick atop Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps. His <kanji>long</kanji> beard doesn't stop at his sandals — it keeps pouring down step after step until it pools at the bottom, where the shrine cats have started napping in it. Nobody has ever found the end of that beard, because it just keeps going, absurdly <kanji>long</kanji>.
nagai-adj.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman's line snags on something and he reels for a full minute before anything surfaces. A kid watching mutters <reading>nah, guy</reading> in disbelief as the catch just keeps coming, and that disbelief is exactly <reading>ながい</reading>, the word for long.

naifu.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker too hungry to wait rams a thin blade sideways into the vending machine's coin slot, prying the stuck snack loose in one clean, mean slice before it even finishes falling. The narrow single-edged tool built for exactly that kind of job is a knife.
naifu.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ナイフ</reading> is written exactly as it sounds - it comes straight from English knife, rounded off into kana, nothing more to it.

naka.meaning_mnemonic: The spear is still lodged dead center in that open square, exactly where you first pictured it — but now imagine trying to yank it back out and finding the square won't let go, gripping tight around the blade buried in its <kanji>middle</kanji>. Whatever's skewered that way isn't sitting near an edge; it's held fast, tucked <kanji>inside</kanji>.
naka.reading_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field a caretaker called <reading>Knocka</reading> rolls a gym mat into a tube and crawls in after a stray ball. The mat pinches shut around her and she bangs the canvas yelling her own name, which is the sound of <reading>なか</reading>, the word for inside.

naku.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the vending machine improbably parked at the top of the mountain trail, dig out your last coin, and watch it get swallowed with a smug beep and no snack in return. Legs shaking, throat tight, staring at that blinking screen — this is the exact moment your face crumples and you start to cry.
naku.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up, a hiker named <reading>Knox</reading> kicks the machine that ate his coin, and it just rings hollow, like a knock on an empty door. He slides down against it and finally lets himself <reading>なく</reading>, sobbing into his sleeve while the machine blinks on, indifferent.

nakunaru.meaning_mnemonic: The supply cabinet at your office has exactly one stapler, and by Friday afternoon it is simply gone — not broken, not borrowed, gone, just <kanji>nothingness</kanji> on the shelf. You check the same empty shelf three times as if it might reappear. That total vanishing, the running-out-to-nothing, is the meaning: to disappear, to run out.
nakunaru.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a woodpecker hammers the same dead branch for hours until it finally splits and topples into the current. The birds go quiet — <reading>knock, no more</reading> — and the fisherman sighs: whatever was there has become <reading>なくなる</reading>, gone for good.

nakusu.meaning_mnemonic: You set your umbrella down for one second on the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, and when you turn back there is only a cat sitting in exactly that spot, looking innocent. The umbrella is not behind the cat, not under the cat, not anywhere. It has simply stopped existing, dissolved into pure <kanji>nothingness</kanji>. That is what it means to lose something.
nakusu.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cat on Grandma Kane's mossy steps has one trick: she'll <reading>knock loose</reading> any offering balanced near the edge, and once it slides past the bell into the dark underneath, the shrine keeper just sighs and says <reading>なくす</reading> — it's gone, no use looking.

namae.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini awning juts out over the sidewalk to greet you before you're even through the door — that's <kanji>front</kanji>, the part that always meets you first. Duck under it and Koichi leans out to fill the gap over his mouth with the one word that was missing: his <kanji>name</kanji>. Front first, then the name.
namae.reading_mnemonic: 名 gives you な and 前 gives you まえ, joined exactly as taught into <reading>なまえ</reading>.

nan.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>what</kanji> kanji still needs no help here. This reading just carries it forward as <vocabulary>what (before counters)</vocabulary>.
nan.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's vending machine, a hiker counts servings of <reading>naan</reading> bread. Before every number he blurts <reading>なん</reading>, as if <vocabulary>what (before counters)</vocabulary> always comes first.
nan.description: なん appears only right before a counter, as in questions about quantity or time. Used alone, 何 takes a different reading instead.

nana-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
nana-v.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a regular named <reading>Nana</reading> orders <vocabulary>seven</vocabulary> onigiri every visit, counting each one aloud as <reading>なな</reading>.

nanatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing. The trailing つ just turns the bare number into a count of objects.
nanatsu.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 七 is read なな, so <vocabulary>seven things</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>ななつ</reading>.

nani.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>what</kanji> kanji needs no help to become a word. Alone, it already means <vocabulary>what</vocabulary>.
nani.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>nanny</reading> at Koichi's konbini opens a mystery tin and blurts <reading>なに</reading>. She still can't name <vocabulary>what</vocabulary> is inside.

nannji.meaning_mnemonic: Put <kanji>what</kanji> directly in front of <kanji>time</kanji> and you get the question itself, <vocabulary>what time</vocabulary>.

nanoka.meaning_mnemonic: String <kanji>seven</kanji> <kanji>suns</kanji> together and you get <vocabulary>seven days</vocabulary>, a full week gone by.

naosu.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the one vending machine refuses to drop its can, jammed sideways in the slot. A hiker rocks it, kicks the base twice, and jiggles the coin return until the can finally thuds free — the machine works again, fixed and repaired, ready for the next exhausted climber.
naosu.reading_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, the till breaks mid-beep and Koichi mutters <reading>now, Sue</reading>, which is exactly what it sounds like — <reading>なおす</reading> — before Sue crouches under the counter with a screwdriver and gets it running again.

naraberu.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's gym teacher makes everyone line up their shoes along the sports field before practice — heel to heel, toe to toe, not one pair crooked. Sei spends ten minutes nudging sneakers into a perfectly straight row, and that patient shove-and-shuffle down the line is exactly what it means to line up.
naraberu.reading_mnemonic: Sei's gym teacher marches down the row of crooked sneakers shouting '<reading>No rebels</reading>!' at anyone out of line, and the command comes out clipped and fast, landing on everyone's ears as <reading>ならべる</reading> before they scramble to straighten their shoes.

naru-become.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a tadpole flops onto a lily pad and refuses to leave. It sits there so long its tail shrinks and legs sprout, and by sunset it hops off the pad a frog. Nobody ever catches the exact moment it happens — one thing just quietly turns into another. That quiet turning, tadpole into frog, is to become.
naru-become.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, containing 「<reading>なる</reading>」.

naru-ring.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the countless cats leaps for a moth and misses, slamming into the enormous mossy bell instead. The whole hillside goes still for a second, then the bell answers — one huge sound rolling down the steps. Nobody rang it on purpose; it simply rang, sound arriving as a consequence, not a choice.
naru-ring.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cat is named <reading>Naru</reading>, and when she yowls at the bell it answers with a tone the locals swear sounds just like her name — <reading>なる</reading> — echoing down the steps every time.

naru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one persistent cat has taken to shadowing her every move — copying exactly how she rings the enormous bell, sweeps the mossy steps, and bows twice before the altar. Nobody assigned it a lesson; it simply watched an expert long enough to learn from her, one gesture at a time.
naru.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane names the shrine cat <reading>Nara</reading>, after the old temple town where she trained as a girl, since it watches her rites with such focus. Every dawn it edges closer to her heels, and by autumn the visitors swear the cat has started to <reading>ならう</reading> her exact bow.

natsu.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, the heat gets so thick that the cicadas scream nonstop and a fat bullfrog finally can't take it anymore — it belly-flops straight into the water fully dressed in someone's abandoned sandals, sending up a wall of spray. That relentless, sweat-soaked heat that drives everyone into the river is summer.
natsu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Koichi complains the heat is unbearable, and Grandma Kane snaps back that it's <reading>not, too</reading> — she's roasting just the same, fanning herself with a shrine pamphlet. The villagers shortened her retort to <reading>なつ</reading>, and that's the season now.

naze.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, one kid stops every teacher to ask なぜ about the rules. He won't take one more step until he knows <vocabulary>why</vocabulary>.

nedan.meaning_mnemonic: At the summit vending machine, legs shaking from climbing every numbered <kanji>grade</kanji> of stair on the way up, you watch the little display flicker between eight hundred yen and eight million before settling. It isn't broken, it's just deciding what altitude is worth. That flickering number, haggling with your exhaustion, is the price you paid to get here.
nedan.reading_mnemonic: Ned the horse trader neighs at dawn every morning before chalking a new number on his cart. Villagers set their clocks by his <reading>neigh-at-dawn</reading> ritual, since that's exactly how you say <reading>ねだん</reading>, the price he's picked for the day.

neko.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, cats already outnumber worshippers, but one has decided the offering bell is a toy. She swats the rope, ducks under the railing, and curls up exactly where the incense smoke is warmest, ignoring every polite attempt to shoo her off. That smug, entitled little squatter is what cat means.
neko.reading_mnemonic: A visitor watches the shrine cat arch and stretch across the warm stone and winces, worried for her <reading>neck, oh</reading> — just as the cat flops flatter, completely unbothered. That half-panicked warning is the shape of <reading>ねこ</reading>, and the cat never once looks up to acknowledge it.

nen-year.meaning_mnemonic: That same scarecrow is still out there, sleeves gone gray, having watched the rice fall and rise through one full circuit of sun and frost. It never counts the seasons one by one — it only marks the moment its whole slow watch loops back to where it started, and that single loop is a <kanji>year</kanji>.
nen-year.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the kanji's own taught sound: 年 is read <reading>ねん</reading>, the same one you already learned for the scarecrow's yearly watch.

neru.meaning_mnemonic: You've hiked all the way up to the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, and the climb wrecks you completely. You slump down against its warm hum, eyes shutting before you even decide to rest, and don't move again until morning. That collapse against the machine is what it means: to sleep.
neru.reading_mnemonic: A hiker called Near always collapses <reading>near</reading> the mountain vending machine, murmuring <reading>ねる</reading> before he even finishes sitting down, and by dawn he's still curled against its warm hum, dead to the world.

ni-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>two</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>two</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.

nichi-day.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the caretaker watches the <kanji>sun</kanji> climb through the window-with-a-bar each morning and chalks one mark onto the great bell for that <kanji>day</kanji>. The temple cats keep swatting the marks off the bronze, so she starts over, one sunrise at a time, tallying days like coins dropped in a jar.
nichi-day.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 日 was already taught as <reading>にち</reading>, and that's exactly the reading this word keeps, unchanged.

nichiyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> is too bright to share the sky, so the very first <kanji>weekday</kanji> takes its name straight from it, becoming <vocabulary>Sunday</vocabulary>.

nigiyaka.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini at midnight should be dead quiet, but tonight the till won't stop beeping, the onigiri shelf is being raided by a dozen elbowing customers, and somebody's abandoned grocery cart is still spinning in the doorway. Noise stacked on noise stacked on noise — that overflowing racket is lively / bustling.
nigiyaka.reading_mnemonic: Back at that same beeping till, a whole herd of yaks squeezes past the onigiri shelf, their knees banging the shelf with every step — '<reading>knee-gear yaks</reading>,' the clerk mutters, watching the chaos spread. That crowded racket is 「<reading>にぎやか</reading>」.

nihon.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, the <kanji>sun</kanji> breaks through the vending machine's fogged window first thing each morning, same as it climbs through any window with a bar across it. Below, the tree's <kanji>origin</kanji> line still marks the very root everything grew from, the first page of the story. Sun rising first over the origin of it all: that's the name given to the whole nation, Japan.
nihon.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps out a stuttering three-note tone every time the register opens, <reading>knee, hone, go</reading>, and the night clerk swears it's saying <reading>にほん</reading> at him on every single sale. Say it three times fast and you'll hear it too.

nihongo.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine steps, dawn breaks and the <kanji>sun</kanji> climbs straight through the gate's window bar, marking a fresh day. Beside it, the tree's origin line still points to the very <kanji>origin</kanji> everything grew from, pressed flat into an ancient book. Then mouths start chanting, stacking speech on speech into a whole <kanji>language</kanji>, spoken over that book, in the land where the sun began. That stacked, sun-born tongue is Japanese.
nihongo.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank crossing, a drill-sergeant crane paces the stepping stones shouting orders: <reading>Knee! Hon! Go!</reading>, bend the knee, grip the handle, go. Villagers repeat the barked count until it blurs into one word, <reading>にほんご</reading>, and that's the reading that sticks whenever someone names the language.

niku.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer piles his arms so high with packages that he can't see over the top, and the automatic door doesn't slide open fast enough — he plows into the glass, packages skidding toward the onigiri shelf while the till keeps beeping through the whole thing. What he was hoarding, glass door and all, was meat.
niku.reading_mnemonic: This word is just 肉 read the ordinary way, <reading>にく</reading>, with nothing added.
