nimotsu.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, Koichi refuses to leave any bag at the bottom, so he hauls every <kanji>thing</kanji> past the vending machine at the summit, knees creaking louder with every step. By the time he collapses at the top, all anyone can see is baggage — two duffels, a rolled tent, and Koichi somewhere underneath it all.
nimotsu.reading_mnemonic: You already know both pieces: 荷 read に, then 物 read もつ, and they lock together as <reading>にもつ</reading>.

nin-counter.meaning_mnemonic: Jin the friendly giant ducks through the door of Koichi's konbini, and a whole line of customers files in behind him, each one a <kanji>person</kanji> striding forward on the same two legs you learned before. Jin taps each striding person on the shoulder as they pass, tallying them one after another — which is exactly what you do when you count people.
nin-counter.reading_mnemonic: When 人 is used as a counter, it still takes the kanji's own on'yomi, unchanged: <reading>にん</reading>.

nishi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Every dusk that squat cage fills up again, wings folding in one after another as the birds settle for the night. You count them home each time the sun dips the exact same direction, and that direction is always <kanji>west</kanji>.
nishi-v.reading_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, a girl in oversized shoes slides for the ball and her kneecap skids across the wet grass. She howls <reading>knee-she</reading> while clutching it, and that howl is <reading>にし</reading>.

niwa.meaning_mnemonic: Behind Sei's school, past the sports field, there's a locked gate nobody bothers with anymore. Squeeze through and you find a <kanji>courtyard</kanji> gone completely wild — tomato vines swallowing the old goalposts, cats sunbathing on a rusted rake nobody put away. Teachers pretend it isn't there. Everyone else just calls it the yard behind the yard.
niwa.reading_mnemonic: In that tangled garden behind the school, a cat pounces off the rusted rake and lands wrong, yowling <reading>knee, wah!</reading> — that garbled yelp is exactly the sound of <reading>にわ</reading>, the overgrown little yard where the school's stray cats actually live.

noboru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat spots the enormous bell rope dangling above and decides the bell tower looks like a throne. Paw over paw, it hauls itself up the mossy steps, then straight up the rope, refusing to stop until it's perched on the bell's crown surveying the cats below — that relentless paw-over-paw haul is what it means to climb.
noboru.reading_mnemonic: Nobu, the shrine cat's owner, snaps at a neighbor asking to borrow his ladder: '<reading>No, borrow</reading> nothing — watch this instead.' He hauls himself up the mossy steps hand over hand, the whole climb echoing through the cats as one long <reading>のぼる</reading>.

nokoru.meaning_mnemonic: After the birthday party ends and the last guest waves goodbye, one lonely slice of cake sits alone on the table, uneaten, crumbs scattered everywhere else. Everyone else got their piece and left; only this slice stayed behind. That staying-behind, the leftover, is the meaning: to remain.
nokoru.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last onigiri on the shelf turns out to be a display fake with <reading>no core</reading> — just rice on the outside, hollow within. Koichi leaves it sitting there past closing, the one item that never sells: it simply <reading>のこる</reading>, remains, night after night.

nomimono.meaning_mnemonic: That same yawning mouth wanders down to the riverbank on a hot afternoon, tips its head all the way back over the water, and doesn't stop until the whole river's worth has vanished down its throat. Food sits forgotten beside it; the only <kanji>thing</kanji> that gaping mouth wants now is to <kanji>drink</kanji>, and it does, all afternoon, without ever closing once.
nomimono.reading_mnemonic: <reading>のみもの</reading> just chains 飲's reading の, the み that follows it, and 物's reading もの.

nomu-v.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, the food radical sits beside that same gaping, thirsty mouth from 飲's story, but now it's not just hanging open — it's tipped straight back over the water, gulping in one long pull. No plate ever touches those lips, only river water pouring straight down, and that greedy tilt-and-gulp is what it means to <kanji>drink</kanji>.
nomu-v.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a garden gnome missing from Koichi's konbini shelf washes up clutching an inner tube and a can. The fisherman hauling him in swears he gasped for a <reading>no-moo</reading>, exactly the sound of <reading>のむ</reading>, before sliding back under, still drinking.

nooto.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a kid staples every loose page from their bag into one brick-thick block and hauls it to class insisting it's still light. The teacher weighs it in one hand, sighs, and writes "notebook" across the cover so nobody has to argue about what to call it again.
nooto.reading_mnemonic: Written in kana exactly as it sounds, straight from the English word notebook — read it as <reading>ノート</reading>, no decoding needed.

noru.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the whole class lines up for the field-trip bus, but one boy refuses to sit until he's counted every seat twice. The driver revs the engine, the line surges forward, and the boy finally hops aboard as the doors hiss shut behind him. That's what it means to ride, to board.
noru.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the driver bellows one rule before the bus leaves: <reading>no rule</reading> about pushing. A boy who never listens hops on anyway, and the driver sighs, muttering <reading>のる</reading> under his breath as the doors close on him again.

nugu.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a raccoon refuses to wade in without stripping down first, peeling a mud-caked jacket off one shoulder at a time and flinging it onto a rock before dog-paddling across. Every animal downstream waits for the splash that means the jacket is finally off and the crossing has begun.
nugu.reading_mnemonic: That riverbank raccoon has a name — the other animals call her <reading>Newgoo</reading> for the sound her claws make peeling wet fabric, a slow squelch like <reading>ぬぐ</reading>. Every time she strips the muddy jacket off before diving in, she drags the sound out long and slow, and the name stuck.

oba.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, an aunt turns up every New Year wrapped in an absurd sheep-print scarf — your <kanji>mother</kanji>'s sister, standing in for the <kanji>uncle</kanji> who usually reads the fortunes. The temple cats scatter, certain a sheep has invaded their mossy steps. Flustered, she throws up both hands and calls out across the courtyard — that startled, scarf-wrapped arrival is exactly who aunt means.
oba.reading_mnemonic: As the cats bolt, she cries <reading>Oh, baa!</reading> — sheep noise, not sheep, just her own flustered yelp. That startled cry, <reading>おば</reading>, is the exact sound of an aunt arriving at Grandma Kane's shrine every single year, scarf and all.
oba.description: The vowel here is short — don't stretch it into the longer sound used for the word for grandmother. They look and sound almost identical on the page but name different relatives, so lean on the mnemonic's short, startled yelp to keep the vowel length honest.

obaasan.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank where the washing happens, an old woman scrubs scarves for the whole village and refuses anyone's help. Children stop to greet her properly before crossing, and she waves them on with damp hands. To everyone nearby, respectfully, she's simply grandmother — polite, warm, and impossible to argue with.
obaasan.reading_mnemonic: おばあさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おばあさん</reading> read straight through.
obaasan.description: おばあさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly woman, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "ma'am" than a strict family term.

oboeru.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the new hire gets handed the entire onigiri shelf and told to have every position memorized by closing time. He stands under the fluorescent lights reciting shelf slots to himself, ignoring the beeping till, until the whole shelf is burned into his skull. That's what memorizing something for good actually takes.
oboeru.reading_mnemonic: He does it by muttering the same flat chant at the shelf, over and over, all shift: oh, bore, you, oh, bore, you. By closing time the chant has worn a groove straight into his memory, and what's left in his mouth is <reading>おぼえる</reading> — the sound of an <reading>oh, bore, you</reading> repeated until it sticks.

ocha.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she pours something pale green and steaming into small cups for every visitor who climbs the mossy steps, cats sniffing at the tray. One sip after the climb and you understand why she never skips this step: <kanji>tea</kanji>.
ocha.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hot can rolls off the shelf and lands right at your feet, steam still hissing from the seam. You yelp <reading>oh, cha!</reading> as it burns your fingers picking it up. That yelp is the reading: <reading>おちゃ</reading>.
ocha.description: Almost always appears with the honorific prefix お attached — daily speech rarely uses the bare form alone, even though it exists in other compounds.

ochiru.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker's phone slips loose from an unzipped pocket and tumbles by itself past the vending machine, bouncing down switchback after switchback with nobody chasing it. Nobody pushed it, nobody <kanji>dropped</kanji> it on purpose — it just goes, all the way down into the ravine below, entirely on its own.
ochiru.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a tanuki named Otchi loses his footing on the loose gravel and yelps "<reading>ouchy</reading>!" as he tumbles past the vending machine. His cry is how you remember <reading>おちる</reading>, the verb for anything that simply falls on its own.

odoru.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a pigeon gets trapped between the automatic doors as they slide open and shut, and starts hopping side to side to dodge them, wings out, feet shuffling under the fluorescent lights by the onigiri shelf. The beeping till never stops. That's dancing.
odoru.reading_mnemonic: Koichi waves a hand at the pigeon and complains about the <reading>odor</reading> it's kicking up mid-shuffle, feathers and dust everywhere. He starts calling the whole routine <reading>おどる</reading> whenever it happens again.

ohayou.meaning_mnemonic: Sei sprints through the school gate half a minute before the bell, hair still flat on one side, and skids past the sports field waving at everyone in one long breath instead of stopping for each person. The greeting comes out squashed together and a little too loud for how early it is — the sound the whole school makes before anyone's fully awake: good morning.
ohayou.reading_mnemonic: おはよう is plain kana, read exactly as spelled — call out <reading>おはよう</reading> the way Sei does, a rushed <reading>oh-hi-yo</reading> tossed over one shoulder while still running.
ohayou.description: This is the casual form, fine for classmates and friends; the polite version adds ございます on the end and is what you'd use with a teacher, a boss, or anyone you don't know well — dropping that ending in the wrong setting reads as overly familiar.

oishii.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, someone microwaves a lopsided onigiri that by all rights should be a disaster. Instead steam curls off it like it came from a five-star kitchen, and three strangers stop scrolling their phones just to watch you eat it. That's what delicious means here.
oishii.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it sounds — just say <reading>おいしい</reading>, no kanji hiding a different reading underneath.

oji.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the point where most people turn back, a man in hiking boots is refilling the lone vending machine himself — turns out it's your <kanji>uncle</kanji>, who apparently owns the machine and hikes up every week just to restock it. Your <kanji>father</kanji> waits at the trailhead with his arms folded. Nobody in the family questions this anymore. That's just what your uncle does.
oji.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a hiker rounds the last switchback and yelps, oh, gee, at the stranger already there. It's not a stranger — it's your uncle, and that startled gasp is exactly <reading>おじ</reading>: <reading>oh, gee</reading>, uncle, fancy meeting you up here.
oji.description: 叔父 marks a younger uncle — your parent's younger brother, or one married in — as distinct from the term for an older uncle, though both get shortened to the same casual address form in speech.

ojiisan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the old bell-ringer finally hands the rope to someone new: a stooped man with a walking stick who has swept the mossy steps every morning for forty years. The cats accept him instantly. The children bow and call him grandfather, and from that day the enormous bell is his alone to ring.
ojiisan.reading_mnemonic: おじいさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おじいさん</reading> read straight through.
ojiisan.description: おじいさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly man, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "grandpa" than a strict family term.

okaasan.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a boy collapses by the lone vending machine, certain he can't take one more step. Then his <kanji>mother</kanji> crests the rise behind him, unbothered, carrying his backpack, her water bottle, and a spare pair of socks, somehow not out of breath. That endless, unglamorous readiness is what mother (polite) means.
okaasan.reading_mnemonic: Driving the mountain trail's last hairpin toward the vending machine at the top, she doesn't slow down. The kids in the back seat brace and yell <reading>oh, car, san</reading> — which is exactly how <reading>おかあさん</reading> sounds, screamed by children who have done this drive with her before.

okaerinasai.meaning_mnemonic: The weary traveler finally reaches the door, walking stick clattering to the floor as the whole house seems to lean forward to catch him. You fling the door open before he can even knock, already shouting the words that make the <kanji>return</kanji> complete: welcome back.
okaerinasai.reading_mnemonic: Regular derivation: the polite prefix お plus 帰（かえ）plus the closing りなさい string together exactly as read, giving you <reading>おかえりなさい</reading>.

okane.meaning_mnemonic: Right before you lift that solid little roof and uncover the stash of gleaming nuggets, someone clears their throat politely — a soft "oh" announcing what's coming. Then out comes the precious <kanji>gold</kanji> that's been tucked away safe underneath, introduced now with the respect it deserves: money.
okane.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist on the mossy steps reaches for the offering box and a shrine cat slaps the hand away. They yelp <reading>oh, Kane</reading> at the old woman by the enormous bell, and that cry is exactly the sound of <reading>おかね</reading>.

okashi.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, someone leaves rice crackers by the bell as an offering. A <kanji>child</kanji> wriggles free of its wrap — arms flung wide, the exact shape that means <kanji>child</kanji> — snatches the whole plate and is found later face-down in crumbs. The monks give up on real food; now they just leave out sweets.
okashi.reading_mnemonic: Behind Koichi's konbini, there's a locked drawer everyone whispers about. Pry it open and you find <reading>おかし</reading> — an entire <reading>cache</reading> of sweets he's been hoarding since spring, more candy than any kid could eat in a year.

okiru.meaning_mnemonic: You fell asleep leaning against the onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini, and the till starts beeping nonstop over a jammed barcode. The noise won't quit, so you peel your eyes open, stagger upright, and blink at the fluorescent lights. That beeping is the whole story: to wake up, to get up.
okiru.reading_mnemonic: Oki the night clerk always oversleeps at Koichi's konbini. Every morning the manager shouts <reading>おきる</reading>, get up, and jangles the shutter key — <reading>oh, key</reading> — until Oki finally rolls off the floor and opens the store.

oku.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane crosses the mossy shrine steps every morning with a saucer of milk, choosing the exact same paw-worn stone by the enormous bell and setting it down without a wobble, right where the cats expect it. That precise, deliberate setting-down is putting or placing something exactly where it belongs.
oku.reading_mnemonic: She lowers the saucer onto a gnarled root of <reading>oak</reading> jutting from the shrine steps, whispering <reading>おく</reading> each time like a little rule for where things go.

okureru.meaning_mnemonic: You wake with the sun already high, sprint to Sei's school still wearing one shoe, and skid into the echoing hallway just as the bell finishes its last ring. Every other seat is filled, every face turned toward the door, toward you, standing there <kanji>late</kanji>.
okureru.reading_mnemonic: Sei tears down the mountain trail toward school, trips over a root by the lone vending machine, and yells '<reading>oh, curry!</reading>' as his lunchbox bursts open — <reading>おくれる</reading> — arriving with rice down his shirt and the bell already silent.

okuru.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine dispenses a paper crane instead of a drink. The hiker who buys it doesn't keep it — she opens her hand and lets the wind carry it down the switchbacks, waving until it's gone. Not keeping something, but launching it off toward someone else: that's what it means to send, to see off.
okuru.reading_mnemonic: A ranger at the mountain trail radios down every hiker who passes the summit, calling them her <reading>oak crew</reading>, and each evening she watches them go, waving from beside the vending machine until the trail is empty — that daily goodbye ritual is <reading>おくる</reading>.

okusan.meaning_mnemonic: At the very top of the mountain trail, a woman leans against the lone vending machine, patient in the shade of an oak, clearly waiting for somebody. Every exhausted hiker who finally staggers up assumes she must belong to whoever shows up gasping right after — and that assumption, someone waiting up there for her other half, is exactly (someone's) wife.
okusan.reading_mnemonic: She waves at the oak baking in the noon sun and calls down the trail, <reading>oak sun</reading> — the greeting that carries all the way to the switchbacks. That call is just how <reading>おくさん</reading> sounds: someone's wife, waiting patiently at the top for him to catch up.
okusan.description: 奥さん is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's wife — never your own. It also gets used casually to address a married woman in general, but it is not what a man calls his own wife.

omoi.meaning_mnemonic: Someone dumps a waterlogged stone lantern on the riverbank and asks for help hauling it home. Two people grab opposite ends, knees buckling, boots sinking a little deeper into the mud with every step, and the third person just watches them struggle: heavy, heavy, heavy, put it down before someone's back gives out.
omoi.reading_mnemonic: He tries to lift the waterlogged lantern off the riverbank by himself and it doesn't budge a centimeter. <reading>Oh my</reading>, he wheezes, letting it thud straight back into the mud — <reading>おもい</reading>, this thing is おもい, somebody else grab the other end already.

omoshiroi.meaning_mnemonic: You step out of Koichi's konbini into that blinding <kanji>white</kanji> flash of morning sun, and just as your eyes adjust, a delivery truck reverses straight into the onigiri sign with a crash. Everyone in line stops chewing to stare, because it's suddenly the most interesting, funniest thing that's happened all week.
omoshiroi.reading_mnemonic: Koichi surveys the flattened sign and mutters, '<reading>Oh, most royal</reading> mess I've ever seen,' and the customers by the till can't stop repeating it, laughing: <reading>おもしろい</reading>, they agree, watching him sweep up onigiri wrappers.

omou.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail you stop dead at the vending machine that has no business being up there, staring at the buttons without pressing any of them for a full minute. Your friend asks what's wrong. Nothing's wrong, you say — you're not doing anything, you're just standing here working through what you think and feel about a can of hot coffee.
omou.reading_mnemonic: Further up that same trail a cow blocks the path and just stares. You stare back, it stares back, and it finally lets out one flat moo. The only thing that comes out of your mouth in reply is <reading>おもう</reading> — that same flat, thinking exhale, an <reading>oh, moo</reading> for whatever's turning over in your head.

onaji.meaning_mnemonic: Two identical customers walk into Koichi's konbini at the same moment, in the same jacket, reaching for the same drink on the same shelf. The clerk rings up one barcode, scans the second item out of habit, and gets an identical receipt down to the second. Everything about the two of them matches, right down to the yawn.
onaji.reading_mnemonic: A hiker reaches the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and meets his own look-alike standing there already — same scar, same missing jacket button. Startled, he blurts his twin brother's name like a catchphrase, <reading>oh, Naji</reading>, which is exactly how the reading <reading>おなじ</reading> sounds, twin and echo both.

onaka.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a man buys every onigiri on the shelf and eats them standing at the counter, one after another, until his shirt stops closing. By the last one his middle has ballooned into a round drum he has to hold with both hands — his stomach, full past reason, the only thing left worth talking about.
onaka.reading_mnemonic: Koichi watches the man's belly swell round as a spare tire and mutters he looks like he's got one strapped <reading>on a car</reading>. The man just groans <reading>おなか</reading>, patting the bulge, and Koichi decides that's as good a name for it as any.

oneesan.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the captain of the school relay team, the one every younger kid looks up to and never dares call by her first name. She lines up the little ones, ties their shoelaces, and lets them win. That respectful, polite way you address someone's honored <kanji>older sister</kanji> is exactly this word.
oneesan.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports day, the team captain warms up by impersonating a horse, letting out an exaggerated <reading>neigh</reading> before every sprint. The younger kids salute her respectfully as <reading>おねえさん</reading>, the neighing captain, and nobody questions it.
oneesan.description: This word is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's older sister, or an unrelated older woman as a term of respect — it is not the plain, private term you'd use among your own family growing up with a younger sibling.

onegaishimasu.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the vending machine hums but won't drop the can until you press both palms together and bow toward it like it's a shrine bell. Everyone on the trail does this — palms pressed, head dipped, asking properly instead of grabbing — and that whole gesture, spoken aloud, is exactly how you ask someone for a favor: please.
onegaishimasu.reading_mnemonic: Oto kneels on the mountain trail and begs the temperamental vending machine, palms pressed together, chanting <reading>oh-nay-gai-shee-mas</reading> until the plea lands as <reading>おねがいします</reading>, her word for please, and the can finally drops.

ongaku.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's enormous bell doesn't just clang once — every cat in the yard has learned to time its own yowl to the ring, overlapping into layers of tone until stray clangs and cat wails resolve into something with rhythm. <kanji>Noise</kanji> agreeing to become rhythm like that is <kanji>music</kanji>.
ongaku.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 音 read おん, plus 楽 read がく, gives <reading>おんがく</reading>.

ongakushitsu.meaning_mnemonic: Down one echoing hallway at Sei's school there's a door nobody opens during class, because behind it a moose is mid-trumpet-solo, hooves stomping the beat, antlers knocking the light fixtures, every note pure <kanji>sound</kanji> bouncing off the tiles. The janitor padded every wall just to contain the daily racket — that padded <kanji>room</kanji> is the <kanji>music</kanji> room.
ongakushitsu.reading_mnemonic: Ask why the moose gets away with it and Sei just shrugs: the walls are soundproofed, so nobody outside hears him <reading>on-gawk-shoot</reading> through his solos — run those three words together and you get <reading>おんがくしつ</reading>.

oniisan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a young man rings the enormous bell for an elderly stranger who can't reach the rope, then carries her offering up the mossy steps himself while the shrine cats trail behind them. Nobody there is related to him, but everyone calls him <kanji>older brother</kanji> (polite) anyway, because that is simply what the word is for.
oniisan.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats climb his leg the moment he sits on the mossy steps, and he winces <reading>oh, knee, sahn</reading> as claws land — which is exactly how <reading>おにいさん</reading> sounds, and exactly why the cats never leave him alone.
oniisan.description: The polite, respectful form used to talk about or address someone else's older brother, or a young man in general as a courteous form of address — contrast with the plain word used only for your own older brother.

onnanohito.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> finally rises from her bow and falls into step beside the two legs she already knows as a <kanji>person</kanji>, the pair of them striding together past the cats toward the enormous bell. Kneeling figure plus striding legs, moving as one down the mossy steps — that's a grown woman.
onnanohito.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのひと</reading>.

onnanoko.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a tiny figure copies the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> pose out on the sports field, except her sweeping arm has curled inward to cradle a swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, little arms flung out against her chest. A pint-sized woman who still has a bundled baby's shape tucked in her arms — that's a girl.
onnanoko.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのこ</reading>.

ookii.meaning_mnemonic: The fisherman still has his arms flung wide, spread even wider today than yesterday, boasting about a catch that somehow grows a little more with every retelling. By the third telling his arms won't close in front of him at all — whatever he caught, it was <kanji>big</kanji>.
ookii.reading_mnemonic: 大 already sounds おお in words like this one, and き＋い are just the ordinary adjective ending, so 大きい reads straight through as <reading>おおきい</reading>.

oriru.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old fisherman poles his boat back to shore, but his cat refuses to get off, digging its claws into the plank. He tips the boat until the cat has no choice, and it tumbles onto the mud, forced to <kanji>descend</kanji> whether it wants to or not, with an offended yowl. That's the picture: reluctant, undignified, but off.
oriru.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the ferryman's cat is named <reading>Oriel</reading>, and every evening she refuses to disembark until he tips the boat. He mutters <reading>おりる</reading>, already off himself, as she finally splashes onto the mud beside him.

orosu.meaning_mnemonic: The shelf from 下 tilts, and the crate riding on it slides toward that dangling mark, sliding <kanji>down, below</kanji> the shelf's edge until it's about to hit the floor on its own. Before that happens you grab the crate and lower it yourself, hand over hand, taking it down deliberately instead of letting gravity finish the job.
orosu.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches above Koichi's konbini loading dock, puffing little flames as a signal. The clerks call back "<reading>oh, rose</reading>!" mishearing his screech for a flower, but they still know to <reading>おろす</reading> the delivery crates, lowering box after box off the truck onto the pavement.

osake.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats curled by the enormous bell always find the one jar the priest forgot to lock away. By the time you arrive for New Year's prayers, three of them are sprawled belly-up on the mossy steps, hiccuping softly, radiating that unmistakable warm reek of alcohol.
osake.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane spots the empty jar and gasps <reading>Oh, sake</reading>, her shocked cry stretching into <reading>おさけ</reading> as she chases the wobbling cats down the mossy steps, the enormous bell clanging behind her the whole way.
osake.description: お酒 means alcohol in general — beer, wine, spirits, anything you drink to get tipsy — not only the rice wine English speakers picture when they hear the word sake.

oshieru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the resident cat keeps hooking a paw around the base of the enormous bell, testing whether today is the day it tips. Grandma Kane never shouts. She crouches down and taps the stone beside it, over and over, every morning, until the cat starts copying the tap instead of shoving. Patient repetition until someone else can do it themselves — that is what it means to <kanji>teach</kanji>.
oshieru.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane repeats the tapping so many mornings that the cats start yowling it back at her, a flat little <reading>おしえる</reading>, oh-shee-eh-ru, and the tourists on the mossy steps swear it sounds exactly like <reading>oh, she'll</reading> — she'll keep doing this forever, patiently teaching.
oshieru.description: 教える covers more than formal instruction — it also means simply telling or informing someone of a fact, like giving directions to a station. The English gloss undersells how broad the everyday use is.

osoi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture someone hauling a shopping cart up the mountain trail, swearing they'll reach the vending machine at the top in five minutes. Forty minutes <kanji>later</kanji> they're still only halfway, one wheel catching on every root. By the time they finally arrive, the machine has sold its last can and the sun is already going down.
osoi.reading_mnemonic: Meet Ozawa, still dragging that cart. Every time someone yells at him to hurry, he just sighs, '<reading>oh, so</reading> tired,' stretching the words out to stall for time — and that long, dragging drawl is exactly the sound of <reading>おそい</reading>.

otearai.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank a door stands with a huge <kanji>hand</kanji> painted on it, fingers spread wide and dripping wet. Everyone in line shakes that dripping <kanji>hand</kanji> before ducking inside to hunt for the toilet. The dripping hand is the whole point of the sign: <kanji>wash</kanji> first, then go — this is the restroom.
otearai.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from its parts: お, 手 read て, 洗 read あら, and い combine to give <reading>おてあらい</reading>.

otokonohito.meaning_mnemonic: Out in the paddy, the <kanji>man</kanji> finally straightens up from the plow, gives his arm one last flex, and starts walking toward Koichi's konbini for something cold — those two legs carrying him off the field are exactly the <kanji>person</kanji> he becomes the second he stops working. Power in the field, then legs on the road: that's a grown man.
otokonohito.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのひと</reading>.

otokonoko.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, a small figure flexes one arm at the vending machine exactly like the <kanji>man</kanji> dragging his plow through the paddy, except his other arm is still tucked into a <kanji>child</kanji>'s swaddle, wriggling loose at his side. A miniature man who hasn't finished unwrapping yet — that's a boy.
otokonoko.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのこ</reading>.

otona.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> striding forward suddenly stops and throws their arms out wide, legs spread as far as they'll go — the stance for showing off something <kanji>big</kanji>. Nobody teaches a kid to stand like that; you grow into needing the room. Standing tall enough to need the whole stance is what makes you an adult.
otona.reading_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby stops wailing the second someone hands him <reading>a tuna</reading> — the calm is instant, like a switch. Jin ducks through the doorway just in time to see it: <reading>おとな</reading>, grown up right in front of him.

otosu.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a boy juggling erasers by the sports field takes aim and flings one straight <kanji>down</kanji> onto his rival's shoe, on purpose, then strolls off whistling. Nobody trips him, nothing slips — he means to send it down, and that deliberate act of sending something down is the whole word.
otosu.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a boy named Otto stands at the sports field fence and shouts "<reading>oh, toss</reading> it here!" before yanking the ball straight down out of the air himself. That shout is how you remember <reading>おとす</reading>, the verb for deliberately dropping something.

ototoi.meaning_mnemonic: Count back <kanji>one</kanji> more <kanji>day</kanji> past yesterday and you land on <vocabulary>the day before yesterday</vocabulary>.
ototoi.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank an <reading>otter toy</reading> washes ashore two days late, stamped <reading>おととい</reading> for <vocabulary>the day before yesterday</vocabulary> it went missing.

otousan.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, red-faced and sweating under the noon sun, a <kanji>father</kanji> hauls a stalled cart the last hundred meters by rope while his kid cheers from beside the lone vending machine. That's the picture pinned to <kanji>father</kanji>, polite: the dad you'd point out respectfully to a stranger, not the tired grumble you'd use at home.
otousan.reading_mnemonic: As he heaves the cart past the vending machine, the kid shouts the word for him, and it lands in your ear as <reading>oh, tow, sun</reading> — dad towing, sun blazing overhead — the same beats as <reading>おとうさん</reading>. That's the polite word for pointing him out to a stranger on the trail, not the plain one for talking about your own.
otousan.description: お父さん (otousan) is the polite, respectful word for father — what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father in conversation. It contrasts with the plain 父 (chichi), which you use only when talking about your own father to people outside the family.

otouto.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the pesky little brother who trails you everywhere, small enough that shopkeepers assume he's still in diapers, always demanding you carry him piggyback until your arms give out. That exact whiny, tag-along presence is what points straight at a <kanji>younger brother</kanji>.
otouto.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the small brother stomps on the same customer's foot twice reaching for onigiri, and the customer yelps <reading>oh, toe, toe</reading> each time. The beeping till clerk sighs and says it again, plain: <reading>おとうと</reading>, always causing trouble.

otsuri.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman reels in his line expecting a fish and instead pulls up a dripping fistful of coins, more than he ever paid to be there. He shrugs, stuffs the extra into his pocket, and keeps casting. That unexpected excess handed back to you is change.
otsuri.reading_mnemonic: Otsu, the riverbank fisherman, always over-tips the ferry boy, then waves off the leftover coins with a cheerful <reading>oh, too rich</reading>! Grandma Kane says his running joke is exactly how you remember <reading>おつり</reading>, the change he never wants back.

otto.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a woman is washing laundry when her <kanji>husband</kanji> wades in fully dressed, chasing a sock that floated loose, soaking his only good shirt in the process. She doesn't even look up — of course that's who waded in after one sock, nobody else would bother. That reliable, faintly ridiculous devotion is (my) husband.
otto.reading_mnemonic: He climbs out of the river dripping head to toe, sock triumphantly in hand, and she just sighs, <reading>Otto</reading>, not again — the exact sound of <reading>おっと</reading>, her name for the husband who always wades in after the laundry.
otto.description: 夫 is the plain way a wife refers to her own husband when speaking to other people — not a word she'd use to call out to him directly, and not used for someone else's husband.

owari.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, a relay race is going fine until the last runner trips over his own shoelace two meters from the tape and just lies there. The whistle blows anyway. Nobody finishes cleanly, but the race is over, and over is over.
owari.reading_mnemonic: A spinning top at Grandma Kane's shrine wobbles slower and slower across the mossy steps until it tips onto its side. A cat watches it go <reading>oh, whirly</reading> one last time before it stops — that stop is 「<reading>おわり</reading>」, the end.

owaru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps go quiet and the cats freeze mid-stretch the instant the enormous bell rings its last, sagging note. Nobody rings it twice — that single dying note is the whole signal that whatever was happening on those steps is done, over, finished, and everyone on the steps knows to stand up and leave.
owaru.reading_mnemonic: One particular shrine cat, Ru, yowls <reading>Oh, wow, Roo!</reading> every time that last bell note dies away, startled it's really over. The yowl blurs into <reading>おわる</reading> — the sound of the exact moment the ceremony ends and Ru stops caring about any of it.

oyasuminasai.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening the shrine cats pile onto Grandma Kane's mossy steps, and one always shoves against the enormous bell just as she pulls the rope, so the whole shrine rings out over the neighborhood at the exact moment she says her nightly line to send everyone home to bed: good night.
oyasuminasai.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it sounds, kana all the way through, so there's no puzzle to solve — just recognize <reading>おやすみなさい</reading> on sight and you already have the reading.

oyogu.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi falls face-first into the river trying to grab a floating onigiri wrapper before it drifts past Grandma Kane's shrine steps. He can't touch the bottom, so he flails, arms churning, head barely above the current, refusing to let go of the wrapper. That desperate, arms-churning motion through water is to swim.
oyogu.reading_mnemonic: Watching him thrash, the cats lined up on the shrine steps cheer him on with what sounds like <reading>oh-yo-go</reading>, as if urging 'oh, go, go!' — close enough to <reading>およぐ</reading> that Koichi adopts it as his own victory shout every time he drags himself back to shore.

pan.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer grabs the last loaf off the shelf right as the till starts beeping, panicking because the shelf is otherwise all onigiri. He hugs it like it's the only bread left in Japan, mutters thanks under the fluorescent lights, and pays before anyone else spots it.
pan.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read: <reading>パン</reading>, borrowed straight from Portuguese pão — no derivation needed.

pasokon.meaning_mnemonic: In Koichi's konbini, beside the onigiri shelf, a customer heaves a slab of grey plastic onto the counter and starts jabbing it the way he jabs the beeping till. Half-finished English stutters out of its little speaker — pa, so, kon — until the whole register short-circuits into a glowing screen full of spreadsheets: a computer, ringing up groceries nobody asked it to buy.
pasokon.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, no kanji hiding underneath — just the borrowed English squeezed down to fit: <reading>パソコン</reading>.

pen.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine sells exactly one item no hiker asked for: a pen that leaks the instant you click it, blooming blue across your knuckles and smearing your name across the summit logbook the second you try to sign it — a pen, and now a permanent one.
pen.reading_mnemonic: ペン is kana all the way through, read exactly as written and borrowed straight from English: 「<reading>ペン</reading>」 is simply pen.

raigetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The rice due to <kanji>come</kanji> up won't be ready until one more lap of the <kanji>moon</kanji> finishes, and that lap is <vocabulary>next month</vocabulary>.

rainen.meaning_mnemonic: Another chevron is about to <kanji>come</kanji>, scratched onto the shield-board for a <kanji>year</kanji> that hasn't happened yet: <vocabulary>next year</vocabulary>.

raishuu.meaning_mnemonic: A crop that hasn't <kanji>come</kanji> up yet breaks the surface on the <kanji>week</kanji> after this one, which is exactly <vocabulary>next week</vocabulary>.

rajio.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the one enormous bell hasn't been rung in months, yet the cats gather on the mossy steps every evening at six, ears flat, tails puffed. Tucked behind the bell sits a cracked wooden box quietly muttering a weather report to no one. The cats, it turns out, have been listening to the shrine's radio the whole time.
rajio.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ラジオ</reading> is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so the reading is simply <reading>ラジオ</reading> itself — nothing to derive.

rei.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the annual bell inspection turns up nothing wrong, and the inspector announces the crack count in his most formal voice: <vocabulary>zero (formal)</vocabulary>.
rei.description: 零 marks the formal, technical zero, used in temperatures, exam scores, and official readings, where everyday speech reaches for a plainer word instead.

reizouko.meaning_mnemonic: Every night at Grandma Kane's shrine, the rice offerings spoil in the heat before the cats even get to them, so the priest wedges a tall humming metal locker in beside the mossy steps. It breathes <kanji>cool</kanji> air and keeps everything frost-stiff till morning. Villagers just call the humming locker the refrigerator.
reizouko.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 冷 read れい, plus 蔵 read ぞう, plus 庫 read こ, which gives <reading>れいぞうこ</reading>.

rekishi.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail turns out to be decades older than the trail itself — dented, rusted, still dispensing drinks with labels nobody's printed in years. Under it, hikers dig up a buried plaque naming every person who hauled supplies up before there was any summit machine at all. Layers of forgotten human effort stacked beneath one ordinary object: that's history.
rekishi.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 歴 read れき, plus 史 read し, gives <reading>れきし</reading>.

renshuu-suru.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, a wren lands by the goalpost and shoos the same three pigeons off the grass, over and over, a hundred times before the whistle even blows. It never varies the routine, never skips a rep — that relentless repeating drill, doing the same motion until it's automatic, is what to practice means.
renshuu-suru.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just those pieces stacked together: 練 read れん, plus 習 read しゅう, plus する, giving <reading>れんしゅうする</reading>.

resutoran.meaning_mnemonic: Someone moors a floating diner to a post on the riverbank so it can't drift off. A chalkboard menu hangs from the mast, and the one waiter wades out in rubber boots to deliver plates. Tourists queue on the bank just to eat somewhere that technically counts as a restaurant, even though it's really a raft with silverware.
resutoran.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>レストラン</reading>.
resutoran.description: レストラン specifically means a Western-style sit-down restaurant. Casual Japanese eateries, noodle counters, and specialty food shops usually go by other names, not this word.

riyuu.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a hiker turns back at the exact same rock every single time, and every time he has a brand new one lined up before anyone even asks — the sun, his knee, a text he needs to send. Stack enough of those up and you've got his <kanji>reason</kanji>, freshly invented, every single climb.
riyuu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 理 read り, plus 由 read ゆう, gives <reading>りゆう</reading>.

roku-v.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing was ever added to the <kanji>six</kanji> kanji, so the <vocabulary>six</vocabulary> word is just that same kanji standing alone.

ryokan.meaning_mnemonic: You cross the riverbank on a rickety ferry, soaked and shivering at the end of a long <kanji>trip</kanji>, and the only <kanji>building</kanji> on the far bank is a lantern-lit lodge with steaming baths and futons laid out. There's nowhere else to go, so you stay the night. That riverside shelter with a bath and a bed is an inn.
ryokan.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 旅 read りょ, plus 館 read かん, gives <reading>りょかん</reading>.

ryokou-suru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>go</kanji> stick figure — legs split wide, one arm swinging forward — never settles for a single step out the door. He straps on a pack and keeps swinging that same arm through town after town, station after station, never breaking stride. Repeating the going, over and over, day after day, without ever stopping to unpack: that ceaseless, restless going is what it means to <kanji>travel</kanji>.
ryokou-suru.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Koichi</reading> hangs a CLOSED sign over the till for the first time in years, laces his boots by the onigiri shelf, and walks out past the beeping doors — the konbini king is finally going to <reading>りょこうする</reading>.

ryokou.meaning_mnemonic: Someone frames a photo of the <kanji>go</kanji> stick figure — caught mid-stride, one arm swinging forward, legs split over unfamiliar ground — and pins it above their desk like a promise. It isn't him going right now; it's the single, saved-up going still waiting to happen, the whole journey folded into one still frame. That pinned promise of a future going is a <kanji>trip</kanji>.
ryokou.reading_mnemonic: Behind the register, <reading>Koichi</reading> tapes up one photo: himself atop the mountain trail, out of breath beside that improbable vending machine. He taps it every morning and says the word, <reading>りょこう</reading> — the one trip he ever took.

ryouri-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi drags a portable stove behind the onigiri shelf and starts frying eggs directly under the beeping till, measuring each yolk against his own cold <kanji>logic</kanji>, ash drifting onto the rice balls, customers stepping over the smoke to pay — until the whole fluorescent-lit konbini smells like dinner, because that chaos is cooking.
ryouri-suru.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 料 read りょう, plus 理 read り, plus す, plus る, gives <reading>りょうりする</reading>.

ryouri.meaning_mnemonic: It's 2 a.m. at Koichi's konbini, fluorescent lights buzzing over the onigiri shelf while the till beeps through a lull. Bored, the night clerk pulls ingredients off the shelves — instant miso, a rice ball, a squeeze of mayo — and assembles them into something new on the counter, rejecting any combo that bends his straight-line <kanji>reason</kanji>. By closing, he's turned convenience-store scraps into an actual dish: cooking.
ryouri.reading_mnemonic: The clerk introduces himself over the counter, 'I'm <reading>Leo Uri</reading>, konbini cooking champion of aisle three.' He says his name so fast it comes out as one word — <reading>りょうり</reading> — which is exactly how you ask for cooking or a dish.

ryoushuusho.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the register light dims like the sinking sun that once taught your hand to write. As it fades, the printer's little arm keeps that same sun-fed urge to <kanji>write</kanji>, scribbling out a curling strip of paper long after the customer's gone. That printed proof of the sale is the receipt.
ryoushuusho.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 領 read りょう, plus 収 read しゅう, plus 書 read しょ, gives <reading>りょうしゅうしょ</reading>.

sagaru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat swats the offering shelf until the charm hanging beneath it swings loose, dropping further and further past the mossy steps — everything about it points one way, straight <kanji>below</kanji> where it used to sit: to go down, fall.
sagaru.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches on the shrine's bell rope, but her weight drags it lower and lower until it dips past the mossy steps — she squawks a mournful 「<reading>さがる</reading>」, her cry sounding just like <reading>saga-ru</reading>, as she watches herself sink: to go down, fall.

sagasu.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini stocks a hundred kinds of onigiri, and today he's misplaced the exact one he wants. He paces the fluorescent-bright aisles, checks behind the beeping till, digs through the shelf twice — turning the whole store over just to search for a single rice ball he's sure is still there.
sagasu.reading_mnemonic: Koichi narrates his own hunt like a soap opera, sweeping a hand across the onigiri shelf: '<reading>Saga's</reading> search for the missing rice ball continues...' he announces to no one, and every time he says it, the line comes out sounding exactly like <reading>さがす</reading>.

sai-age.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps are lined with birthday candles instead of stone lanterns, one candle burning on every step. The shrine cats trot past blowing each one out in turn, and the shrine keeper explains he isn't counting steps at all — he's counting years old (counter), the same tally kept every birthday.
sai-age.reading_mnemonic: 歳 does not change its sound in this counter; it keeps the reading you already learned for the kanji: <reading>さい</reading>.

saifu.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone wading across loses their footing, and a slim leather fold flies from their pocket mid-splash. Coins scatter into the current and bills drift downstream like paper boats, but the fold itself washes up on the bank, empty and dripping — proof that whatever it once held, it's still a wallet.
saifu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 財 read さい, plus 布 read ふ, gives you <reading>さいふ</reading>.

saigo.meaning_mnemonic: The trailing runner never catches up — race after race he crosses last, one leg forever dangling <kanji>behind</kanji> him. Meet after meet he never places anywhere but there: dead last, the <kanji>utmost</kanji> end of the results board, right where <kanji>after</kanji> always plants him.
saigo.reading_mnemonic: At the finish line, the runner who's always after, always behind, finally stumbles in, gives one long <reading>sigh</reading>, and is waved through with a flat <reading>go</reading> — sigh, go, <reading>さいご</reading>, last place, race over.

saisho.meaning_mnemonic: Before Grandma Kane opens the shrine gates, one scrawny cat drags itself onto the bell platform and lets out an enormous, theatrical sigh — stretching, yawning, groaning at the sunrise. Nothing at the shrine happens before that sigh; the monks wait for it, the other cats wait for it. It's the <kanji>utmost</kanji> edge of the day, its very <kanji>beginning</kanji>.
saisho.reading_mnemonic: Locals nickname that daily ritual the <reading>sigh-show</reading> — say it fast and it becomes <reading>さいしょ</reading>. It's the first performance of the morning at the shrine, and by shrine law nothing else is allowed to start before it airs.

sakana.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman casts his line for hours and reels in nothing but weeds, until a sudden tug nearly drags him into the water — he hauls back to find something flopping on the bank, gasping right alongside him. That flopping, gasping catch is the entire reason anyone stands at a riverbank all afternoon: fish.
sakana.reading_mnemonic: The fisherwoman working that same riverbank, <reading>Sock Anna</reading>, wades in after a lost sock and something latches onto her bare foot instead of the fabric — she yelps out the same sound as her own name, <reading>さかな</reading>, and from then on that's just the word for fish.

samui.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail the vending machine hums alone in the wind, and a stray dog presses its whole body against the machine's warm metal side, shivering so hard its bark comes out broken and stuttering instead of sharp. That shudder, the cold that gets into your bones from the outside air, is the meaning.
samui.reading_mnemonic: A hiker named Sam reaches the vending machine at the summit with his teeth chattering so hard the words come out garbled, over and over, until he finally zips his coat. Hear that chatter as <reading>さむい</reading>: <reading>some moo, eh</reading>, repeated until the shivering finally stops.

san-v.meaning_mnemonic: There's no gap between the <kanji>three</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>three</vocabulary> word — write one and you've written the other.

sanpo-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening a stray dog checks the same three streets in the same order — the bakery, the vending machine, the bridge — not hunting for anything, just <kanji>walking</kanji> them because the walking itself is the point. No errand starts the loop and no errand ends it; it just circles the block and lets itself back home. That aimless, looping stroll, taken for its own sake, is what it means to take a walk.
sanpo-suru.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 散 read さん, plus 歩 read ぽ, plus す, plus る, gives <reading>さんぽする</reading>.

sara.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone at the riverbank campsite balances their food on flat stones fished out of the water, one apiece, since nobody packed real ones. It works fine until the stones tip over the second a fish bone hits them. What the trip actually needed was a proper plate.
sara.reading_mnemonic: Sara refuses to eat off river stones like the rest of the campers and packs an actual dish for every single meal. The others tease that of course <reading>Sara</reading> brought her own <reading>さら</reading> - it's practically her name.

satou.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone drops a paper packet off the little footbridge, and instead of sinking it dissolves mid-air into the current, turning a whole stretch of water thick and slow, the fish drifting through it like it's honey — that's what falls into your tea as sugar.
satou.reading_mnemonic: Sei's homeroom teacher introduces herself as <reading>Sato</reading>-sensei, then skips the chalkboard and just pours a spoonful into her tea to prove the name: <reading>さとう</reading>, she says, tapping the packet, sweet like she is.

satsu-counter.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the librarian stacks returned homework workbooks so high on one cart that the bottom shelf buckles and the whole tower slides across the echoing hallway floor, spine over spine, until it rams the trophy case. She doesn't reshelve them — she just counts how many books fell, one after another, in that same skidding stack.
satsu-counter.reading_mnemonic: 冊 is regular here: the reading you already learned for the kanji itself is the whole word, <reading>さつ</reading>.

sayounara.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, an old bell only gets rung once a year, at the one moment everyone agrees a season has truly ended. Nobody rings it for a quick trip to the vending machine and back. When it finally tolls, mossy steps empty, cats scatter, and the whole shrine seems to exhale: goodbye.
sayounara.reading_mnemonic: Picture <reading>さようなら</reading> as someone slowly waving from a departing ferry, calling out "<reading>sigh-oh-nara</reading>" until the shape of them disappears past the riverbank.
sayounara.description: This word carries real finality — Japanese speakers reach for it when a parting is long, permanent, or dramatic (moving away, a breakup), not for the daily goodbye to a coworker or friend you'll see tomorrow, where a lighter phrase fits better.

seito.meaning_mnemonic: That same patch of earth where a seed splits open into <kanji>life</kanji> now stretches out as a schoolyard, planted with row after row of identical green shoots, all still too short to see over the fence. They're not finished yet — still rooted, still waiting their turn to grow — and that half-grown state is exactly what a pupil is.
seito.reading_mnemonic: 生 gives せい and 徒 gives と, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>せいと</reading>.

seki-seat.meaning_mnemonic: A heron wades to the exact same flat rock on the riverbank every single evening, shoves aside any duck already perched there, and refuses to fish from anywhere else. It has, unmistakably, claimed its seat, and nothing short of a flood will move it.
seki-seat.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just this kanji's own taught sound: 席 is read <reading>せき</reading>, exactly as you already learned it.

sekken.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the resident cats bats a pale, chalky slab off the mossy steps and it tumbles straight into the offering basin, foaming white as it rolls under the water until the cat backs away, thoroughly appalled at what it started. A stone that lathers the moment it touches water is soap.
sekken.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 石 read せっ, plus 鹸 read けん, gives <reading>せっけん</reading>.

semai.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the onigiri shelf until the aisle behind it chokes down to nothing — one shoulder in, one shoulder out, and the till starts beeping because somebody's stuck sideways. He wedges a mop bucket into the last gap out of spite and now there isn't even room to breathe: narrow, cramped, narrow, cramped, nobody move.
semai.reading_mnemonic: Sammy tries to squeeze past the onigiri shelf sideways and gets wedged solid between two racks while the till keeps beeping at him for no reason. <reading>Sammy</reading> can't move an inch, and everyone shuffling past just mutters the same thing at him: <reading>せまい</reading>, せまい, you picked the worst aisle.

sen-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>thousand</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>thousand</vocabulary> word are one and the same character, doing double duty as itself.

sengetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The one already <kanji>ahead</kanji> of you finished its <kanji>moon</kanji>-lap before you did, and that finished lap is <vocabulary>last month</vocabulary>.

sensei.meaning_mnemonic: The legs that always stride out <kanji>ahead</kanji> of everyone reach the classroom first, plant themselves at the front, and refuse to sit down. Beneath their feet is the same patch of ground where a seed cracks open into <kanji>life</kanji> — because this is the one person whose ideas take root in you and grow. That's a teacher.
sensei.reading_mnemonic: 先 gives せん and 生 supplies the same せい you know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student — stack them together and you get exactly 「<reading>せんせい</reading>」.

senshuu.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever strode <kanji>ahead</kanji> already crossed the <kanji>week</kanji> before this one, and that finished lap is <vocabulary>last week</vocabulary>.

sentaku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Every basket of clothes at the riverbank ends the same way: someone dunks the pile in the current to <kanji>wash</kanji> it, scrubs a shirt against a flat rock, and chases a runaway sock bobbing downstream before it drowns — the whole soggy, splashing chore of getting clothes clean is doing the laundry.
sentaku-suru.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman wades in to net a runaway sock and hollers <reading>Send sock, sure!</reading> — his gruff cry for <reading>せんたくする</reading>, as he wrings it out and pins it up to dry with the rest of the wash.

setsumei-suru.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till locks up mid-beep and nobody knows why. The new clerk grabs a marker, draws arrows all over a torn onigiri wrapper, and holds it up to the confused line of customers in the <kanji>bright</kanji> fluorescent light, mapping error code to fix one scribble at a time. That's the whole job here: to explain, arrow by arrow, until the confusion drains out of the room.
setsumei-suru.reading_mnemonic: Put the known readings together in order: 説 as せつ, 明 as めい, then する, and you get <reading>せつめいする</reading>.

shashin.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a dozen cats sprawl across the mossy steps, and just as the great bell tolls, a bulb pops and freezes every yawn and twitching tail at once, the whole <kanji>true</kanji> moment trapped flat and still forever. That frozen instant, kept for good, is a photograph.
shashin.reading_mnemonic: A tourist barges into the shrine's hush, camera raised, and the old priest just hisses <reading>shush in</reading> before you break it — too late, the shutter already clicked. He hands back the camera; the saved file reads simply <reading>しゃしん</reading>.

shatsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer leans too far over the counter to grab an onigiri and his loose top catches on the price scanner by the till. The register beeps furiously, over and over, as if trying to ring up the fabric itself, until Koichi peels the sleeve free and holds up the wrinkled shirt like it just came off the shelf.
shatsu.reading_mnemonic: シャツ is written the way it sounds — no kanji to decode, just read the kana straight across as <reading>シャツ</reading>.

shi-num.meaning_mnemonic: Four (alt) is simply the <kanji>four</kanji> kanji on its own, so the kanji and the <vocabulary>four (alt)</vocabulary> word mean exactly the same thing.

shichi-num.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>seven (alt)</vocabulary> word are one and the same, meaning exactly what the kanji already taught you.

shigoto.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody has to haul crates up the steep mountain trail to refill that one improbable vending machine at the summit, every single day, rain or shine, boots blistering, back aching under the load — they <kanji>attend</kanji> that machine like a post, every crate another <kanji>matter</kanji> to haul, so that grinding, thankless climb up and back down again is what work means.
shigoto.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 仕 read し, plus 事 read ごと, gives <reading>しごと</reading>.

shigotoba.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi never really leaves his konbini. The fluorescent lights buzz all night, the onigiri shelf never empties, and he sleeps propped against the beeping till, still <kanji>attending</kanji> between customers. Every <kanji>matter</kanji> in that cramped bright box — from the door to the register — has become the one <kanji>place</kanji> that is entirely his workplace, no separate word needed.
shigotoba.reading_mnemonic: You already know the pieces: 仕 as し, 事 as ごと, 場 as ば, which line up as <reading>しごとば</reading>.

shikashi.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats sprawl fast asleep across every mossy step, completely unbothered by the enormous bell hanging right over their heads. However, the instant a visitor's hand touches the bell rope, every single cat bolts upright at once and scatters. That flip from total calm to sudden chaos, with nothing gradual about it, is however.
shikashi.reading_mnemonic: Kana straight through — sound out <reading>しかし</reading> exactly as written and you have already got the reading.

shiken.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps fill every February with silent students ringing the one enormous bell, clapping twice, and begging the cats for luck. The weight of it all — one bell, one prayer, one date circled on the calendar for weeks — is exactly what an exam is: the single test everything has been building toward.
shiken.reading_mnemonic: A student rings Grandma Kane's enormous bell so hard a cat topples off the railing, then stands there muttering over and over, <reading>しけん</reading>, convincing herself <reading>she can</reading> pass tomorrow's exam if the bell just rings back loud enough.

shimeru.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at Grandma Kane's shrine, the last visitor leaves and the ancient gate groans on its hinges. The caretaker leans her whole weight into it until the two heavy halves meet with a dull clang, sealing the mossy steps off from the night and the cats out. That final clang is the meaning: to close.
shimeru.reading_mnemonic: The caretaker's name is Shizu, and when she shimmers the bronze gate shut at dusk, the metal catches the last orange light and seems to glow all along its seam. She <reading>shimmers</reading> it closed every single night — say <reading>しめる</reading> and picture that glowing gate swinging to.

shinbun.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, someone <kanji>new</kanji> in town stands beaming beside a fresh stack of printed pages, and every cat under the big bell presses an ear to the stack like it's a gate, straining to <kanji>hear</kanji> what's inside before anyone thinks to ask. By the time the bell rings, the whole shrine already knows what's inside those pages pressed flat — the newspaper.
shinbun.reading_mnemonic: 新聞 keeps both taught readings back to back, so read it as <reading>しんぶん</reading> — new, then hear.

shinpai-suru.meaning_mnemonic: You leave the house and immediately start replaying the stove, the door, the iron — did you actually turn them off? By the time you reach the corner you've invented three new disasters that haven't happened yet. That spiral of manufactured dread, dragging you back home just to check, is what it feels like to worry.
shinpai-suru.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its pieces stacked together: 心 read しん, plus 配 read ぱい, plus す and る, giving <reading>しんぱいする</reading>.

shinsetsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist misses the mossy top step and goes down hard, shin <kanji>cut</kanji> open on the stone. Before they finish wincing, an old woman appears from nowhere, hoists them up, and walks them the rest of the way to the bell, never once mentioning her own bad knees. That unasked-for shin-saving is what kind means here.
shinsetsu.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 親 as しん plus 切 as せつ gives you 「<reading>しんせつ</reading>」.

shinu.meaning_mnemonic: Deep on the back shelf of Koichi's konbini, past its printed deadline, the oldest onigiri finally gives out — filling gone grey, wrapper gone limp, the little countdown sticker flashing red one last time before going dark. Koichi bows his head over it for a solid ten seconds. It has died.
shinu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 死 read し plus the verb ending ぬ, carried straight through as <reading>しぬ</reading>.

shio.meaning_mnemonic: Every dawn at Grandma Kane's shrine, the temple cats watch her fling a scoop of coarse white grains across the gate, a purifying toss meant to sting bare skin. One greedy cat licks a stray grain from the stone, recoils hard, and spends the hour draining the well dry. That sharp mineral bite on its tongue is salt.
shio.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane hands her shrine attendant Ren a sack for the purification toss. He trips on the steps, and it bursts everywhere as he yelps '<reading>She, oh!</reading>' watching grains fill his sandals — that yelp is exactly <reading>しお</reading>, salt.

shiro-color.meaning_mnemonic: You're still blinking from that blinding ray outside Koichi's konbini, and when your eyes finally adjust, the whole street looks bleached — the cars, the sidewalk, even the shopkeeper's apron drained of every color into the same flat <kanji>white</kanji>. That's the word for what you're staring at.
shiro-color.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone drags a bedsheet through the shallows to rinse out a grass stain, wringing it out and snapping it flat against the current. It bleaches paler with every pass until it's blinding, and the launderer just mutters <reading>show row</reading> at the glare — the closest an English mouth gets to <reading>しろ</reading>, the reading for this exact shade of white.

shiroi.meaning_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, that same blinding morning ray never fades — it keeps hitting the onigiri shelf until every wrapper on it bleaches to the exact same shade of <kanji>white</kanji>. The till keeps beeping uselessly, unable to tell one product from another anymore.
shiroi.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the gym teacher blows her whistle so hard it slips loose and bounces into a bucket of chalk dust. The cloud that erupts sends the whole team sneezing out a ragged <reading>shrew, eee</reading>, which is exactly <reading>しろい</reading>, the word for white.

shiru.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the vending machine at the summit restocks like magic — until you catch the delivery man radioing ahead to a friend at dawn. Once you've seen him do it, you can't pretend not to anymore; the secret clicks into place and stays there. That sudden, permanent click, the moment the secret becomes yours, is what it means to know something.
shiru.reading_mnemonic: A shrew has been staking out those delivery crates for weeks and finally works out that the truck always arrives at dawn. <reading>しる</reading>, it seems to squeak, sounding just like <reading>shrew</reading> — now it knows exactly when to dart in before the machine even opens.
shiru.description: 知る marks the moment something becomes known, not the ongoing state of knowing it — for an ongoing "I know," learners need the continuous て-form instead of this plain form standing alone.

shita-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone balances a shelf mid-air while doing the laundry, and the little mark dangling off underneath it stops waiting — it drops, plop, straight into the current. Everything about that shelf still leans toward the space it fell from: <kanji>down</kanji>, <kanji>below</kanji> the surface, gone.
shita-v.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a clerk crawls behind the beeping till to coat the sticky floor with tar. A dropped onigiri rolls into the wet stripe, fluorescent lights buzzing, and from the floor she mutters <reading>she tar</reading>, which is exactly the sound of <reading>した</reading>.

shitsumon-suru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine you climb the mossy steps, grab the rope on the enormous bell, and haul it down hard enough to scatter every cat on the grounds. That's the only way anyone up there notices you've got something to <kanji>ask</kanji> — the bell itself answers nothing, it just announces that a <kanji>question</kanji> is on its way. That deliberate, rope-hauling demand for attention before you ever open your mouth is what it means to ask a question.
shitsumon-suru.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 質 read しつ, plus 問 read もん, plus す, plus る, gives <reading>しつもんする</reading>.

shitsumon.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, one customer plants himself at the register and <kanji>asks</kanji> about every single item on the shelf — the onigiri's expiration, why the till beeps twice, whether the till itself has feelings. Koichi answers thirty of these before the line behind reaches the door, and there's no sign of them stopping.
shitsumon.reading_mnemonic: Watching them pile up, Koichi mutters to the next person in line, <reading>she's too much</reading> — and the words blur into <reading>しつもん</reading>, the very thing holding up his till: one more question, then another, then another.

shitsurei-suru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a monk barges through a crowd of cats mid-ceremony, gives the enormous bell one stiff bow, and backs straight out through the gate before the abbot can even turn around. That clipped, apologetic retreat — bow, mutter, gone — is exactly what to excuse oneself means: leaving politely before you've overstayed the room.
shitsurei-suru.reading_mnemonic: You already know the pieces: 失 as しつ, 礼 as れい, then す and る, which line up as <reading>しつれいする</reading>.

shizuka.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps lead up to one enormous bell that nobody dares ring — even the cats stop mid-stride and flatten their ears, padding past on silent paws so nothing disturbs the hush. Not a chime, not a meow, not a footstep. That held-breath stillness is quiet.
shizuka.reading_mnemonic: A cat named Shizuka naps under that same enormous bell, and visitors tiptoe past whispering '<reading>she's-zoo-kah</reading>, don't wake her' so as not to break the hush. That whispered warning carries 「<reading>しずか</reading>」.

shokuji-suru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats gather every dusk under the little tent-roof shelter that is, as you already know, a roof made entirely of dinner. Tonight it's a full sit-down affair: bowls set in a row, tails tucked, nobody leaving until the tray's been properly cleared, one official <kanji>matter</kanji>. That polite, four-legged sitting-down to <kanji>eat</kanji> is what the word describes — an actual meal, not just a snack.
shokuji-suru.reading_mnemonic: Add the readings in order — 食 as しょく, 事 as じ, then する — and you already have <reading>しょくじする</reading>.

shokuji.meaning_mnemonic: At exactly noon a bell rings through Sei's school, and dozens of <kanji>eat</kanji> tents pop up along the hallway floor — the same roof-made-of-dinner shelter you already know, one for every student ducking in to eat. Trays pile up under each roof until the bell rings again and reports the heap as one official <kanji>matter</kanji>. That whole stretch, from first bite to last, is the meal.
shokuji.reading_mnemonic: A student named Shoko checks her watch in the echoing hallway and gasps '<reading>Shock, gee</reading>, is it that late already?' — she's smelling the trays before she sees them. That gasp is exactly <reading>しょくじ</reading>: meal.

shorui.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the sun sinks in the window behind the register the way it always does, and a hand starts to <kanji>write</kanji> on its own, filling page after page. But tonight it doesn't stop at one notebook — it keeps going until the whole counter is buried under stacked, filled pages: a mountain of documents nobody asked for.
shorui.reading_mnemonic: You already know both halves from the kanji: 書 is しょ and 類 is るい, so the word reads <reading>しょるい</reading>.

shoukai-suru.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the new transfer student gets dragged in front of the class by the homeroom teacher, who cups both hands around her mouth like a game-show host unveiling a prize. Name, hometown, hobby — she rattles off all three before the poor kid can say a single word himself. That shove-and-announce routine is what it means to introduce someone.
shoukai-suru.reading_mnemonic: Line up the readings you already know — 紹 as しょう, 介 as かい, then す and る — and they simply become <reading>しょうかいする</reading>.

shukudai.meaning_mnemonic: Every night, Koichi finds a fresh stack of workbooks wedged onto the onigiri shelf, exactly where the rice balls should be — someone keeps swapping snacks for problem sets nobody asked for. He bags them for customers anyway, grumbling that unfinished pages on today's <kanji>topic</kanji> waiting for you at home, whether you want them or not, is exactly what homework is.
shukudai.reading_mnemonic: You already know both pieces in order: 宿 as しゅく, then 題 as だい, lining up as <reading>しゅくだい</reading>.

shumi.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's one true hobby is chasing the shrine cats with a broom, shouting them off the mossy steps every morning — then, the instant they scatter, she sits right down where they were and sighs happily, savoring the <kanji>taste</kanji> of that chase, surrounded by the very cats she just chased. That ritual, pointless and adored, is what a hobby actually is.
shumi.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 趣 read しゅ, plus 味 read み, gives <reading>しゅみ</reading>.

shuukan.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the steep mountain trail, you retrace the boxy calendar loop of the <kanji>week</kanji> with one finger, looping toward the vending machine glinting at the summit. Each loop finished, the gate's caught sliver of sun marks the <kanji>interval</kanji> before the next starts, and by the top you've climbed through several whole weeks of loops.
shuukan.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 週（しゅう）plus 間（かん）simply combine, giving you <reading>しゅうかん</reading> straight from readings you already know.

shuumatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>week</kanji> finally reaches its <kanji>end</kanji>, and that end is the <vocabulary>weekend</vocabulary>.

sobo.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till goes quiet as an elderly woman — an <kanji>ancestor</kanji> in her own right, and someone's <kanji>mother</kanji> long before she became a grandmother — counts her coins one by one. Koichi leans over to the new hire and says simply: that's my grandmother, in for her onigiri. No polite title, no fuss — just family, plain and direct, the way you describe your own grandmother to someone else.
sobo.reading_mnemonic: This word takes 祖's reading そ and 母's reading ぼ and fuses them together, giving 「<reading>そぼ</reading>」: (my) grandmother.
sobo.description: 祖母 is how you refer to your own grandmother when speaking to someone outside the family — plain and humble, with no polite title attached. It isn't what you'd call her directly, or use for someone else's grandmother, both of which take an address term instead.

sochira.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway, a student points not at herself but at the spot where her friend already stands, and calls it <vocabulary>that way</vocabulary>.

sofu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the old man who rings Grandma Kane's one enormous shrine bell every single morning, out of habit rather than faith, then complains for an hour that his arm hurts. That specific, grumbling, ritual-bound old man, the <kanji>ancestor</kanji> of your <kanji>father</kanji>, is exactly your grandfather.
sofu.reading_mnemonic: After ringing the enormous bell, the old man collapses onto the shrine steps and announces he's <reading>so full</reading> — of aches, not food. The cats ignore him as he mutters it again, <reading>そふ</reading>, and refuses to get up.

soko.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank you point across the water at one exact rock, not far off and not your own feet. That single spot is <vocabulary>there</vocabulary>.

sonna.meaning_mnemonic: Someone across the riverbank is smacking a shirt against a rock over and over. You can't believe anyone still washes clothes <vocabulary>that kind of</vocabulary> way.
