sono.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank your friend holds up a fish still flapping, and you can only call it <vocabulary>that (+ noun)</vocabulary>, because the fish is stuck to their hands, not yours.

sora.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail sits improbably alone, no building for a mile around it, just a cable running to nowhere and a stretch of blue that starts at the machine's roof and doesn't stop. Hikers reach the summit less for the drinks than to stand there and stare straight up into all that open <kanji>sky</kanji>.
sora.reading_mnemonic: At the summit vending machine, a hawk seen every clear afternoon <reading>soars</reading> straight up until it's a speck, and the hikers waiting on their drink call it their <reading>そら</reading> bird, because it never comes down until the whole open expanse above the machine is empty again.

sore.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat refuses to leave the steps and just flicks its tail toward the bell across the yard. Whatever sits too far to reach is always <vocabulary>that one</vocabulary>.

sorede.meaning_mnemonic: The onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini goes completely empty during the lunch rush, the till keeps beeping at customers who have nothing left to buy, and so the clerk flips the sign to closed without waiting for anyone's approval. Cause tips straight into effect with no gap between them, no hesitation, no other option — that domino roll is and so.
sorede.reading_mnemonic: Plain kana again — read <reading>それで</reading> just as it is spelled and the sound is the entire answer.

sorekara.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker collapses at the vending machine improbably parked at the mountain trail's summit, drains an entire can without pausing for breath, wipes their mouth on a sleeve, and only then turns to look at the view spread out below. That gap between finishing the can and turning around is the whole word: after that, first one thing happens, then the next.
sorekara.reading_mnemonic: This word is pure kana — sound out <reading>それから</reading> exactly as it is written and you already have the reading, no detour needed.

soshite.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the crossing only works one stone at a time: you step onto the first rock, wait for your balance, then the next, then the next. Someone yells directions from the far bank — first this stone, then that one, then the last — and the whole crossing becomes one long chain of and-then, and-then, and-then, until you're standing on the other side.
soshite.reading_mnemonic: そして is written exactly as it's read — <reading>そして</reading>, straight through, with no kanji hiding a different sound underneath.

soto.meaning_mnemonic: That same figure is still at the slanted gate, one foot already past the threshold — but now picture them finally committing, both feet clearing the fence, the gate swinging shut behind them for good. Whatever was inside is someone else's problem now; they're standing in the open air, fully and firmly <kanji>outside</kanji>.
soto.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank a washer pins the last wet sheet, then a crab clamps her big toe and she hops the length of the mud barking <reading>so-toe</reading> with every hop, which is exactly <reading>そと</reading>, the word for standing outside in the open air.

souji-suru.meaning_mnemonic: Every cat at Grandma Kane's shrine tracks paw-prints across the moss, and every morning she attacks the steps with a broom twice her height, scattering leaves, sweeping cobwebs off the enormous bell, scrubbing stone until it shines — that relentless morning ritual is what it means to clean.
souji-suru.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane scrubs the mossy shrine steps and barks at a lounging cat, <reading>Soap, geezer, sure!</reading> — her raspy shout for <reading>そうじする</reading>, and the cat finally slinks off so she can finish cleaning.

sugu.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the steep mountain trail sits one improbable vending machine. The instant a hiker spots it through the trees, he breaks into a sprint — no pause for the view, no catching his breath, straight up the last slope immediately, because a cold drink that close cannot wait even one more step.
sugu.reading_mnemonic: 「<reading>すぐ</reading>」is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so you just read it as it appears — no kanji to decode.

suiyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Water</kanji> floods the middle <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> of the week, leaving it soaked through as <vocabulary>Wednesday</vocabulary>.

suki.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi rings up the same rice ball at his konbini every single evening, though the shelf is stocked with a dozen other kinds. He doesn't compare, doesn't browse — just walks straight past the beeping till to the one he always gets, because some things you're simply fond of and no substitute will do.
suki.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail in midwinter, Sei straps skis on right by the vending machine and grins 「<reading>すき</reading>」 before pushing off downhill — the crunch of the <reading>skis</reading> against fresh snow is the sound of someone doing exactly what they love.

sukoshi.meaning_mnemonic: You've already watched someone take a bite out of small: slice one more dot off that hooked little shape and next to nothing survives. Pinch what's left between two fingers — that scrap, that residue, the near-nothing you can still hold onto — is exactly <kanji>few</kanji>. A little is whatever remains after almost everything else is gone.
sukoshi.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, never asks the crowd for much. Before every trick he holds up one white-gloved finger and requests just <reading>a skosh</reading> of hush, a skosh of powder, a skosh of anything at all. That signature request is <reading>すこし</reading> — a little, exactly his size, never more.

sumimasen.meaning_mnemonic: Sei knocks over an entire display at Koichi's konbini reaching for a drink, cans rolling under the beeping till in every direction. She freezes, hands up, apologizing to Koichi and to the three customers she nearly took out — one word covering the mess, the noise, and the bruised dignity: excuse me, sorry.
sumimasen.reading_mnemonic: Hear <reading>すみません</reading> as Sei's voice cutting through the clatter, rushed and apologetic: "<reading>soo-mee-mah-sen</reading>, soo-mee-mah-sen" — over and over as the cans keep rolling.
sumimasen.description: This one covers both a sincere apology and a polite way to get someone's attention (like flagging down a waiter), so the same word that says sorry for a mess also opens a request — context, not the word itself, tells you which.

sumu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture someone circling apartment listings for months, rejecting every one — too small, too loud, too far from the shrine — until one day they just stop circling. They unpack the boxes, hang a calendar on the wall, and stay put. That's the gap between visiting somewhere and actually living there: eventually you settle in and <kanji>reside</kanji>.
sumu.reading_mnemonic: A hulking <reading>sumo</reading> wrestler wanders into Grandma Kane's shrine one afternoon, likes the mossy steps and the cats, and simply never leaves. He builds a tiny hut by the bell and starts paying the shrine rent every month. That's <reading>すむ</reading> — to live, to reside.

supootsu.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school field has one announcer who only ever learned a single English word, so before every event — race, ball game, swim meet — he grabs the microphone and bellows スポーツ, because that one borrowed word already covers every game you could name: sports.
supootsu.reading_mnemonic: スポーツ is a loanword written exactly the way it sounds, straight from English into kana: <reading>スポーツ</reading>.

supuun.meaning_mnemonic: In the cafeteria at Sei's school, someone catapults a lump of mashed potato clean across the room with a spoon during lunch, and it lands with a wet slap on the sports-field banner outside the window. Every year the students blame a new first-year, and every year it's the same bent spoon.
supuun.reading_mnemonic: スプーン is written exactly as it sounds — <reading>スプーン</reading> — a katakana borrowing of the English word <reading>spoon</reading>, no decoding needed.

suru.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports day, one kid volunteers for every single event before anyone else can answer: relay, tug-of-war, clean-up, all of it. By the final whistle he's just standing in the middle of the field doing the next unasked-for thing, because doing is the only setting he owns.
suru.reading_mnemonic: する is written exactly the way it sounds, plain kana with nothing to decode — just <reading>する</reading>.

suteki.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat that normally swats everything off the mossy steps stops mid-swat, sits down, and just stares at one stone lantern glowing gold in the evening light. Even the cranky, destructive cats agree on this one: it's lovely, it's wonderful, it's worth sitting still for.
suteki.reading_mnemonic: That same cat gets nicknamed <reading>sue-tech</reading>, because anything shiny short-circuits her, and she freezes at the lantern glow while everyone around her mutters <reading>すてき</reading> before she can even blink.

suugaku.meaning_mnemonic: The swaddled child still sits under the canopy of scribbled lessons, but today someone dumps a whole crate of numbers onto the roof. They slide down through the notes, stack themselves into columns, and pile up in the child's lap until <kanji>study</kanji>-time is nothing but numbers. That mess of numbers under the lesson-canopy is mathematics.
suugaku.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a girl named Sue gawks at a chalkboard someone has covered edge to edge in equations overnight. She just stands there, and <reading>Sue gawks</reading> is exactly how you remember 「<reading>すうがく</reading>」, mathematics.

suupaa.meaning_mnemonic: A shopping cart rolls out the automatic doors hauling forty bags of rice, an entire side of beef, and a wobbling pyramid of soap boxes, because an ordinary grocery run won't cut it here. One roof, every aisle, everything in bulk — the store is proud enough of the scale to call itself super for it: a supermarket.
suupaa.reading_mnemonic: スーパー is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>super</reading> and you've already said <reading>スーパー</reading>, nothing to derive.

suwaru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, two frozen visitors drop straight onto the mossy steps, planting themselves on the same patch of ground exactly like before, refusing to move an inch closer to the bell. Cats pile onto their laps and pin them there. That's exactly what it means to <kanji>sit</kanji> — plant yourself and stay.
suwaru.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a duck named Sue plants herself on the washing stone and will not move, even as the current tugs her tail. Wash-water soaks her feathers. She just squawks <reading>sue-wah-roo</reading> and stays put, which is exactly the sound of <reading>すわる</reading>.

suzushii.meaning_mnemonic: You haul yourself up the mountain trail, drenched, and finally reach the lone vending machine at the top. Before you even press a button, its compressor exhales a blast of chilled air across the back of your neck, and the whole sweaty afternoon evaporates into one cool, refreshing breath.
suzushii.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine, a hiker named <reading>Suzy</reading> holds her water bottle to her cheek and sighs, dragging the word out like the cool air itself: <reading>すずしい</reading>, she says, every time the breeze finally reaches her.

tabemono.meaning_mnemonic: That tent pitched over a heaped tray — the shelter you duck into when you're hungry — gets dragged whole onto Sei's school sports field for a picnic, roof and all. The whole team ducks under it at once, and every dish sitting under that roof, from the rice down to the last pickle, gets <kanji>eaten</kanji> before the bell rings. Any <kanji>thing</kanji> that ends up under that tent is, simply, food.
tabemono.reading_mnemonic: <reading>たべもの</reading> just chains the readings you already know: 食 as た, べ as written, and 物 as もの.

taberu.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini is closing, and the last customer ducks under the peaked tent-roof from 食's story — the shelter built entirely out of dinner, rice and side dishes heaped under the eaves. There's nothing else you can do under a roof like that but sit down where you're standing and <kanji>eat</kanji>, so that's exactly what closing time forces on him.
taberu.reading_mnemonic: 食 already gives た, べ gives べ, and る closes it out, so to eat becomes <reading>たべる</reading> exactly as those three pieces already spelled it.

tabun.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the sports field scoreboard flickers between <kanji>many</kanji> different numbers all afternoon, and nobody on the sidelines can <kanji>understand</kanji> which one is actually correct. Ask a teacher and all you get is a shrug: probably the higher number, maybe not, hard to say for certain. That shrug, refusing to commit either way, is probably, maybe.
tabun.reading_mnemonic: This one is plain kana too — read <reading>たぶん</reading> exactly as it is written and there is nothing left to derive.

tadaima.meaning_mnemonic: Sei drops her bag the second she's through the door after school, sports-field mud still on her shoes, and calls out into the hallway before her shoes are even off. Nobody answers right away, but she says it anyway, announcing herself to a house that already knows her. That first shout through the door is the whole word: I'm home.
tadaima.reading_mnemonic: Written exactly as it sounds — read the kana straight through and you get 「<reading>ただいま</reading>」.

taihen.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, the <kanji>big</kanji> stick-figure kid takes a running start for the long jump, sails clean over the sandpit, and lands hard enough to <kanji>change</kanji> the whole field's layout — snack stand flattened, half the scoreboard gone. The coach just stares at the wreckage, clipboard still raised. That kind of day is what this word means: tough, awful.
taihen.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 大 as たい plus 変 as へん gives you 「<reading>たいへん</reading>」.

taiiku.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the sports field gets roped off every single morning into lanes, hurdles, and a rope-climb nobody wants to attempt, all before homeroom even starts. Nobody is teaching a subject out there — they are just making bodies move, sweat, and complain in unison before the bell rings. That daily, compulsory shoving of the <kanji>body</kanji> through drills is physical education.
taiiku.reading_mnemonic: Just line the two known kanji readings up in order: 体 as たい plus 育 as いく is <reading>たいいく</reading>.

taitei.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman named Tai washes the same net every morning. Mostly he hauls up nothing but weeds, and usually that's exactly the day he decides to give up — right before the one big fish finally shows up. So he keeps going, mostly, usually, forever.
taitei.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly as it sounds — picture tidy <reading>Tai</reading> scrubbing his net at the riverbank to get the reading <reading>たいてい</reading>.

takai-adj.meaning_mnemonic: Stand beneath that same tower with its yawning mouth of an entrance, except today the mouth is a ticket booth, and the price climbs one more floor every time you crane your neck to look up. By the top the ticket costs a fortune — the building was always both <kanji>tall</kanji> and <kanji>expensive</kanji> at once.
takai-adj.reading_mnemonic: 高 already sounds たか in words like this one, and い is just the ordinary adjective ending, so 高い reads straight through as <reading>たかい</reading>.

takusan.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini restocks the onigiri shelf every morning, but today the delivery truck backs up too far and dumps three times the usual order. Onigiri spill off the shelf, stack on the floor, and pile up by the register until Koichi can't see the counter anymore. Customers wade through rice triangles just to check out — that's not a stocking error, that's a lot.
takusan.reading_mnemonic: たくさん is written exactly the way it sounds, kana only, nothing to decode: <reading>たくさん</reading>.

takushii.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail is so steep that hikers stop believing in the vending machine at the top — until a taxi comes crawling up the switchbacks behind them, meter running, wheels spinning on loose gravel. It pulls up right next to the machine and idles patiently, because someone actually ordered a taxi to fetch canned coffee from the summit.
takushii.reading_mnemonic: This word is a loanword borrowed straight from English "taxi" and written in katakana exactly as it's read: <reading>タクシー</reading>.

tama-ni.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine cats swarm the mossy steps every single day, certain of scraps. But the enormous bell above the steps only tips over and rings once in a great while — a stray gust, a startled crow — and when it does, every cat scatters, because that bell only ever rings occasionally.
tama-ni.reading_mnemonic: 「<reading>たまに</reading>」is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so you just read it as it appears — no kanji to decode.

tamago.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the delivery truck arrives before dawn and unloads crate after crate of impossibly round, pale ovals, still warm from the truck's engine. Koichi holds one to the fluorescent light, taps it once, and it cracks open — bright yolk sliding across the counter: egg.
tamago.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the fat shrine cat curls into the offering bowl every morning. Someone finally claps and shouts <reading>Tama, go!</reading> — it slinks off, revealing one warm egg underneath. That shout is the reading: <reading>たまご</reading>.

tanoshii.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a dozen cats chase a dropped paper fan down the mossy steps, tumbling over each other and clanging the enormous bell by accident on the way, its clatter ringing out like wild <kanji>music</kanji>. Visitors abandon their prayers just to watch, laughing, and that whole chaotic scramble is exactly what fun and enjoyable feels like.
tanoshii.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane laughs so hard at the cats that she slips and lands on the steps, showing off a <reading>tanned knee</reading>, and declares between giggles that this is the most <reading>たのしい</reading> afternoon she's had all year.

taoru.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone finishing the dishes flings a soaked cloth overhead to dry it in the wind, and it sails wide, landing draped square across a passing fisherman's shoulders, soaking through his shirt before he's even noticed. That oversized wet cloth everyone keeps grabbing for and missing is a towel.
taoru.reading_mnemonic: <reading>タオル</reading> is written exactly as it sounds - a loanword from the English towel, squeezed into kana, nothing to decode.

tatsu-v.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's echoing sports field, the coach blows the whistle and every player plants their feet on the ground exactly like before, refusing to budge an inch, rooted upright in a straight line. Nobody sits, nobody wobbles — the whole team just <kanji>stand</kanji>s there until the whistle blows again.
tatsu-v.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's fluorescent konbini, a bag of frozen potato tots bursts beside the onigiri shelf when the till beeps. They skitter under the door. The night clerk drops to his knees and scoops, hissing <reading>tots</reading> with every grab, which is the sound of <reading>たつ</reading>.

te-v.meaning_mnemonic: That same <kanji>hand</kanji> is still hanging out mid-air, wrist and all, waiting for the shake nobody's ever finished. It doesn't close, it doesn't wave — it just stays there, open-palmed, being exactly the shape it always was. That patient, unshaken shape is the word for hand.
te-v.reading_mnemonic: Same kanji, same lesson: 手 already gave you two readings, and this word just borrows the plain <reading>て</reading> reading straight off it.

teeburu.meaning_mnemonic: Two fishermen haul a wide, flat plank out of the river and can't be bothered carrying it back to camp, so they wedge it level across four boulders right there on the bank and eat lunch off it. Every trip after, they head straight for the same plank on the same four rocks. They never call it a plank again, it's their table.
teeburu.reading_mnemonic: This word is a straight loanword from the English word for table, written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>テーブル</reading>.

tegami.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a <kanji>hand</kanji> reaches across the water and drops a folded sheet of <kanji>paper</kanji> into a second <kanji>hand</kanji> waiting on the far bank, which folds it again and passes it to a third — the page crossing hand to hand until it reaches you, refolded and ready to read: a letter.
tegami.reading_mnemonic: Koichi wraps a sticky gummy candy inside a folded note at the konbini register and mutters <reading>the gummy</reading> as he slides it across the counter — the customer unwraps it, and taped underneath, waiting to be read, is a <reading>てがみ</reading>.

teinei.meaning_mnemonic: A new clerk at the library re-folds every origami crane the kids abandon on the returns desk, squaring each corner twice before setting it down straight. She bows to a stack of overdue books like they're guests arriving late. Nothing about her is rushed — every motion is polite, every motion is careful.
teinei.reading_mnemonic: The other clerks nickname her <reading>tay-nay</reading> for how she irons every library ticket flat before filing it, and the sound became the word itself: <reading>ていねい</reading>, meticulous and polite, exactly the way she squares those corners.

tenki.meaning_mnemonic: Look up past the ceiling stretched over everyone's outstretched arms — the <kanji>sky</kanji> itself — and you'll see it has moods. When that same curling wisp of <kanji>spirit</kanji> that rises off a hot bowl of rice thickens into cloud, or thins and vanishes, the sky is telling you what's coming: today's weather.
tenki.reading_mnemonic: 天 already gives you てん and 気 already lends Kiki's き — stitch them together and you get <reading>てんき</reading>, weather.

terebi.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail breaks down one rainy week, and its cracked screen fills with fuzzy grey static instead of dispensing canned coffee. Hikers keep climbing anyway, huddling round the glowing box, because somehow it has started showing Sei's sports day live from the valley below. Nobody's brave enough to unplug the trail's new TV.
terebi.reading_mnemonic: <reading>テレビ</reading> is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so the reading is simply <reading>テレビ</reading> itself — nothing to derive.

tesuto.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, hikers find one improbable vending machine that only accepts jokes — feed it a bad enough pun and it judges you before dispensing a drink. That single machine standing between you and relief, checking whether you measure up before it lets you pass, is exactly a test.
tesuto.reading_mnemonic: テスト is a loanword from English "test", written and read exactly as it sounds: <reading>テスト</reading>.

tetsudau.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini till is buried under boxes he can't shift alone, so you hold up your <kanji>hand</kanji>, fingers spread the way you always picture it, and slide it under the heaviest crate just before it tips, the weight passing from his grip to yours like a message that has to <kanji>transmit</kanji> hand to hand. You're not doing his job for him — you're only lending a <kanji>hand</kanji>, which is exactly what helping means.
tetsudau.reading_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, your friend can't lift the net alone, so you jog over saying '<reading>let's do</reading> this together' — <reading>てつだう</reading> — and grab the other end before he drops it.
tetsudau.description: 手伝う specifically means pitching in on a task that's mainly someone else's — helping with chores, homework, or work — rather than a general word for rescuing or assisting in any sense.

tobu.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a cat sunning itself beside the vending machine is startled by a hiker's dropped can, and it doesn't just scurry off — it launches clean over the machine in one motion, all four paws leaving the ground at once. That single clean launch off the ground, whether across a gap or straight up, is to fly or jump.
tobu.reading_mnemonic: As the cat sails over the machine, it clips a tuba someone left leaning against it, and the horn lets out a low <reading>toh-buh</reading> honk mid-air — the exact sound the hikers now shout as <reading>とぶ</reading> every time that cat launches itself again.

toire.meaning_mnemonic: The bell rings at Sei's school and the hallway turns into a stampede — everyone sprinting for the same door before the next class starts. Whoever gets there first slams it shut, and the rest line up outside, jiggling, staring at their shoes: the single most fought-over room in the whole building, the toilet.
toire.reading_mnemonic: Written and read exactly as it sounds, letter for letter: <reading>トイレ</reading>.

tokei.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane is sick of craning her neck at the shrine to track <kanji>time</kanji>, so she catches the sun mid-crawl above the steps and coils its slow arc into a circle small enough to nail above the bell. Now <kanji>time</kanji> ticks around a tidy face instead of crawling across the sky — she has hung herself a clock.
tokei.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer stubs his toe on the wall clock and yelps <reading>toe-kay</reading> before glaring up to see exactly how much time he wasted wincing — that wall clock is <reading>とけい</reading>.

tokidoki.meaning_mnemonic: You're back at the shrine watching the sun mark the <kanji>time</kanji>, but instead of climbing straight up like always, it stutters, vanishing behind a cloud, popping back out, vanishing again. That broken, doubled version of <kanji>time</kanji>, ticking on and off instead of running straight, is sometimes.
tokidoki.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a bird named Toki rings the huge bell in a stuttering double knock, and the caretaker mutters <reading>okey-dokey</reading> each time, but only when Toki bothers to show up, which is <reading>ときどき</reading>, sometimes, never on a schedule.

tokoro.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a toucan named Toco stubs her toe on the exact same rock every single hike. She stops, taps it twice, and declares that spot the <kanji>place</kanji> — not the trail, not the view, just the one stubbed patch of ground she keeps returning to.
tokoro.reading_mnemonic: Toco's toe finds the same rock every hike, and she barks out her toe-corral: <reading>ところ</reading> — <reading>toe-corral</reading> — the small fenced-in place at the top of the trail that belongs only to her stubbed toe.

tomaru-stay.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker named Tomo reaches the vending machine at the top of the steep mountain trail just as the sun drops. His legs refuse another step down, so he unrolls a mat beside the machine, uses his backpack as a pillow, and settles in to stay overnight, listening to the machine hum its one lonely song until morning.
tomaru-stay.reading_mnemonic: Tomo stands frozen on the dark trail, torn between climbing down and waiting for dawn. He mutters, 'I'll stay till <reading>tomorrow</reading>' — the cold swallows his words into one sound, exactly like <reading>とまる</reading>, and he plants his boots and doesn't move again.

tomaru.meaning_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle grinds up the mountain trail with his shell stacked full of sample doors, aiming for the vending machine at the top. Right at the steepest switchback he plants one foot flat against the gravel and freezes — the same <kanji>stop</kanji> pose the trail already taught you — and won't haul his doors another step until someone flags him down.
tomaru.reading_mnemonic: 止（と）＋ま＋る spell out <reading>とまる</reading> exactly the way you already learned to read 止 — the readings just fall into place, no new story needed.

tomeru-stop.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's onigiri cart breaks loose and rolls for the door. You don't chase it — you do what the mountain trail already taught your foot: plant it flat and hard, right in the cart's path. The wheels ram your ankle and jam dead, frozen mid-roll. That's your foot learning to <kanji>stop</kanji> something other than itself.
tomeru-stop.reading_mnemonic: 止（と）＋める gives you the reading <reading>とめる</reading> straight from the と you already know for 止 plus the plain める ending — nothing new to memorize here.

tomodachi.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a stranger reaches for the last onigiri the exact moment you do. Neither of you lets go. You end up splitting it on the curb outside, silent and suspicious of each other, until one bite in you're both laughing about it — and just like that, you've made a friend.
tomodachi.reading_mnemonic: 友 gives とも and 達 gives だち, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>ともだち</reading>.

tonari.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat claims the mossy step by the bell, and a second cat — never asked, never invited — plants itself immediately beside the first, close enough their tails touch. Every single day it's the same two steps, side by side, the second cat permanently attached to whichever step the first one picks. That fixed, right-beside-you position is what the word means.
tonari.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>tawny</reading> cat has taken over the step <reading>となり</reading> — right next to — the shrine bell, and hisses at anyone else who tries to sit there, as if the neighboring step belongs to it alone.

too.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ten</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>ten things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so counting up to ten is all this one ever means.
too.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini he stubs his <reading>toe</reading> on the shelf ten times, yelping <reading>とお</reading> each time, and swears the broken onigiri come to exactly <vocabulary>ten things</vocabulary>.

tooi.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail is so far away that by the time you reach it, the drink inside has gone flat from age. Every switchback just reveals another switchback waiting behind it. The summit never gets closer, only farther.
tooi.reading_mnemonic: Near the summit, a hiker stubs her toe on a root and yelps <reading>toe, ee!</reading> — the echo bounces off ridge after ridge, because the peak above her is <reading>とおい</reading>, so far that the echo outlasts the climb itself.

tooka.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> the sun climbs through its window and finds you at the shrine steps, raising both hands a little higher than yesterday, palms open like the <kanji>ten</kanji>-shaped cross you make once all your fingers are up. Nine sunrises of half-raised hands pass before the tenth, when both hands finally form that perfect cross overhead — ten days of raising, and it's the tenth.
tooka.reading_mnemonic: This word takes 十's reading とお and 日's reading か and fuses them together, giving 「<reading>とおか</reading>」: the 10th, ten days.

tori.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the vending machine that shouldn't be there, something small and feathered dive-bombs a hiker's rice ball straight out of his hand and is gone before he can react. He never even sees it land — just a blur, a gap in the air, and an empty wrapper. That blur is what bird means.
tori.reading_mnemonic: The hiker shouts that the thing just <reading>tore</reading> his rice ball clean out of his hand, and the guide behind him laughs — everyone's shout sounds like that the first time it happens. That's <reading>とり</reading>: the sound of something snatching your lunch and vanishing before you can name it.

toru.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker's hand shoots out for the last can of coffee sliding off the vending machine tray. The lid rim catches her sleeve and tears a clean slit through the fabric before the can lands in her palm. She doesn't stop to check the damage. She just needed to take the can, grab it before anyone else could.
toru.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a fat calico waits till no one's looking, then leaps onto the tray and <reading>tore</reading> a rice cracker off the plate before Grandma can shout. The bell swings from the impact. That cat has taken more crackers than anyone, and everyone calls the theft by its sound: <reading>とる</reading>.

toshokan.meaning_mnemonic: You step into a hall of shelves stretching past where the light reaches, the whole <kanji>building</kanji> given over to paper. Every page began the same way: someone let the sun sink over their desk while their hand kept moving, filling line after line to <kanji>write</kanji> — even a hand-drawn <kanji>map</kanji> to nowhere ends up bound and shelved here. Multiply that by ten thousand desks and stack it under one roof — that's a library.
toshokan.reading_mnemonic: 図（と）＋書（しょ）＋館（かん）combine directly into <reading>としょかん</reading>.

totemo.meaning_mnemonic: A tiny turtle named Toby plants all four feet under one pebble and grunts like he's hoisting a boulder, veins bulging, shell trembling with effort. Everyone watching can see it's just a pebble, but his groaning insists the weight is very, very much more than that.
totemo.reading_mnemonic: とても is written just the way it sounds, plain hiragana carrying the word straight across: <reading>とても</reading>.

tsugi.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's lone vending machine, a line forms mid-slope. Each hiker steps up, buys a drink, and steps aside without a word, and the one standing there simply becomes whoever is next before the machine even finishes humming. Nobody skips ahead; the queue just moves forward one body at a time.
tsugi.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine, Sei mutters <reading>two geese</reading> under his breath every time someone new steps up — his private way of marking whose turn is next. By the fortieth hiker it's worn into a chant, and that chant is exactly how you say <reading>つぎ</reading>.

tsugou.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school reschedules the exam for the exact hour the sports field floods and the vending machine jams — three disasters stacking into one tidy circumstance. The teacher just shrugs and cancels class: how convenient the timing turned out to be. That's circumstances, and convenience, in one word.
tsugou.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 都 read つ, plus 合 read ごう, gives <reading>つごう</reading>.

tsuitachi.meaning_mnemonic: The flat line of <kanji>one</kanji> sits right against the <kanji>day</kanji> mark on the calendar. That opening pair is always the <vocabulary>1st of the month</vocabulary>.
tsuitachi.reading_mnemonic: Every <reading>ついたち</reading>, landlord <reading>Sweetie Tachi</reading> pounds on the door, because rent is only ever due on the <vocabulary>1st of the month</vocabulary>.

tsukau.meaning_mnemonic: A boy borrows the last bat from the school equipment shed and swings so hard at the first pitch that the handle snaps clean in half. He shrugs, jogs to get the spare, and swings that one too. Nobody taught him to be gentle with things — only that if it exists in that shed, you use it until it's someone else's problem.
tsukau.reading_mnemonic: The school somehow owns one elderly cow, kept behind the sports field for reasons nobody remembers. When the mower breaks, the coach ropes her to the cart and hollers to use the cow — students hear <reading>tsu-cow</reading>, and it sticks: that's exactly what's happening, they <reading>つかう</reading> the cow to drag the cart.

tsukeru.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a broken keychain flashlight sits in the discount bin by the register until a bored customer clips two fresh batteries onto its back and thumbs the switch. The little bulb sputters, then catches, glowing steady in his hand. That double motion — snapping something onto a thing and waking it up — is the meaning: to turn on, to attach.
tsukeru.reading_mnemonic: つける is written in kana exactly as it sounds, with no kanji hiding underneath: <reading>つける</reading>.

tsuki-v.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane climbs her mossy shrine steps and looks straight up: there's the same sliver she already knows, the <kanji>moon</kanji> that fattens and fades to mark off a whole <kanji>month</kanji>. Tonight she isn't tracking the calendar at all, just staring at the sliver itself — and that sliver, on its own, is simply the word moon.
tsuki-v.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the kanji's own <reading>つき</reading>, the same sound you already attached to that crescent, carried straight into the word.

tsukue.meaning_mnemonic: A moving crew wedges a single office desk through the automatic doors of Koichi's konbini because it wouldn't fit anywhere else, bolting it down beside the onigiri shelf. Now Koichi rings up rice balls sitting behind a proper desk instead of a bare register. Every clerk after him just calls it the desk.
tsukue.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a janitor hauls a heavy desk down the echoing hallway, grunting <reading>Sue, cooey!</reading> with every shove until the hallway chants it back. By the time the desk scrapes into the classroom, the chant has worn a groove: <reading>つくえ</reading>, the sound of a desk landing where it doesn't fit.

tsukuru.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone has spent all afternoon weaving wet reeds into a raft, tying each bundle with more reeds pulled from the mud. It wobbles, it leaks a little, but it floats when she pushes it past the shallows. She didn't find a raft down here. She built one, piece by piece, from whatever the river handed her.
tsukuru.reading_mnemonic: A cuckoo at the riverbank spends the whole morning weaving twigs into a nest, calling its own name the entire time it works — <reading>cuckoo</reading>, <reading>つくる</reading>, over and over, like it's narrating the job. By evening the nest holds together on its own, twigs it wove into something it made from nothing.

tsuma.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a man climbs the mossy steps every evening expecting to be first, and every evening his own wife is already there ahead of him, feeding the shrine cats without a word of announcement. He never has to ask where she is — she is simply, quietly, always a step ahead of him. That settled certainty is (my) wife.
tsuma.reading_mnemonic: He calls up the steps, <reading>Sue, ma!</reading>, thinking he's found Grandma Kane — but it's his own wife who turns around, cat in her arms. That startled beat is the sound of <reading>つま</reading>: realizing, again, that his wife got there first.
tsuma.description: 妻 is the plain, slightly formal way a man refers to his own wife when talking to other people — it is not a word used for someone else's wife, and not one he'd use calling out to her directly.

tsumaranai.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a substitute reads the safety manual aloud in a flat monotone for the entire period, and by the second page three students are asleep on their desks while one just counts ceiling tiles. Nothing happens, nothing changes, and that flat, empty stretch of nothing is boring.
tsumaranai.reading_mnemonic: つまらない is written exactly as it sounds, kana only, nothing to decode: 「<reading>つまらない</reading>」 reads precisely the way it looks.

tsumetai.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank someone dunks a can of juice into the current to <kanji>chill</kanji> it, forgets about it for an hour, and pulls it back out numb-fingered and gasping. The metal has gone shockingly cold to the touch, far colder than the air around it ever was, and that's the meaning: cold, the kind you feel through your skin.
tsumetai.reading_mnemonic: A man at the riverbank loosens his necktie in the heat and dunks the end of it in the current to cool off, then yanks it back out gasping at how it stings his fingers. That yelp is <reading>つめたい</reading>: <reading>too, my tie</reading>, dripping and cold enough to hurt.
tsumetai.description: 冷たい also describes a person, not just an object — a cold, distant, unfriendly manner. The same word that fits icy river water fits an icy attitude. This entry teaches the physical, to-the-touch sense; the personality sense is a common extension you'll run into later.

tsutaeru.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail your legs give out, so you cup your hands and shout the whole message to the hiker just above you. She shouts it to the next, who shouts it to the next, until it reaches the vending machine waiting at the summit and prints out your exact sentence. Nobody up there invented anything — they only <kanji>transmitted</kanji> it, unchanged. That uphill, word-for-word relay is what it means to convey or tell.
tsutaeru.reading_mnemonic: A tutor is stationed halfway up that same mountain trail, relaying every word radioed down from the summit vending machine without changing a syllable of it. Say her job fast — tutor, tutor — and it collapses into <reading>つたえる</reading>, the <reading>tutor</reading> whose only task is passing the message on exactly as it was given.

tsuyoi.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker on the mountain trail stops at the summit vending machine, wraps both arms around it, and simply picks the whole humming thing up off its concrete pad to shake loose a stuck can. Nobody films it. Nobody comments. He just sets it back down and keeps walking, unmistakably <kanji>strong</kanji>.
tsuyoi.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, the same hiker hoists the vending machine overhead one-armed and lets out a flat, matter-of-fact roar — “<reading>TSU-YO-EE</reading>!” — the sound the whole trail now associates with anyone that <reading>つよい</reading>.

tsuzuki.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the little television behind the register freezes on a soap-opera cliffhanger just as the till starts beeping. The customer refuses to pay until the show comes back. Nobody moves, nobody rings anyone up, everything just waits for the continuation.
tsuzuki.reading_mnemonic: A raccoon named Zuzu patrols the riverbank looking for the <reading>zoo key</reading> that reopens the closed exhibit gate. She finds it wedged under a rock, holds it up, and the sign flips to 「<reading>つづき</reading>」 — to be continued tomorrow.

uchi.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at Grandma Kane's shrine, the stray cats pile into one shivering heap on the mossy steps — not because any cat owns the place, but because the heap itself is the point. Ask an outsider cat to squeeze in and the whole pile hisses as one; ask one inside where home is, and it just presses closer. The heap is home.
uchi.reading_mnemonic: This word is pure kana, spelled exactly the way it sounds, so <reading>うち</reading> needs no decoding — just read it as written.
uchi.description: うち means home in the sense of your own group or household, not just a building. Japanese speakers use it to mark insiders against outsiders, so it can describe a company, a team, or a family circle as easily as a physical house — a nuance the English word 'home' does not carry on its own.

ue.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a goat drags the vending machine past the summit, still climbing — its hooves pointing the same way as that little mark rising off the ground: skyward. It won't stop until there's nothing left <kanji>above</kanji> it but open sky, which is exactly <kanji>up</kanji>.
ue.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Oo-eh</reading>, groans a repairer on a wobbly ladder at the mountain trail's vending machine, fingers shy of a can jammed in the top slot. The ladder walks sideways, his arms shake, and that strain is the sound of <reading>うえ</reading>, the word for up, for whatever hangs above your reach.

ugokasu.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a rowboat sits beached and refuses to budge. Sue plants both feet in the mud, braces against the hull, and shoves until it finally slides free into the current. The boat never moves itself — Sue is the one who moves it, which is exactly what it means to <kanji>move</kanji> something.
ugokasu.reading_mnemonic: As the hull finally scrapes free, someone on the bank yells <reading>a go-car, Sue!</reading> — cheering her on, and about as close as English gets to <reading>うごかす</reading>, moving something that wouldn't move on its own.

ugoku.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, someone parks a go-kart beside the lone vending machine and wanders off for a drink. By the time they turn back, the kart has already rolled halfway down the slope on its own, nobody behind the wheel, nothing pushing it — it's simply started to <kanji>move</kanji>.
ugoku.reading_mnemonic: Watching the driverless kart trundle downhill, you swear its engine mutters <reading>a go-kart</reading>, which is about as close as English gets to <reading>うごく</reading> — the sound of something moving all by itself.

umareru.meaning_mnemonic: The same shoot that broke through the earth in the story of <kanji>life</kanji> keeps climbing past where anyone was watching, until one morning it splits its last husk open in the sun and unfurls a leaf nobody planted. No ceremony, no announcement — something that wasn't there yesterday is simply, suddenly alive: it has been born.
umareru.reading_mnemonic: At school, Sei is put in charge of the class tomato plant, certain nothing will come of it. Weeks later she sprints down the hallway insisting <reading>you're merely</reading> looking at a seed one day, and then — <reading>うまれる</reading> — a whole red tomato hangs off the vine she swore was empty.

umi.meaning_mnemonic: A fisherman leaves one bucket of water by his back door to rinse his boots, but it rains so hard overnight that the bucket overflows and never stops — by morning his whole street sits underwater, waves lapping at the mailbox. One forgotten bucket, given enough time, became an entire sea.
umi.reading_mnemonic: Sei wades into the riverbank current on a school trip, certain it's shallow, until the ground vanishes and cold water rushes to her shoulders. She yelps <reading>ooh, me</reading>, right before the current sweeps her toward the open <reading>うみ</reading> the river was hiding all along.

unten-suru.meaning_mnemonic: A vending-machine restocker's truck grinds up the mountain trail's switchbacks in first gear, engine screaming, cans rattling in the back, aiming for the one machine improbably parked at the summit. Nobody walks this delivery route — someone has to sit behind the wheel and wrestle it up every hairpin <kanji>turn</kanji>. That's the whole job: to drive, all the way to the top.
unten-suru.reading_mnemonic: Nothing irregular here: 運 is うん, 転 is てん, plus する, and the whole word reads <reading>うんてんする</reading>.

ureshii.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last onigiri on the shelf is about to expire right at closing time. He snatches it seconds before the till locks him out, laughing out loud in the empty, fluorescent-bright aisle. That giddy, undignified triumph over a single rice ball is what happy and glad mean here.
ureshii.reading_mnemonic: Koichi clutches the onigiri and yelps <reading>Ooh, retch-she!</reading>, the exact sound of <reading>うれしい</reading> — the customers behind him in line assume it's pure joy, not the heartburn that follows right behind it.

uru.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that same street vendor leaning back on his two kicked-out legs, sign propped above his stacked goods, still shouting prices at everyone who walks past. He never once stops to hand over money himself — only to unload what's piled in front of him onto whoever stops. That relentless shouting-and-unloading is exactly what it means to <kanji>sell</kanji>.
uru.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a kangaroo named Roo leans on the lone vending machine and stuffs warm cans into her pouch to sell to gasping hikers. The pouch jams. She tips backward with a long <reading>oo-roo</reading>, which is exactly the sound of <reading>うる</reading>.

ushiro.meaning_mnemonic: The runner is still frozen mid-stride, string trailing off his heel from a race that never seems to end. Now picture the whole pack has finished and gone home, and he's still out on the empty course, a few permanent steps back from where everyone else stood. That's his spot for good — <kanji>behind</kanji> the group, always trailing after.
ushiro.reading_mnemonic: An <reading>usher</reading> at Sei's school assembly grabs every latecomer at the door, and instead of the empty front seats, walks them all the way to the back — <reading>うしろ</reading> — where they stand behind the whole crowd for the rest of the ceremony.

uta.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a hiker collapses in front of the lone vending machine and won't take another step. Her friend starts humming, then breaks into a full song about the cold drinks waiting at the summit. By the second verse the hiker is back on her feet, still humming, powered entirely by the song.
uta.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine, her friend keeps saying <reading>you oughta</reading> sing along before every button press, until the hikers are chanting it back in rhythm — <reading>oughta</reading>, <reading>oughta</reading> — and the phrase warps into <reading>うた</reading>, the machine's tinny jingle playing the actual song.

utau.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat leaps onto the giant bell rope and yowls straight down the mossy steps, scattering pigeons off the roof. A second cat joins in an octave higher, then a third, until the whole shrine sounds like a badly rehearsed choir. That's singing.
utau.reading_mnemonic: The lead cat lets out a long, warbling <reading>oo-ta-oo</reading> into the bell rope, and by the second verse every cat on the mossy steps is repeating that exact howl — <reading>うたう</reading> — like a chorus line nobody auditioned for.

wakai.meaning_mnemonic: A new gym teacher shows up at Sei's school looking barely older than the students, sprinting laps around the sports field twice as fast as anyone else and still bounding up the bleachers two at a time after the whistle blows. The staff room can't agree on whether to call him sir or classmate. Everything about him says young.
wakai.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway, Sei radios a teacher on an old <reading>walkie</reading>-talkie to ask why the new gym teacher looks like a student. The reply crackles back: he just is <reading>わかい</reading>, young.

wakaru.meaning_mnemonic: A shrine cat drags a ball of string down the mossy steps so badly knotted that nobody can find an end to it. The woodcutter sets the whole mess on his block, and the sword comes down: the knot falls open in two leaning <kanji>parts</kanji>, and every loop inside is suddenly plain. Split a thing and you <kanji>understand</kanji> it.
wakaru.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a kangaroo has jammed its head into the lone vending machine. A hiker sets down his pack, lifts a picnic wok, and <reading>whacks a roo</reading> once on the rump. The animal pops free with a hollow clang, which is the sound of <reading>わかる</reading>.
wakaru.description: The thing understood takes the subject particle, not the object particle — English speakers reach for the object one for months. It stretches to knowing a fact or recognising a person, and on its own it does the work of got it.

warau.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron dives for a fish, misses, and cartwheels straight into the mud. It stands back up wearing a lily pad like a hat, holding a look of total dignity, as if nothing happened. That straight-faced dignity in total defeat is what gets you — you cannot help it, you laugh, then grin the whole walk home.
warau.reading_mnemonic: On the mossy shrine steps, a street performer named <reading>Wara</reading> attempts to out-sing the enormous bell. It is so off-key that even the cats flee, and Grandma Kane doubles over, unable to stop laughing — <reading>わらう</reading>, over and over, until she's wiping her eyes.

warui.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a cat knocks a straw laundry basket clean off the washing rock, and it drifts downstream with the current, contents soaking through. Nobody wades in after it. Whatever comes back out of that basket later — waterlogged, torn, ruined beyond fixing — is the exact picture of bad.
warui.reading_mnemonic: The cat leans too far off the riverbank wall chasing the basket, wobbles, and topples in with a flailing <reading>“Wall, ooh-ee!”</reading> Its shriek on the way down lands close enough to <reading>わるい</reading> that everyone on the bank agrees: that fall looked bad.

wasureru.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the cats buries the spare bell clapper under the mossy steps, fully intending to dig it back up. It naps in the sun instead. Days later it noses around all the identical mossy steps with no idea which one, the whole plan having genuinely gone out of its head.
wasureru.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane crouches by the steps and asks the cat plainly: was you really the one who buried it? The cat just blinks, having forgotten the entire errand. That blank <reading>was you, reru</reading> stare, empty of any answer, is exactly <reading>わすれる</reading>.

watar.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a mossy stone bridge arches over the carp pond, and an old monk crosses it every morning on his daily <kanji>transit</kanji>, at the exact moment the bell tolls, timing his steps to the sound. One morning he pauses to feed the pond cats, forgets the bell, and has to hustle to cross before it stops ringing.
watar.reading_mnemonic: The monk crossing the bridge is nicknamed <reading>Walter</reading> by the tourists, and Grandma Kane calls out <reading>わたる</reading> every morning to hurry him across the mossy stones before the bell finishes tolling.

watashi.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>private</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>I / me</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
watashi.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hoarder snatches the last piece of sushi and snaps <reading>わたし</reading>, which sounds just like <reading>what a sushi</reading>, because only <vocabulary>me</vocabulary> gets to eat it.

watashitachi.meaning_mnemonic: Each <kanji>private</kanji> stash belongs to one person, but stand a whole row of them side by side and that row becomes <vocabulary>we</vocabulary>.
watashitachi.reading_mnemonic: You already know 私 reads わたし, so adding たち turns <vocabulary>we</vocabulary> into <reading>わたしたち</reading>.

watasu.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank the current is too fast to wade, so instead of crossing yourself you stretch out and hand the umbrella straight across to the woman waiting on the far bank, letting the umbrella make the <kanji>transit</kanji> you can't. She catches it one-handed, dry the whole time — you didn't cross the river, you handed it over.
watasu.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat drags a stray pot of stew up the mossy steps and dumps it at your feet. '<reading>What a stew</reading>,' you mutter — <reading>わたす</reading> — as Grandma Kane scolds you for feeding the shrine cats her prized dinner.

yakkyoku.meaning_mnemonic: Hikers stagger up the mountain trail certain the summit vending machine only sells sports drinks, but this one's shelves are stocked with bandages, cough drops, and bottles of <kanji>medicine</kanji> instead. A local hiker who restocks it twice a week finally admits she carries the whole supply up on her own back, running it like a one-woman <kanji>bureau</kanji> — the trail's unofficial pharmacy, open only when she feels like climbing.
yakkyoku.reading_mnemonic: Everyone on the trail calls her <reading>やっきょく</reading> — it started as an exhausted climber gasping <reading>'yuck, yo, cure'</reading> at the sight of her bandage stash, and it stuck so hard the vending machine now has it taped above the coin slot.

yakusoku.meaning_mnemonic: A yak on the mountain trail solemnly holds out one sock to you and refuses to let go until you swear to bring the other one back next week. That solemn oath — the yak's one sock held hostage until you keep your word — is a <kanji>promise</kanji>, an appointment you can't wriggle out of.
yakusoku.reading_mnemonic: Line up the readings you already have — 約 as やく, then 束 as そく — and you get <reading>やくそく</reading>.

yama-v.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, legs burning, you stop and count peaks the old way: three ridges, the middle one tallest. Except now it isn't ink on a page — it's rock under your boots, wind in your ears, and a vending machine glowing improbably at the summit. You've hiked straight into the shape that means <kanji>mountain</kanji>.
yama-v.reading_mnemonic: Near the mountain trail's summit, a hiker spots the one vending machine wedged onto a ledge that shouldn't hold anything and backs away breathing '<reading>yah-mah</reading>' at the sight. That startled breath is <reading>やま</reading>, the word for the whole slope under his boots.

yasai.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning Grandma Kane sets a fresh offering on the shrine steps, but this time it isn't rice or dried fish — it's a heap of raw produce, and the shrine cats sniff it once, turn their tails up, and stalk off toward the bell instead. Not even a temple cat will touch it. That offering nobody at the shrine wants is vegetables.
yasai.reading_mnemonic: <reading>やさい</reading> is just 野's reading や plus 菜's reading さい, chained together as written.

yasashii.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat drops a whole fish at her feet like it's nothing — no hunting story, no fuss, just here you go. She barely blinks. Everything about the exchange takes no effort at all, the easiest gift she's ever received.
yasashii.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane offers the cat a plate of sushi in return. It just shrugs, like accepting would say <reading>yeah, sushi</reading>, sure, whatever — refusing would take effort it doesn't have. That shrug is the sound of <reading>やさしい</reading>.

yasui-adj.meaning_mnemonic: The woman is still kneeling safe under her own roof, and today she's turned the whole house into a shop. Rent is nothing, worry is nothing, so she chalks every price down to nothing too, hanging a sign over the door: everything in here is <kanji>cheap</kanji>, because peace of mind never cost her a thing to begin with.
yasui-adj.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a whole shelf of dented onigiri packs gets marked down at closing time, and a regular grabs an armful, grinning <reading>yah, sue me</reading> at the register as the total comes to almost nothing. That grin is exactly <reading>やすい</reading>, the word for a price too good to pass up.

yasumu.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the top of the mountain trail expecting the vending machine, but the same <kanji>rest</kanji> person is still slumped against the tree, arms crossed, a note pinned to the bark reading back tomorrow. Everyone else keeps hiking past; this one has turned a five-minute breather into calling off the whole day. That is 休む: to rest, to take a day off.
yasumu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a washerwoman dunks a heavy futon and the current yanks it straight downstream. She lunges after it, swallows a mouthful of cold river, and comes up on her knees sputtering <reading>yes, um</reading> between coughs, which is exactly the sound of <reading>やすむ</reading>.

yattsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>eight</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>eight things</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
yattsu.reading_mnemonic: A toy <reading>yacht</reading> capsizes on the riverbank and spills <vocabulary>eight things</vocabulary> into the current. The kid wading after it yells <reading>やっつ</reading> as they float away.

yobu.meaning_mnemonic: Sei stands at one end of the empty sports field and cups his hands to shout across it. His voice ricochets down the echoing hallways behind him, bouncing off lockers, doubling back twice before anyone comes running — that's what it takes to call someone from clear across the school, to invite them over.
yobu.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone wades in too deep and calls out <reading>yo-boo</reading> for help, the sound skipping across the water until it lands as <reading>よぶ</reading> — close enough that everyone within earshot comes running to invite themselves into the rescue.

yoi.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a formal inspector in white gloves lifts each onigiri to the fluorescent light, cross-checking it against a clipboard before she'll stamp the wrapper. Nothing leaves the shelf without that stamp. This is the paperwork version of saying something is good — the one you'd write in a report, not say to a friend over the till.
yoi.reading_mnemonic: The inspector never just nods — she barks the verdict for the record, <reading>“Yo, E!”</reading> she calls, stamping the wrapper as she says it. That clipped, official shout is exactly how <reading>よい</reading> sounds: approval formal enough to file away.
yoi.description: よい is the full, uncontracted form of the same word — the one that shows up in formal speech, writing, and set phrases, while everyday conversation overwhelmingly shortens it to いい instead.

yokka.meaning_mnemonic: Pacing off all <kanji>four</kanji> walls of that doorless room already burns a whole <kanji>day</kanji>. Four walls at a day apiece add up to <vocabulary>four days</vocabulary>.

yoku.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail sits one lone vending machine, and the same hiker keeps reappearing at it, not once but again and again, always pausing to gulp his drink down slowly and thoroughly. He climbs often, and every time, he drinks well.
yoku.reading_mnemonic: よく is plain kana, read and written exactly as <reading>よく</reading>, nothing more to derive.

yomu.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini till goes quiet — the merchant has abandoned his onigiri shelf and is hunched over the register receipt instead, lips moving syllable by syllable down the tiny print. Wares untouched, eyes locked on the page, mouth shaping every line he isn't selling. That hunched, silent scanning is the whole picture of learning to <kanji>read</kanji>.
yomu.reading_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, a cow named Yoko wanders in from nowhere and parks herself on the pitcher's mound with a paperback. Nobody can get her to move until she finishes the page, mooing a flat <reading>yo, moo</reading> at anyone who interrupts, which is exactly <reading>よむ</reading>, and refusing to budge until the chapter ends.

yon-v.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>four</kanji> kanji is the <vocabulary>four</vocabulary> word — nothing added, nothing changed to get here.
yon-v.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a hiker counts his water bottles. His huge <reading>yawn</reading> comes out sounding just like <reading>よん</reading> — he's short exactly <vocabulary>four</vocabulary>.
yon-v.description: Native speakers use this reading rather than the kanji's other reading, because that other reading sounds identical to the word for death and is avoided when counting aloud, especially in hospitals and elevators.

yoru.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school gates lock shut the moment <vocabulary>night</vocabulary> falls, leaving the sports field dark and silent.
yoru.reading_mnemonic: A ghost at the riverbank moans 「<reading>よる</reading>」, which sounds just like calling <reading>your</reading> name, right as <vocabulary>night</vocabulary> falls.

yotei.meaning_mnemonic: On the whiteboard in Sei's school hallway, someone has drawn out every practice, exam, and holiday for the whole term in tidy boxes, weeks <kanji>beforehand</kanji>, nothing left to chance. Students stop and check it before doing anything else. That fixed grid of what's coming next is the plan, the schedule.
yotei.reading_mnemonic: The reading follows straight from the kanji: put 予 as よ in front of 定 as てい and the compound is <reading>よてい</reading>.

yottsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>four</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>four things</vocabulary> word share the same number, but the added つ turns a bare digit into four items you can point at and count.
yottsu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a collector proudly shows off four half-sunk <reading>yachts</reading>, insisting that's exactly why everyone says <reading>よっつ</reading> when they mean <vocabulary>four things</vocabulary>.

youji.meaning_mnemonic: You have exactly one afternoon and four separate errands — a form, a package, a shrine offering, a lost cat — and a goose at the riverbank follows you between every stop, honking each one as an official <kanji>matter</kanji>, as if supervising your business for the day. Four errands, one honking overseer: that's the whole word, errand, business, sorted.
youji.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 用 read よう, plus 事 read じ, gives <reading>ようじ</reading>.

youka.meaning_mnemonic: Flip the calendar past <kanji>eight</kanji> pages, each one a <kanji>day</kanji>, and you have flipped through <vocabulary>eight days</vocabulary>.

yowai.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi tries to twist the cap off a bottle of tea at the konbini counter and simply cannot do it. He braces the bottle against the register, grits his teeth, asks the customer behind him for help. She opens it without looking up from her phone, one twist, done. He was just weak.
yowai.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a character wading across the stepping stones gets his ankles knocked out from under him by the current and pitches sideways into the shallows, letting out a thin, defeated “<reading>yo-wa-ee</reading>” as he goes down — the sound that means someone's <reading>よわい</reading>.

yoyaku-suru.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a yak shoulders its way to the onigiri shelf <kanji>beforehand</kanji>, plants a hoof on the exact spot it wants, and refuses to budge even when customers stack up behind it. Claiming a spot ahead of everyone else, locking it in with a <kanji>promise</kanji> before anyone can take it, is exactly what to reserve means.
yoyaku-suru.reading_mnemonic: Add the readings in order — 予 as よ, 約 as やく, then する — and you already have <reading>よやくする</reading>.

yuki.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the path turns white — not sand, not ash, just cold pale flakes settling on your shoulders and melting the second they land. It piles on the vending machine's roof, on the railing, on your shoes, until the whole trail is buried under it. There's one word for that pale, cold covering: snow.
yuki.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail the vending machine jams, burying a hiker under white flakes from its coin slot. She digs through the cold pile shouting <reading>you, key</reading> — hunting her dropped key — and every shout comes out sounding exactly like <reading>ゆき</reading>.
yuki.description: ゆき is also an extremely common Japanese given name for girls, so outside of weather talk it will usually be someone's name rather than the word for snow.

yukkuri.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old turtle decides to wash a single sock, letting the current do the work while it dozes on a warm rock. The whole chore takes the entire afternoon, and nobody hurries it along, because that unbothered, whole-afternoon pace is exactly what slowly and leisurely means.
yukkuri.reading_mnemonic: 「<reading>ゆっくり</reading>」 is plain kana from front to back, so you read it exactly as written — no shortcuts, no detours, same unhurried pace as the word itself.

yume.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the vending machine at the summit isn't real — it never has cold drinks, it's always one more switchback past your last break, and it vanishes the moment you actually reach the top. Everyone who's hiked that trail knows the machine at the peak is only ever a dream.
yume.reading_mnemonic: At the base of the mountain trail, a sign reads '<reading>you may</reading> rest here, traveler' — but climb further and the exact same sign keeps reappearing, word for word, at every switchback. Hikers swear the trail itself is a <reading>ゆめ</reading>, a dream that only pretends to have an end.

yuubinkyoku.meaning_mnemonic: The cats at Grandma Kane's shrine have turned the mossy steps into a sorting <kanji>office</kanji>, handy enough now to count as pure <kanji>convenience</kanji>, stacking twigs, feathers, and dead beetles beside the enormous bell. Visitors expecting incense get a paw stamping their sandal instead, like a receipt. By evening prayers the pile is sorted, labeled with cat hair, and ready for pickup.
yuubinkyoku.reading_mnemonic: 郵（ゆう）＋便（びん）＋局（きょく）combine directly into <reading>ゆうびんきょく</reading>.

yuugata.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini dims its lights and marks the onigiri shelf half price exactly when <vocabulary>evening</vocabulary> falls, every single day.

yuumei.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports field, one student's <kanji>name</kanji> gets called over the loudspeaker so many times — first place, then an encore, then again for the yearbook photo — that it starts echoing down the hallways on its own, and strangers who never set foot on that field find themselves repeating it too. A name that outgrows the mouth that gave it is famous.
yuumei.reading_mnemonic: This word simply stacks the readings you already know: 有 as ゆう plus 名 as めい gives you 「<reading>ゆうめい</reading>」.

zasshi.meaning_mnemonic: The onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini gets restocked every hour, but the rack beside it never does — gossip pages, fishing weeklies, and a torn coupon insert all wedged into one groaning shelf the clerk just calls 'the magazine,' singular, because nobody has ever managed to tell where one issue ends and the next begins.
zasshi.reading_mnemonic: 雑 (ざっ) plus 誌 (し) combine directly to give <reading>ざっし</reading>.

zenbu.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the new monk doesn't leave one coin behind. He tips the entire offering box onto the mossy steps, sweeps every last piece from each <kanji>section</kanji> of the box into his sack, and pats the empty box twice to prove it: nothing remains inside. He took the <kanji>whole</kanji> thing, every part of it — that's the idea.
zenbu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just its kanji stacked together: 全 read ぜん, plus 部 read ぶ, gives <reading>ぜんぶ</reading>.

zenzen.meaning_mnemonic: You haul yourself up the mountain trail certain of one reward: the vending machine waiting at the top. You press every button. Nothing happens — it's empty, every slot glass-eyed and blank, and the silence answers you plainly: there was never anything up here to begin with, not at <kanji>all</kanji>.
zenzen.reading_mnemonic: A monk called <reading>Zen</reading> sits at Grandma Kane's shrine promising perfect stillness. Asked if he's ever startled, he says <reading>ぜんぜん</reading> — not at all — right as the enormous bell crashes down beside him, and he doesn't blink.

zero.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's team loses eleven to nothing, and the scoreboard just flashes the English word for it: <vocabulary>zero</vocabulary>.

shi-city.meaning_mnemonic: You come back to that town square: banners still snapping over the stalls, the vendor still slamming his pot shut so nobody smells the stew for free. Now there is a clerk too, desk wedged between two stalls, stamping permits and zoning the pavement. A <kanji>market</kanji> that grows this far hires staff, draws a boundary, and calls itself a <kanji>city</kanji>.
shi-city.reading_mnemonic: Nothing new to learn here: the word is the kanji standing on its own, so it simply takes the reading you already have for it, <reading>し</reading>.
shi-city.description: Read this way it is the administrative unit — the city that collects your bins and follows the place name on an address, not the general idea of a big built-up area. The character's other reading carries the market sense.

ooi.meaning_mnemonic: The hedgehog is still out on its balcony with the fork, and the plate of moons has become a leaning tower that wobbles each time it adds another. Nobody counts them now. You glance at the stack and it answers for itself — which is <kanji>many</kanji> made into the word you say about a pile: there is a lot of that.
ooi.reading_mnemonic: By the riverbank, someone tries to count the ducks crowding the shallows and gives up halfway through, throwing up their hands and groaning <reading>oh, oy</reading> at how many keep paddling into frame. That groan is exactly <reading>おおい</reading>, the word you reach for the moment counting stops being worth it.
ooi.description: Unlike English many, this word usually sits at the end describing the subject — you say the people are many rather than putting it in front of the noun. Placed directly before a noun it sounds off in most sentences.
